ALEX MURDAUGH MURDER SAGA LANDS RIGHT BACK WHERE IT STARTED BEFORE NEXT LOWCOUNTRY COURTROOM BATTLE

The filing described a July 7 Webex conference involving defense attorneys, prosecutors, SLED forensic scientists and Othram CEO Dr. David Mittelman following a June 29 hearing to discuss the proposed testing.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Alex Murdaugh, convicted of killing his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, in June 2021, sits during a hearing on a motion for a retrial, Tuesday, Jan. 16, 2024, at the Richland County Judicial Center in Columbia, S.C. (Tracy Glantz/The State via AP, Pool)

The defense further argued SLED had "articulated no scientific basis" for repeating testing already performed on the evidence. Attorneys wrote another round of STR testing could permanently reduce the amount of DNA available for independent analysis.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

"There is no scientific reason on the current record to consume additional reserve sample material to obtain a second STR result," the filing states. "Absent some articulated basis for believing repeat STR testing will produce new or different information, the only apparent effect of allowing SLED to proceed is to consume irreplaceable sample material before Othram ... has the opportunity to test it."

The defense also renewed its criticism of SLED's handling of forensic evidence, citing previous disputes over blood evidence recovered from one of Murdaugh's T-shirts as further justification for independent testing.

Paul, Alex, Maggie and Buster Murdaugh at a sporting event. Alex, was convicted of fatally shooting his wife and son. (Facebook)

ALEX MURDAUGH'S DOUBLE MURDER CONVICTION UNANIMOUSLY OVERTURNED BY SOUTH CAROLINA SUPREME COURT

The memorandum estimated Othram could complete its analysis within 60 to 90 days at Murdaugh's expense.

Last month, prosecutors urged a judge to reject Murdaugh's latest requests for independent DNA testing and expanded access to electronic case materials while he remains in prison awaiting retrial.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

In the June filings, prosecutors opposed two motions from Murdaugh's legal team: one seeking independent DNA testing tied to evidence recovered from beneath Maggie Murdaugh's fingernails and another requesting permission for Murdaugh to review case materials electronically while incarcerated.

The filings come as Murdaugh prepares for a second murder trial after the South Carolina Supreme Court overturned his convictions in May, finding former Colleton County court clerk Rebecca "Becky" Hill engaged in jury tampering that compromised his right to a fair trial.

Murdaugh was convicted in March 2023 of murdering his wife, Maggie, and son, Paul, at the family's Colleton County hunting estate in June 2021. The jury also found him guilty of two weapons charges.

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

articles.title: Taylor Sheridan's 'Lioness' season 3 is an action-packed saga loaded with violence and carnage
articles.excerpt:
"Landman" star Andy Garcia touted show creator Taylor Sheridan's distinctive talent for dialogue, character development and a unique worldview in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Season three of "...
articles.body_text:
"Landman" star Andy Garcia touted show creator Taylor Sheridan's distinctive talent for dialogue, character development and a unique worldview in an interview with Fox News Digital.

Season three of "Lioness" will shock fans by taking things to unprecedented levels.

TAYLOR SHERIDAN RETURNS TO MOVIES AFTER FIVE YEARS WITH NASA THRILLER, POLITICAL DRAMA

ZOE SALDAÑA SAYS TAYLOR SHERIDAN 'REALLY SEES WOMEN' AS LIONESS SEASON THREE HITS PARAMOUNT+

NEW LIONESS SEASON 3 TRAILER SIGNALS TAYLOR SHERIDAN IS TAKING THE PARAMOUNT+ SERIES TO NEW HEIGHTS

Zoe Saldaña as Joe in Lioness season 3, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. (Lauren "Lo" Smith/Paramount+)

It's no secret that I'm a big fan of Sheridan's work and I love the gritty and dark CIA/military series starring Zoe Saldaña, Nicole Kidman, Michael Kelly and a lot of other incredibly talented actors and actresses.

The lead up to season three of "Lioness" has been boosted by some outstanding trailers and previews promising a new mission for Joe and her hardened team.

Well, I had the opportunity to get an advanced look at several of the early episodes of season three, and I can confidently say the stage is set for season three to be the most explosive one yet.

Season one dealt with a terror target, season two focused heavily on the cartels and a high stakes mission in Iran and season three is taking viewers to a new enemy staring down America:

Nicole Kidman as Kaitlyn in episode 2 of season 3 of Lioness, streaming on Paramount+ in 2026. (Ryan Green/Paramount+)

I am going to keep this review spoiler free because season three is simply too great and too fast paced for me to want to ruin anything.

What I will say is that season three doesn't just keep the same energy as the previous two. It elevates it, and the season one premiere features an action sequence involving the CIA and Delta Force commandos that rivals the season two premiere, which I've said many times is the best action sequence in the history of TV.

It's honestly incredible how plugged in Sheridan is when it comes to the shadowy world of special operations. The tactics, movements, the way dogs are utilized and communication all feel very real. Even the gear the characters carry is about as real as it will ever get.

The action sequence in the season three premiere also reminded me a lot of the tunnel scene in "Sicario." Very similar vibe, but way more violent and action-packed. Did I mention the drones? Yeah, get ready for several terrifying moments that reflect how wars are now fought.

Season three also utilizes multiple timelines, and manages to do something that rarely happens with that technique:

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK CULTURE COVERAGE

It flows naturally and isn't at all confusing.

Also, Ian Bohen and Elizaveta Neretin are fresh additions to the cast in season three. Bohen plays a Delta Force operator, and Nereten.......well, let's not ruin anything for anybody.

Austin Hébert as Randy and James Jordan as Two Cups in Lioness, episode 2, season 3, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. (Ryan Green/Paramount+)

Overall, Sheridan has created another masterpiece of a season through the episodes I've seen. New villains, new faces and a new level of action and carnage. I can't recommend it enough, and I absolutely can't wait to see what happens the rest of the way. Send me your predictions at David.Hookstead@outkick.com.

David Hookstead is a reporter for OutKick.

articles.title: World Cup: FIFA studying impact of expanding to 64 teams for 2030 edition
articles.excerpt:
FIFA is studying whether to expand the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams for the 2030 edition in a move that could reshape football’s showpiece tournament when it celebrates its centennial.

World footbal...
articles.body_text:
FIFA is studying whether to expand the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams for the 2030 edition in a move that could reshape football’s showpiece tournament when it celebrates its centennial.

World football’s governing body wants to appoint an independent agency to assess the ambitious expansion plan, which would add another 16 nations to ⁠a tournament that had already grown from 32 to 48 teams in 2026.

“FIFA wishes to appoint an independent agency to determine whether and how expanding the FIFA World Cup from 48 to 64 participating national teams, starting with the 2030 edition, would impact on the tournament proposition,” it said in a research brief seen by the news agency Reuters.

South American confederation CONMEBOL had officially proposed hosting the 2030 World ‌Cup with 64 teams last year, allowing more countries the opportunity to join in the celebrations for the tournament’s centennial edition.

The 2026 edition in the US, Canada and Mexico was the first since 1998 to move away from the 32-team format, adding four more groups and an extra knockout round in the process, resulting in 104 matches over more than five weeks.

The accelerated study comes on the heels of FIFA’s plan to create a $20bn subsidiary to run the World Cup and its other events with external investors, a move that has attracted criticism and a ⁠UEFA decision to boycott FIFA events.

Al Jazeera has contacted FIFA for comment.

UEFA President ⁠Aleksander Ceferin said last year that expanding the World Cup to 64 teams was not a good idea.

The European governing body’s position has not changed since then, while Asian Football Confederation President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa had also voiced opposition, questioning last year where further expansion ⁠might end.

FIFA’s proposed analysis is meant to assess whether the proposed expansion can strengthen the tournament or whether concerns such as competition dilution, calendar congestion, operational complexity and market saturation ⁠outweigh the potential benefits.

The study will examine the potential impact of expanding ⁠the tournament to 64 teams, including the effects on the competition, competitive balance, qualification, player welfare and the international calendar.

It will also estimate the revenues that could be generated from ticket sales, sponsorship and media rights under the proposed format.

“The final recommendation should demonstrate not only whether a 64-team tournament ‌can generate incremental value, but whether that value is sustainable,” the document added.

FIFA said a decision on selecting the agency would be made on August 14 and they would have only four weeks to deliver their analysis by September 11.

The ‌2030 ‌World Cup is being jointly hosted by Morocco, Portugal and Spain, while Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay will host one match each to celebrate the tournament’s 100th anniversary.

FIFA is already facing a dispute with its confederations due to a plan to sell stakes in World Cups and other events to private investors.

articles.title: NSW should compensate elderly woman whose public housing was inundated with sewage, ombudsman finds
articles.excerpt:
Ombudsman finds Homes NSW acted unreasonably and recommended additional payment for distress and suffering

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An elderly public housing tenan...
articles.body_text:
Ombudsman finds Homes NSW acted unreasonably and recommended additional payment for distress and suffering

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

An elderly public housing tenant whose home was damaged by sewage overflows will be fully compensated by the New South Wales government after it disposed of her personal belongings without her consent and failed to properly support her insurance claim.

The NSW Ombudsman on Friday published its report after an investigation in which it found Homes NSW acted unreasonably in how it handled the tenant’s contaminated belongings and “failed to provide full and accurate information to the insurer”.

The woman, whose name and suburb were not made public, had lived in the unit for more than 15 years. She reported three successive sewage overflows within three months, which saw raw sewage enter the property.

After the third incident she was relocated, but her belongings remained in the contaminated unit for two months before being boxed up and moved to a vacant property.

The furniture, household items, and family heirlooms were not cleaned nor returned to her, despite Homes NSW telling her “she would be actively involved in the decision to keep or dispose of any items”.

She was later told “she would be adequately compensated” through an insurance claim, according to the report. When the claim was lodged, the insurer denied liability and offered a small “goodwill” payment.

The report found Homes NSW’s failure to provide the insurer with “full and accurate information” which contributed to the rejection of the claim.

The Ombudsman’s recommendations included an apology and full compensation “in accordance with her itemised compensation claim”. It also recommended an additional payment for “the distress and suffering she experienced while trying to resolve her claim over more than five years”.

Homes NSW has accepted all of the recommendations and will implement them by next month, according to the report.

The senior deputy ombudsman for complaints and investigations, Kate Anderson, said the findings and recommendations come after identifying “inadequate policies and procedures in place”.

“There were several points where there was inadequate communication to her about … what next steps were going to follow and then those steps were ultimately not followed,” she said.

Anderson said the case demonstrated the importance of ensuring agencies were able to “listen to their complainants”, particularly when they should “have engaged with this particular individual to reach a conclusion on this complaint far earlier”.

“This individual actually had very good record of the possessions that she had and the respective value of them, which ultimately was not taken into consideration,” she said.

“At all points, people should be treated with courtesy and respect and the situation that materialised here really demonstrated that ultimately by the time it had come to us, the tenant had been trying to resolve it herself with Home NSW for a number of years and hadn’t been able to get an effective resolution.”

A spokesperson for Homes NSW said it “sincerely apologises to the tenant affected” and acknowledged “the distress, inconvenience and impact the situation has had on them”.

Homes NSW has since introduced “a number of changes to how we deliver maintenance and repairs with the aim of improved tenant satisfaction, including establishing an in-house call centre to manage repair requests”, the spokesperson said.

articles.title: These boots are the safest for US wildland firefighters. Fewer and fewer can afford them
articles.excerpt:
The handcrafted leather boots are a century-old tradition – but with money tight, the cost of up to $800 is harder to justify

For 18 years, one of the most important relationships in Luke Mayfield’s ...
articles.body_text:
The handcrafted leather boots are a century-old tradition – but with money tight, the cost of up to $800 is harder to justify

For 18 years, one of the most important relationships in Luke Mayfield’s life was with his boots. As a hotshot – one of the US’s elite firefighting crews sent deep, on foot, into wildfires – Mayfield hiked a thousand miles a fire season in his boots, stood in them 16 hours a day and slept near them on assignments that lasted weeks in terrain no truck could reach.

Like every wildland firefighter, he learned the rituals of their upkeep: how to grease them, how to lace them, how soon before the season to break in a new pair so the blisters came during training instead of on duty.

“For all that, they really are the best boots for the job,” Mayfield says. “It’s crazy to me that that’s the case, considering it’s 2026.”

The boot in question is a very particular object, and it has barely changed in more than a century. Eight inches of full-grain leather, minimum, laced high to protect against cuts and hot ash. A sole rated to take heat that could melt an ordinary shoe. A tall, stacked heel that bites into a slope going up and holds the foot steady coming down.

While there are some newer parts, such as fire-resistant Technora threads that self-extinguish in seconds, the majority of the boot is still made the traditional way: by hand, at a small constellation of family workshops in the Pacific north-west. One of them, White’s Boots in Spokane, Washington, is credited with originating the design in 1939, as a variation of the logger boot they had been making since the early 1900s.

It’s part artisan history, part law; many of the boot’s heritage aspects were built into guidelines the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) released for certification.

Despite the rigorous standards of certification, the boots are not a guarantee. Stand too long in hot ash and the heat eventually conducts through the sole; crews call it hot foot. When he was a young firefighter, Mayfield recalls, the lugs on his boots melted clean off.

In the face of these conditions, the boots were made to be rebuilt rather than replaced. A good pair can last the better part of a decade – but that craftsmanship comes at a price. Fire boots of the highest caliber can cost $800 a pair, with less expensive models in the $300-$500 range.

Those sums would be trivial on the budget sheet of the federal government, but Washington DC is rarely the buyer. In fact, the US’s wildland firefighters are largely responsible for equipping themselves.

Part of that is due to a surprising, and consequential, bureaucratic classification. Until only recently, the US government did not formally consider wildland firefighters to be firefighters at all. On paper, they were forestry technicians.

That designation carried genuine weight. It helped keep the burden of equipping the workforce on the “forestry technicians” themselves; the word “fire” did not appear in their job title and neither, reliably, did the government’s duty to outfit them.

The costs that do get covered aren’t shared evenly, either. How a crew is funded and equipped can vary sharply from one to the next, as a function of which agency or region a firefighter happens to land in. Mayfield says he once ran a hotshot crew with six figures in discretionary spending, while a comparable crew a few hundred miles south, in a different region, made do with a small fraction of that.

All of these issues are contributing to a problem of retention. The US interior department acknowledged in 2025 that compensation “has not kept pace” with the work, with firefighters “finding it increasingly difficult to remain in these jobs”. Until recently, wages ran so low that in 2021 the government moved to ensure a floor of no less than $15 an hour.

Demand on these firefighters is only mounting. The US Forest Service no longer references a fire season; it now speaks of a “fire year”. “What used to be a three-month job can be eight months-plus of fighting fire, away from your family,” Mayfield says.

That churning workforce is still, all things considered, a market. The federal wildland firefighting force has stayed essentially flat for more than a decade; about 11,000 people work at the forest service, with several thousand more across the interior agencies. For the handful of companies that still make fire boots by hand, that is not, whatever the price tag might suggest, a particularly lucrative model.

No one understands that better than the people making the boots. Shuyler Mowe, CEO of Spokane-based Nicks Handmade Boots, founded in 1964, thinks his boots are, if anything, underpriced. “People are always like: ‘Wow, your boots are $600,’” he says. “These should be, like, $2,000!”

Mowe’s thoughts are less a complaint than an accounting. The Technora fire-resistant thread is notably difficult to work with; the leather used in the boot is considerably thicker than any consumer boot and, consequently, more difficult to shape; the boot is left on a mold, called a “last”, shaping the leather more effectively, for longer than is practical at scale.

“It’s a lot of these little things that add up to a completely different product,” Mowe says. Being overbuilt is the point – everything is thicker and heavier than it strictly needs to be, which helps a pair bounce back after multiple rebuilds and last for years. “You’re paying for the institutional knowledge.”

The birthplace of that knowledge is White’s, the company where Nicks’ founder learned the trade before striking out on his own in the 60s. (“The Coke to our Pepsi,” Mowe jokes.) White’s has been making boots since 1853, longer than the US Forest Service has existed.

Making the boots is a work of craft. It takes 2,000-3,000 pairs before someone is any good at hand-welting, says Eric Kinney, White’s president (and a bootmaker of 26 years). “Everyone thinks they can do it until they try it for a while.” In all but a handful of White’s Boots’ 168 years, the company has been run by a bootmaker.

White’s Smokejumper model is still considered the gold standard; it was first worn in 1939 by Francis Lufkin, one of the country’s first smokejumpers – elite firefighters who parachute in to remote wildfires – and bought for about a week’s pay. Nearly a century later, that’s the cost ratio White’s has maintained for their premier line.

“The price has stayed true to that course throughout its history,” says Kinney. “Seven hundred and seventy-five dollars is probably on the low end for a week’s pay, but that’s what we’re selling them for.”

That price has held even as the business model has shifted. White’s once stocked 6,000 pairs of its hand-welted Smokejumper; now, it sells closer to 1,500 a year. Demand has been redistributed across White’s other construction styles, which still move from 10,000 to 15,000 annually, according to Kinney – but the premium, handmade boot that once defined the company is being squeezed.

For many firefighters, the boots are getting harder to justify. A pair built to last a decade only pays off for someone fighting fire hard and long enough to wear it out – and a younger, increasingly transient workforce means fewer feet will be around to do so.

Mayfield himself made that same calculation; by the time he reached hotshot captain, he says, he had blown through two pairs of White’s in a single season, $600 apiece. Fed up, he moved to Nicks. When those also suffered damage years later, he was convinced to try out the boots that his newer crewmates were turning to: a hunting boot at half the price. His feet, he says, felt good immediately, without the need to break in stiff shoe leather. He hasn’t gone back – but he hasn’t gotten rid of his old boots, either.

“I have a fully rebuilt pair of Nicks sitting in my garage,” Mayfield says. “If I were cutting trees down and all that stuff, I would want people in a taller leather boot, because accidents happen. I fully recommend that.”

Mayfield is far from alone. There are now a number of companies making boots like his new pair: lighter hunting-style boots often manufactured in Italy, without a long break-in period. Many of those boots also sidestep NFPA certification, and may be less durable in the long term. That tradeoff matters less to a workforce that often turns over within a few seasons. To adapt, White’s is preparing to release an Italian-made boot of its own. “It’s a great-looking boot, just not our traditional stuff,” Kinney says.

For his part, Kinney is looking to steward the Pacific north-west boot tradition through his tenure. “I’ve probably got seven or eight years left at the company,” he says. “We’re doing everything we can to do it the same way on the high-end, hand-welted stuff. We’ll see what happens in 10 years.”

There has been genuine movement on the government side. In March 2025, after years of temporary patches, Congress made permanent the first major pay raise in decades, and the current administration has since moved to extend hazard pay to more of the work. But reform reached the pay and stopped at the boots.

A stipend meant to cover boots has sat at $500 since 2020. The most basic piece of equipment the job requires – the one thing between a person and hot ground – is still something firefighters buy themselves, made by a shrinking number of highly skilled hands.

articles.title: Monica Lewinsky has one request for critics nearly 30 years after White House scandal
articles.excerpt:
Activist Monica Lewinsky told Fox News Digital that her personal definition of power has evolved over the years.

Monica Lewinsky has evolved since the White House scandal – and she hopes critics one ...
articles.body_text:
Activist Monica Lewinsky told Fox News Digital that her personal definition of power has evolved over the years.

Monica Lewinsky has evolved since the White House scandal – and she hopes critics one day can, too.

Lewinsky, 53, credited time and patience as her saving graces while reflecting on challenges from her past during an appearance on the "All the Cool Girls" podcast.

"I think that coming into my 50s was amazing and just the shedding of worries," she told co-hosts Laura Brown and Kristina O'Neill.

MONICA LEWINSKY'S LINDSEY GRAHAM TRIBUTE DRAWS CRITICISM AND PRAISE FOR PLACING PEOPLE OVER PARTY: EXPERT

Monica Lewinsky reclaimed her own narrative years after a White House scandal. (Monica Schipper)

"I mean that whole … joke about 'I don't give anymore f---s,' and it's like you really start to give fewer and fewer f---s, and you settle into acceptance in a way that has been really reassuring for me."

Unlike the critics, the podcast host moved on from past discretions to reclaim not only her life, but also her own story.

"In terms of the people who still have old, old beliefs, I wish they would get some new jokes because, I mean, 30 years of the same jokes, Jesus," she said. "Or 28 years. We're not at 30 yet."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Monica Lewinsky pleaded for critics to find a new joke nearly 30 years after highly-publicized scandal. (Amy Sussman/Getty Images)

Lewinsky was 21 years old when she began an unpaid internship at the White House in July 1995. She turned 22 that summer, and her sexual relationship with former President Bill Clinton, who was 49 at the time, began in November 1995.

It was only after she confided in a Pentagon co-worker, Linda Tripp – who secretly recorded their conversations, which were then used in Paula Jones' sexual harassment lawsuit against Clinton – when the affair became public fodder.

During a January 1998 White House news conference, Clinton famously denied the affair, and stated, "I did not have sexual relations with that woman, Miss Lewinsky," and Lewinsky subsequently went into hiding due to public humiliation.

Bill Clinton was impeached while serving as the 42nd president. (House Judiciary Committee/Getty Images)

The subsequent impeachment trial against the 42nd president began in January 1999 and ended Feb. 12. While Clinton was impeached by the house, he was acquitted of perjury and obstruction of justice charges.

While the scandal made headlines for years, Lewinsky only truly began reclaiming her identity in the last decade.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"I feel really grateful. I'm really grateful, and I'm excited," she said. "It's when I step away and I look at my own story objectively – or as objectively as one can – it is pretty extraordinary to still be here, like physically still here, and to have been able to help shape how people see me more and understand me more and connect with me in ways that are meaningful. It's bonkers."

Monica Lewinsky previously recalled the toll of receiving negative energy from "billions of strangers" over the years. (Robin L. Marshall)

Themes surrounding authority and control have remained a constant in Lewinsky's life post scandal.

"I think of power in two different ways. There's the power that someone has and they use, that impacts other people's power," Lewinsky explained to Fox News Digital earlier this year.

"Then there's the power that someone has in connection to themselves and that's a lot more like strength."

She added, "People often think of resilience as being linear, and it is so much more like a spiral. You will move forward, you'll go back, and move forward ... you'll go back, and I think it's, again, people have to be patient with themselves."

Tracy Wright is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital. Send story tips to Tracy.Wright@fox.com.

articles.title: Iran strikes tankers under US escort in Hormuz strait as Trump gathers cabinet to discuss war
articles.excerpt:
Energy prices have soared again since fighting between US and Iran resumed two weeks ago as conflict spreads across Middle East

Iran has said it struck two tankers trying to pass through the strait o...
articles.body_text:
Energy prices have soared again since fighting between US and Iran resumed two weeks ago as conflict spreads across Middle East

Iran has said it struck two tankers trying to pass through the strait of Hormuz under the escort of the US military as Donald Trump gathered his cabinet to discuss the stalling war and rising prices as midterm elections in the US loom.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Friday that the “non-compliant oil tankers … were struck and brought to a halt, while four other oil tankers quickly changed course and returned to their previous positions”. The military body said the ships had tried to pass through the strait via an “undeclared route” and under US aerial escort.

Iran and the US have said ships should pass through the strait via two competing routes, with Iran bombing ships that take the southern route, close to the coast of Oman, and the US bombing ships that violate its blockade of Iranian ships and ports.

The strait has been almost completely closed to traffic since Iran and the US returned to fighting two weeks ago, sending energy prices soaring. On Thursday, the price of crude oil pushed past $90 a barrel when the US struck Iran in retaliation for its targeting of US bases in Jordan.

Fighting continued on Friday, with the Kuwaiti defence ministry reporting that it had shot down Iranian drones targeting “vital and military facilities” without any casualties.

In Lebanon, the Israeli military carried out a huge detonation overnight near the ancient Beaufort Castle. It said it was targeting Hezbollah tunnels and infrastructure. The explosion was heard across south Lebanon and covered nearby towns in ash, while photos showed the affected area levelled by the force of the blast.

Lebanese officials accused Israel of violating the ceasefire by carrying out the detonation. The Israeli military said it was ensuring the security of its northern residents.

Trump has tried to open the strait of Hormuz by force, but increasingly intense US strikes on Iran have yielded few results. The price of gas and groceries remain high in the US as a result of the energy disruption, complicating Republicans’ chances at the ballot box in November’s midterm elections.

On Friday, Trump brought his cabinet together at the Camp David retreat in Maryland to try to chart a path forward for the war. The White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, said at a briefing last week that the cabinet meeting would be “a lot of fun and something different for the cabinet to experience together”.

Top of the agenda will be the Iran war, which Trump promised would last a few weeks but has now dragged on for five months. A Reuters-Ipsos poll this week found that one in three Americans support the war, the lowest polling since the war began.

Support in Congress is also waning, with the US Senate narrowly rejecting a symbolic vote to express disapproval of the war. The war powers resolution asking the president to stop the war failed in a 49-50 vote. 
 Inflation caused by the war is a boon for Democrats, who are hoping to wrest control of the house from the Republicans.

Energy companies have posted record profits as a result of the conflict, with ExxonMobil’s profits doubling and Chevron reporting more than five times its profits in the same time period last year.

articles.title: Why the under on runs looks like the smart baseball play when Pirates visit the Reds tonight
articles.excerpt:
Pittsburgh Pirates pitcher Jared Jones was on his way to making MLB history on Wednesday night, but he found himself in the wrong chapter of the book. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)

Yeste...
articles.body_text:
Pittsburgh Pirates pitcher Jared Jones was on his way to making MLB history on Wednesday night, but he found himself in the wrong chapter of the book. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)

Yesterday did not go as expected. I lost one game between the Giants and Padres as Robbie Ray spun a gem in what could be his last start for the squad. Sometimes you run into that, and all you can do is tip your cap to the other team. I'll suck it up and move on, and hopefully get some of that money back here today as we play the Pirates vs. the Reds.

The Pittsburgh Pirates seem to be in a similar cycle this season. They have one step forward and then one back. I suppose the good news is that they aren't going one step forward and two steps backward. They are exactly at .500 coming into today's game, sitting at 55-55 for the year. The final 52 games of the season will tell the story of whether this year is successful or not. Maybe that's harsh, because this still should be a step-forward season, and one they can use for momentum moving forward.

Pittsburgh Pirates starting pitcher Paul Skenes (30) watches from the dugout in the sixth inning of the MLB National League game between the Cincinnati Reds and the Pittsburgh Pirates at Great American Ball Park in downtown Cincinnati on Thursday, Sept. 25, 2025. (Sam Greene/The Enquirer / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

I've written about the importance of Pittsburgh being aggressive in using this window for them to make a consistently good team. If they don't, guys like today's starter, Paul Skenes, will start looking for ways off the team. Skenes is 9-9 for the season with a 3.65 ERA and a 1.06 WHIP. This is the worst season of his young career, but all of his numbers are 31st in the Majors or better. He has been worse on the road than at home, but not terrible. This has been a tough month for Skenes; he has allowed 17 earned runs in 27.2 innings of work. He has faced the Reds twice this season and allowed five earned runs in 10 innings of work.

The Cincinnati Reds took a step back this season after making the postseason. They started the season hot out of the gate. This team was 20-11 after April came to an end. Since then, they have gone 30-46. To start May, they lost eight consecutive games and went 4-13 to start the month. To start the second half of the season, they've gone 8-5. Perhaps the All-Star Break is what the team needed to make some adjustments.

Cincinnati Reds starting pitcher Hunter Greene (21) pitches against the Chicago Cubs in the second inning at Great American Ball Park on May 23, 2025. (Katie Stratman/Imagn Images)

There is more than enough time to make a run at the postseason, but they'll need to get some better performances from their pitching staff. The Reds do have some good pitchers, so the adjustments can be made. Today's starter, Hunter Greene, is one of the better young arms in the league, but he has struggled since he came into their rotation in early July. He has allowed 17 earned runs in 21.2 innings this season. In fairness to him, he has two quality starts and two disasters. Pirates hitters are batting .200 against him over 55 at-bats.

We have two aces on the mound, guys who have, or could someday, win Cy Young awards. However, neither has been exactly impressive when it comes to consistency. Skenes has struggled all month. Greene has allowed 14 earned runs in two starts, and three earned runs in his other two. Which version of these pitchers is showing up?

Jake Fraley #27 and Elly De La Cruz #44 of the Cincinnati Reds celebrate after Fraley hit a home run in the second inning against the Atlanta Braves at Great American Ball Park on June 23, 2023 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Dylan Buell/Getty Images)

The Pirates haven't been playing great baseball lately, so it is really hard to back them, even with Skenes on the mound. The Reds have been terrible at home — 24-30. I think the smarter option here is to take the under eight runs. Both teams know the importance of this game, and both starters will know how crucial it is to give their team a chance. Neither team has great numbers against the opposing starter, so I'll back the under eight.

articles.title: Police chief resigns days after deadly shooting in US city of Seattle
articles.excerpt: Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes has resigned less than a week after a deadly shooting at one of the US city’s largest summer festivals as questions have mounted over the authorities’ handling of its ...
articles.body_text:
Seattle Police Chief Shon Barnes has resigned less than a week after a deadly shooting at one of the US city’s largest summer festivals as questions have mounted over the authorities’ handling of its aftermath.

Mayor Katie Wilson announced Barnes’s resignation on Thursday and named Deputy Chief Andre Sayles, a police officer with more than two decades of law enforcement experience, as interim chief.

The move came after three people were killed and four injured, including a two-year-old boy, in a shootout on Sunday at the annual Bite of Seattle food festival.

Dozens of police officers were already providing security at the event, and court documents said at least one officer saw a 15-year-old suspect firing into the crowd and quickly persuaded him to surrender. Police are still searching for at least one other suspect.

The shooting unfolded while Barnes was attending a law enforcement conference outside the city in the northwestern state of Washington.

While Wilson praised officers’ response at the scene, saying it likely saved lives, she said the city’s communication with the public in the hours that followed fell short.

Police posted about the shooting on social media shortly after it began but then went nearly five hours without providing another public update, leaving residents uncertain about whether there was an ongoing threat. The city also failed to send alerts through its emergency notification system while Wilson herself mistakenly announced that two suspects had been taken into custody before later retracting the statement.

“What I did not fully understand in that moment was how little information had reached the public or the press since the incident began,” Wilson said in a video statement on Thursday. “Had I known that, I would have pushed for an immediate briefing rather than waiting for a press conference to be organised.”

Barnes, in a statement released by the mayor’s office, described serving as Seattle’s police chief as “an honor” and said he hoped the transition would allow the department to refocus on “addressing youth gun violence and preventing more tragedies”.

The resignation followed hours of speculation over Barnes’s future with supporters saying he had resisted calls from Wilson to step down. Earlier in the day, Barnes told The Seattle Times that whether he remained chief was “up to the mayor”.

Several Black community organisations, including the Seattle NAACP and the Urban League of Metropolitan Seattle, urged Wilson not to make Barnes, the city’s second Black police chief, “a scapegoat for the complex challenges of public safety”.

They credited him with improving relations between police and the community, reducing gun violence and strengthening the department’s operations. Several City Council members also backed Barnes, pointing out that Seattle has now had four police chiefs in less than three years.

Barnes was appointed in late 2024 by former Mayor Bruce Harrell after leading the Madison Police Department in the northern state of Wisconsin. When Wilson, a democratic socialist who had previously supported defunding the police, took office this year, she kept Barnes in the role, signalling she did not plan to dramatically change the city’s public safety strategy.

Barnes’s resignation was announced as Seattle prepares for another major weekend event with the annual Seafair festival set to begin on Friday.

articles.title: Investigators believe Iranian hackers are likely behind cyberattack on Minnesota water systems: report
articles.excerpt: Retired Navy SEAL Mike Sarraille discusses the expanding U.S.-Iran conflict after a reported cyberattacks on Minnesota water systems and military strikes, stressing the crucial importance of securing ...
articles.body_text:
Retired Navy SEAL Mike Sarraille discusses the expanding U.S.-Iran conflict after a reported cyberattacks on Minnesota water systems and military strikes, stressing the crucial importance of securing global shipping lanes.

U.S. investigators believe a cyberattack that targeted dozens of water systems in Minnesota this week likely was orchestrated by Iranian hackers, a report said.

Minnesota IT Services (MNIT) said the "coordinated cyberattack targeted operational technology at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems" on Sunday and Monday, but the Minnesota Department of Health is "not aware of any active requests from Minnesota cities to have their residents modify their drinking water usage."

U.S. and state officials and others familiar with the incident told The New York Times that Iranian hackers were likely behind the cyberattack.

The newspaper reported that three state officials briefed on an investigation into the cyberattack said the tradecraft used and the absence of a ransom demand led analysts to initially determine Iran was involved. Officials also cautioned that the assessment could change as more data is collected by investigators, according to the newspaper.

"The FBI is aware of recent public reporting around Water and Wastewater sectors. The FBI and our interagency partners are fully engaged to protect critical infrastructure and we remain well-equipped to protect against cyber threats of all varieties," the FBI said in a statement to Fox News Digital on Friday.

IRAN-LINKED HACKERS TARGET US MEDICAL TECH COMPANY

A water tower is seen Thursday, July 30, 2026, in Plymouth, Minn. A cyberattack targeted operating technology at more than 30 water systems in Minnesota, including Plymouth's, earlier this week, state officials said. (Ellen Schmidt/AP)

The newspaper reported that the hackers targeted infrastructure used to manage and monitor water towers operated by municipal governments.

The mayor of the city of Braham, Nate George, said on Monday, a "plant operator found that the water tower was calling for water, but the well was not operating."

"After learning that similar problems were occurring in at least four other Minnesota communities, Braham staff determined that the plant’s computerized control system had been compromised," he continued.

"Public works isolated the affected system, restored a backup, and restarted the plant within approximately 90 minutes. While the plant was offline, residents continued receiving water from the city’s water tower. City administration temporarily requested that residents conserve water to prevent the tower’s limited supply from being exhausted," George added.

In a statement shared with Fox News Digital, MNIT noted that "the investigation remains active, and Minnesota has not attributed the activity to a specific actor."

MNIT said it "continues to collaborate with federal, state, local, Tribal, and private-sector partners to investigate the attack, support affected communities, and strengthen the security of Minnesota's critical infrastructure."

"Cyberattacks against critical infrastructure require a coordinated, whole-of-government response," John Israel, MNIT assistant commissioner and Minnesota chief information security officer, said in a statement. "MNIT is working side by side with our partners to share intelligence, support affected communities, and help utilities restore operations safely while strengthening defenses against future attacks."

LIVE UPDATES ON IRAN WAR: TRUMP ANNOUNCES HAMAS DISARMAMENT DEAL WHILE SAUDI ARABIA LAUNCHES RED SEA DEFENSE COALITION

A woman is seen holding an Iranian flag during a religious ceremony during Eid al-Adha on May 26, 2026, in Qom, Iran. Iran is believed to be behind recent cyberattacks in Minnesota, a report said. (Majid Saeedi/Getty Images)

Israel told the Times that the breach was first detected Sunday and that hackers targeted 36 municipal water systems.

"Minnesota was one of the early detectors of this, but we’re seeing that this same threat activity has likely been occurring in other states throughout the nation," he was quoted as saying.

Nick Andersen, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s (CISA) acting director, told the newspaper that the agency was aware of "multiple potential incidents affecting local water utilities."

In the days leading up to the incident, CISA issued an advisory warning U.S. organizations of "ongoing Iranian-affiliated cyber activity targeting internet-connected operational technology (OT) devices."

"Iranian cyber actors continue to target U.S. critical infrastructure, and the FBI is committed to identifying, disrupting, and imposing costs on those responsible," Assistant Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Division said in the advisory.

A water tower in Plymouth, Minn. (Ellen Schmidt/AP)

It stated that a "group of Iranian-affiliated actors" has "targeted devices spanning multiple U.S. critical infrastructure sectors, including Water and Wastewater Systems, Energy and Government Services and Facilities, to include local municipalities."

Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Trump defends $1.8bn slush fund that is holding up Todd Blanche confirmation
articles.excerpt:
President calls for former personal defense lawyer to be ‘immediately approved’ as attorney general

Donald Trump has defended controversial plans for a $1.8bn slush fund even as they threaten to dera...
articles.body_text:
President calls for former personal defense lawyer to be ‘immediately approved’ as attorney general

Donald Trump has defended controversial plans for a $1.8bn slush fund even as they threaten to derail the nomination of his former personal lawyer Todd Blanche for US attorney general.

Blanche “should be immediately approved” by the US Senate, the president declared in a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday morning, defending the payout scheme proposed by his officials in the Department of Justice as it holds up Blanche’s confirmation.

Blanche, who has been serving as acting attorney general since Trump fired Pam Bondi in April, has been lined up to take the job permanently.

Under agreements to resolve a long-shot $10bn lawsuit filed by Trump against the US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) over the leak of his tax returns, the justice department proposed the creation of a secretive fund – to be awarded with no restrictions to allies of the president – and barred the IRS from auditing his tax returns.

Democrats and some government watchdogs, however, are calling it a slush fund, and have warned it could end up paying out to defendants convicted over their role in the January 6 Capitol riot.

While Blanche later said the slush fund was dead after an extraordinary backlash, two Republicans on the Senate judiciary committee – John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina – have demanded assurances in writing that the fund will never be activated before they back his confirmation as attorney general. Blanche has not given them that assurance, and the committee’s vote to advance his nomination was postponed this week as a result.

“I felt that they should be given compensation for what has been done to them,” Trump wrote of his supporters, whom he described as “a group of people treated so badly in our Nation’s history”, adding: “I gave up any payments for myself, which would have been substantial … I will always feel that these victims of government abuse should be paid back for what they were forced to endure, their lives have been ruined!

“John Cornyn never had a problem with the so called ‘Fund’ … until after I decided to Endorse and Support his Republican Primary opponent,” Trump wrote. That opponent, the Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton, beat Cornyn by roughly 28 points in May, ending Cornyn’s Senate career and making him the first Texas Republican senator to lose a renomination bid.

Blanche was previously Trump’s personal defense lawyer, representing him in the New York hush-money case and other criminal matters, before joining the justice department as Bondi’s deputy.

Judiciary committee Democrats have said Blanche privately told the senator Dick Durbin that pushing for the fund had been a mistake. He has also faced questions over his firm’s past payments from a Trump-aligned political action committee and his handling of the Epstein files.

The Senate majority leader, John Thune, has said he expects the nomination to come back for a vote once Cornyn and Tillis are satisfied. Trump has said he is willing to pull Blanche’s name temporarily and resubmit it later, once Cornyn and Tillis are “out of office”, while keeping Blanche on as acting attorney general in the meantime.

articles.title: Chelsea fined $13.5m for FA breaches, avoid Premier League points deduction
articles.excerpt:
Chelsea have been ‌‌fined £10m ($13.41m) by the English Football Association (FA) after admitting to multiple ⁠⁠historical breaches ⁠⁠of regulations, the governing body has said.

The breaches were se...
articles.body_text:
Chelsea have been ‌‌fined £10m ($13.41m) by the English Football Association (FA) after admitting to multiple ⁠⁠historical breaches ⁠⁠of regulations, the governing body has said.

The breaches were self-reported by Chelsea following their takeover by US investor Todd ⁠⁠Boehly and private equity firm Clearlake Capital in May 2022.

The Premier League club avoided a points deduction after successfully appealing part of the original ⁠⁠punishment. However, Chelsea will face a suspended two-window registration ban through to June 30, 2027.

After reviewing the case, an independent Regulatory Commission initially imposed a suspended six-point deduction, but that sanction was later set aside on appeal.

“Chelsea ‌‌FC admitted to 74 breaches of FA Rule E1.2 prior to a hearing and an independent Regulatory Commission imposed a six-point deduction, which was to be suspended until 30 June 2027, and a £10m ($13.41m) fine,” Friday’s FA statement said.

“The club appealed against the suspended points deduction and an independent Appeal Board allowed the appeal ⁠⁠and set aside this sanction following a further hearing.”

Rule ⁠⁠breaches included of regulations relating to third-party investments and on working with intermediaries, among others.

The £10m ($13.41m) fine was not subject to appeal, with the FA adding that the full ⁠⁠amount will be directed towards grassroots football initiatives.

“In 2022, the club self-reported potential historical rule breaches to ⁠⁠all applicable regulators,” Chelsea said in a statement.

“Following ⁠⁠that report, it has worked openly and transparently with all regulators, including voluntarily and proactively disclosing many thousands of documents.”

The latest sanction follows other financial penalties imposed on Chelsea for ‌‌historical regulatory violations.

In March, the club was fined a record £10.75m ($14.4m) for breaches of Premier League regulations.

Chelsea were also handed a one-year first-team ‌‌transfer ‌‌ban, suspended for two years, along with an immediate nine-month ban on academy player transfers.

The West London club have lifted the English top flight trophy on six occasions, but not since 2017, and have won the UEFA Champions League twice, in 2012 and 2021.

articles.title: Ryan Gosling's family-first philosophy reshaped his Hollywood career: experts
articles.excerpt: Ryan Gosling and Sandra Hüller on epic adventure, science included, theme of being brave with challenging projects and how Goslings space wardrobe is a "love letter" to the late Val Kilmer in "Real Ge...
articles.body_text:
Ryan Gosling and Sandra Hüller on epic adventure, science included, theme of being brave with challenging projects and how Goslings space wardrobe is a "love letter" to the late Val Kilmer in "Real Genius"

Ryan Gosling is officially joining the Marvel Cinematic Universe as Ghost Rider, marking the latest chapter in a career evolution that the actor has linked directly to fatherhood.

Earlier this month, Gosling, 45, made a surprise appearance during Marvel Studios' panel at San Diego Comic-Con where it was announced that he will be starring as the titular motorcycle-riding supernatural hero in a standalone "Ghost Rider" movie slated for release in 2028.

Gosling's casting comes as the three-time Oscar nominee continues to embrace blockbuster franchises after spending years building his reputation in some of Hollywood's darkest, most critically acclaimed dramas.

MARVEL STAR VINCENT D’ONOFRIO SAYS HE ‘CAN’T DO’ KINGPIN TRANSFORMATION ANYMORE

Ryan Gosling's family-first philosophy sparked his career evolution, according to experts. (Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images)

The actor has previously shared that his pivot toward lighter, more mainstream projects was intentional, explaining that his priorities changed after becoming a parent. Gosling shares daughters Esmeralda, 11, and Amada, 10, with his longtime partner, Eva Mendes, 52.

During a 2024 interview with The Wall Street Journal, Gosling said he avoids psychologically heavy roles because he wants to be emotionally present for Mendes and their daughters.

"I don’t really take roles that are going to put me in some kind of dark place," Gosling said. "This moment is what I feel like trying to read the room at home and feel like what is going to be best for all of us. The decisions I make, I make them with Eva, and we make them with our family in mind first."

‘DUCK DYNASTY’ STAR SADIE ROBERTSON HUFF ADMITS ‘FEARS’ OVER PUTTING HER KIDS ON REALITY TV

While speaking with Fox News Digital, PR expert Sarah Schmidt shared her view that Gosling's family-first approach has reshaped not only the types of roles he is taking, but the purpose behind them.

"He began picking lighter roles to keep his mood stable for his family and also create art that they can be a part of," the president of Interdependence PR said.

Gosling spent years building his reputation in critically acclaimed dramas before becoming a blockbuster leading man. (Lloyd Bishop/NBC via Getty Images)

Paul Dergarabedian, head of Marketplace Trends for Rentrak, said Gosling's evolving priorities reflect a broader pattern among actors whose careers change alongside their personal lives.

"It does feel as though he is gravitating toward movies that his kids could actually see and enjoy," Dergarabedian said. "That kind of evolution is not unique as we have seen it with other actors as they get older, start families, and begin making choices that reflect where they are in life, how they see the world, and how they want to be perceived both personally and professionally."

Gosling's shift toward family-friendly entertainment signals a full-circle career moment for the actor, who made his debut as a child performer on the Disney Channel's "The All-New Mickey Mouse Club." He later appeared in the children's TV shows "Are You Afraid of the Dark?" and "Goosebumps."

During a 2011 interview with The New York Times, Gosling recalled that he decided to pursue "serious acting" at age 19. After making his mainstream breakthrough in the hit 2004 romantic drama "The Notebook," the Canada native went on to establish himself as one of Hollywood's most respected dramatic actors with critically acclaimed films, including "Half Nelson," "Blue Valentine," "Drive," "The Place Beyond the Pines," "Blade Runner 2049" and "First Man."

Gosling shares daughters Esmeralda and Amada with his longtime partner, Eva Mendes, who he met on the set of "The Place Beyond the Pines." (Sonia Recchia/Getty Images)

In recent years, Gosling has charted a different course with starring roles in audience-friendly movies including "Barbie," "The Fall Guy," and "Project Hail Mary," and his upcoming turns in "Star Wars: Starfighter" and "Ghost Rider."

Ryan McCormick, co-founder of Goldman McCormick PR, said he believes Gosling has earned the creative freedom to balance blockbuster franchises with prestige films.

"Ryan has not only built a career of acclaimed roles, those films are often box office successes," McCormick told Fox News Digital. "He has attained a rare status where he can do a sandbox film like 'Ghost Rider' and also take a dramatic or independent role without any one performance limiting his future choices."

Dergarabedian noted that Gosling's career has long defied easy categorization, citing his performances in 2011's "Crazy, Stupid, Love" and 2016's "La La Land."

"Gosling has always been far more versatile than any single role would suggest," Dergarabedian said. "He has shown he can do comedy, as he did so memorably in ‘Crazy, Stupid, Love.'"

"Of course, he proved he could carry a musical with ‘La La Land,'" he added.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Gosling said that "La La Land" was the first project he chose because of his children. (Dale Robinette/Lionsgate)

Dergarabedian pointed to Gosling's starring role in Nicolas Winding Refn's "Drive" as a pivotal moment that expanded audiences' perception of him beyond romantic leads and demonstrated his ability to tackle darker, action-oriented material.

"You really cannot put Gosling in a box. He has been able to move between genres and tones with a level of ease that very few actors can match," Dergarabedian said. "All that being said, you can definitely see a shift in tone at this stage of his career."

Gosling previously shared that "La La Land" was the first project he chose that reflected his changing priorities after becoming a father. While speaking with The Wall Street Journal, Gosling recalled thinking of how Esmeralda and Amada would enjoy watching him prepare for the role.

"It was just sort of like, ‘Oh, this will be fun for them, too, because even though they’re not coming to set, we’re practicing piano every day, or we’re dancing, or we’re singing,'" Gosling said.

The philosophy carried over to 2023's "Barbie," which Gosling said resonated with his daughters, who were already immersed in the world of Barbie dolls before he signed on to play Ken.

"Their interest in Barbie and their disinterest in Ken was an inspiration," Gosling said. "I thought they were already making little movies about their Barbies on the iPad when it happened, so the fact that I was going off to work to make one too, we just felt like we were aligned."

The actor said his daughters inspired him to star in "Barbie." (Courtesy Warner Bros. Pictures)

Though some fans initially criticized Gosling's casting as Ken, arguing he was too old to portray Barbie's iconic counterpart, the actor ultimately won over audiences with a performance that became one of the film's biggest highlights. "Barbie" went on to gross more than $1.4 billion worldwide and Gosling earned an Oscar nomination for best supporting actor, cementing the film as both a commercial and critical triumph.

Schmidt told Fox News Digital that she believes the film fundamentally changed the trajectory of Gosling's career.

"Gosling proved that just because he began his career as a critically acclaimed darling does not mean that he cannot also be an international franchise and blockbuster star," she said.

"'Barbie' paved the way," Schmidt continued. "Prior to that, Gosling was a serious actor who occasionally moonlighted in a rom-com. As it turns out, Ken can carry a billion-dollar movie. He was funny and self-aware, and it did not cost him any of his hard-earned credibility."

Gosling has continued to embrace projects that his daughters can share with him. While promoting "Project Hail Mary," he revealed that Esmeralda and Amada occasionally voiced his alien co-star Rocky during rehearsals and became some of the sci-fi adventure movie's earliest viewers.

Gosling said his daughters helped him by sometimes voicing Rocky when he was filming "Project Hail Mary." (Jonathan Olley © 2026 Amazon Content Services LLC. All Rights Reserved.)

"Sometimes when I was working, and I needed to sort of switch things up or whatever, my kids would come in, and I had an earpiece in my ear, and they would talk for Rocky, so I could talk to them as Rocky," Gosling told People in March.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"And there's some moments in the movie where I'm laughing or I'm just so charmed by him, which is like, it's actually my kids talking to me and helping me out," Gosling continued.

"They've seen many cuts of this film," he added of his daughters. "They've given me many notes."

Marvel's "Ghost Rider" marks the latest chapter in the blockbuster era that Gosling has spent years building. Gosling's role as Johnny Blaze/Ghost Rider in the superhero movie will also reunite him with director Shawn Levy after the two previously collaborated on "Star Wars: Starfighter," which hits theaters in May 2027.

"Wow, is this really happening?" Gosling told the crowd at Comic-Con after being unveiled as Ghost Rider by Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige.

"As you know, this is a character I’ve wanted to play for a very long time," he said.

Gosling is starring in Marvel's "Ghost Rider," which will be released in 2028. (Jesse Grant/Getty Images for Disney)

Schmidt told Fox News Digital that she believes Gosling has found a way to balance artistic credibility with commercial success without losing sight of the priorities that reshaped his career.

"He became a dad first, actor second," Schmidt said. "He is building a filmography legacy that his kids can be part of and proud of."

Meanwhile, Dergarabedian said he believes Gosling's recent choices have also cemented his place among Hollywood's biggest stars.

"He has become a go-to actor for huge, audience-friendly studio films and major franchises because he occupies such a unique position within the public eye," Dergarabedian said. "He has credibility, he has charm, he has range, and he has that elusive movie-star quality that is increasingly rare today."

Ashley Hume is an entertainment journalist for Fox News Digital and Fox Business who covers breaking news, celebrity culture, major industry events and the business of entertainment.

articles.title: Approval for China’s mega embassy in London was lawful, UK court rules
articles.excerpt:
A British court has ruled that the planned construction of a new Chinese “mega” embassy in central London can go forward, and dismissed a lawsuit pleading the contrary.

The ruling by the High Court o...
articles.body_text:
A British court has ruled that the planned construction of a new Chinese “mega” embassy in central London can go forward, and dismissed a lawsuit pleading the contrary.

The ruling by the High Court on Friday rejected the legal challenge brought earlier this month by The Royal Mint Court Residents’ Association, which alleges that the embassy’s development poses human rights risks to residents, including Chinese critics and dissidents.

Two judges ruled remotely that the residents’ “claims are … dismissed”, saying the housing minister and the London district of Tower Hamlets had acted lawfully by granting planning permission in January.

China’s plans to build the embassy on the site of the two-century-old Royal Mint Court, located near the Tower of London, were approved shortly before ex-Prime Minister Keir Starmer visited China.

The residential association, which represents families and businesses in about 100 properties close to the proposed site, said the presence of the embassy could result in “terror” attacks, repression of protests, and claimed that the facility could be used to spy on and enforce “draconian” Chinese laws on UK territory.

The association further raised concerns about the risk of a fire, pointing out that the UK government would not be able to enforce British safety obligations because of diplomatic immunity.

“Beijing thinks this judgement is the final word. It isn’t. The appeal is already in the works,” Luke Pollard, head of the residents’ association, said in a statement.

“If they expect us to roll over and allow our own capital to become a CCP power centre, they have completely misjudged the strength of opposition to this mega embassy.”

Beijing bought the site of the historic former Royal Mint, next to the Tower of London, in 2018 for a reported $327m.

The 20,000-square-metre (215,000-square-foot) site is set to become the largest embassy complex in the United Kingdom by area.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, as well as the London Borough of Tower Hamlets, defended their position, saying they had “conscientiously and carefully had regard” to residents’ concerns in their planning.

President grapples with finding a resolution to Middle East conflict that has pushed up gasoline prices ahead of vital midterm elections

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

President Donald Trump will convene a cabinet meeting later today at his ⁠Camp David retreat as he grapples with how to resolve his war against Iran.

He will also be keen to find a way to bring down gasoline prices as the Republicans head into ⁠the November ​midterm elections.

This will be only his third trip ⁠to Camp David during his second term, with Trump largely having stayed away from the mountaintop presidential retreat in western ⁠Maryland.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt ​told reporters at a briefing last ‌week that this would ‌be the 13th Cabinet meeting of Trump’s second term and that it ‌would be “a lot of fun and something different for the cabinet to experience together.”

The agenda for the meeting will likely focus heavily on foreign policy, Reuters reported. Trump is engaged in tit-for-tat strikes against Iranian targets with no end in sight to a conflict that the president initially projected would ‌last just a few weeks but is now five months old.

The Iran war has sent gasoline prices spiraling and taken a ​toll on his popularity across the US. This week, a Reuters-Ipsos poll found just one in three Americans support the war, the lowest in the poll since the conflict’s early days.

In another foreign policy development, Trump on Thursday night announced that his so-called “Board of Peace” reached an agreement for the complete ⁠disarmament of Hamas ​militants and other armed groups in Gaza. Israel has yet to respond officially to the plan.

President Donald Trump has said he may pull Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney-general until senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis leave office. The Republicans have demanded written assurances about the settlement of the president’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service. Cornyn recently lost the GOP primary in Texas and Tillis is not seeking reelection.

The US Senate narrowly rejected a largely symbolic effort to check Donald Trump’s war in Iran, as a war powers resolution directing the president to end hostilities failed in a 49-50 vote.

The House Democratic Women’s Caucus called on Thursday for an ethics committee investigation of Republican congressman Max Miller, a former Trump aide who has been accused of domestic abuse by his ex-wife and former girlfriend.

New polling commissioned by Fox News shows Texas Democrat James Talarico narrowly ahead of the state’s Trump-backed Republican attorney general, Ken Paxton, in their contest for a seat in the US Senate.

In this week’s episode of Politics Weekly America, host Jonathan Freedland delves into leftwing Democrats’ political moment in the sun – Zohran Mamdani’s rise in New York City, Abdul El-Sayed’s progressive campaign in Michigan and the buzz of whether New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez will run for president in 2028.

Freedland sits down with Bhaskar Sunkara, the president of the Nation magazine and founding editor of Jacobin, to talk about whether Democratic socialism is shifting from the political fringe to the mainstream and how swing voters will respond.

You can watch or listen on the Guardian’s website or find it wherever you get your podcasts.

A new survey of voters in 18 congressional toss-up districts by the Working Families Party showed voters, and especially independents, want candidates who challenge the political system.

The survey found 80% of voters agreed that elected officials care more about wealthy donors and powerful interests than people like them. When given a choice between a generic candidate who is an experienced elected official who focuses on “practical reforms” who gets funding from established groups and party donors, or a “political outsider who says the system is broken” who calls for changes to the status quo, the outsider wins by 14 points in the poll, including among independents and moderates.

“The survey does not show that every progressive policy or organizational cue is equally effective,” a polling memo from the Working Families Party says. “Instead, it points to a broader candidate posture: challenge concentrated power, demonstrate independence from party leadership, and connect change to material improvements in people’s lives.”

The Working Families Party, a progressive minor political party that’s growing in recent years, concludes that advocating for changing the political system instead of a conventional move toward the political center in a competitive district is a more winnable strategy.

“The strongest candidate in this environment is therefore not simply the most progressive or the most moderate,” the memo says. “It is the candidate who can credibly demonstrate that they are independent of entrenched power, willing to challenge their own party, and focused on delivering meaningful improvements for working people.”
