articles.title: The Jacksonville Jaguars opened training camp with an amazing message about God on their social media
articles.excerpt: Riley and Steve dive into why the COVID era changed athletes, how media outlets treat Christian and conservative viewpoints, why softball has become such a powerful example of public faith, and why sp...
articles.body_text:
Riley and Steve dive into why the COVID era changed athletes, how media outlets treat Christian and conservative viewpoints, why softball has become such a powerful example of public faith, and why sports gambling may be one of the biggest threats to the integrity of athletics today. Steve also discusses his book Godball, the rise of outspoken Christian athletes, and why sports may be one of the last true meritocracies in American culture. Subscribe for more conversations on truth, faith, sports, women’s rights, and culture.

In a sports landscape that has included some biological males not only competing against, but sharing locker room space with biological females, leagues littering their fields or courts with stenciled woke signage, and teams celebrating Pride nights, wearing Pride warmup jerseys and even Pride-themed uniforms, we present the Jacksonville Jaguars this week.

The Jaguars, in case you are unfamiliar, are an NFL team in one of the league's smaller markets. They're also the defending AFC South champions.

And they're also the organization that put this on X this week:

That's quite a banger to start training camp.

SAN FRANCISCO GIANTS FANS PROTEST AND SHAME CHRISTIAN PITCHERS FOR BIBLE VERSES ON PRIDE NIGHT CAPS

A Jacksonville Jaguars helmet is seen during an offseason workout on May 30, 2023, at TIAA Bank field in Jacksonville, Florida. (James Gilbert/Getty Images)

The post was seen 1.9 million times as of Thursday evening after being posted at 10:18 a.m. on Wednesday.

The Jaguars boast around 857,000 followers on X, which is modest by NFL team standards. Their estimated average posts are viewed by anywhere from 20,000 to maybe 35,000 people.

Patrick Mahomes of the Kansas City Chiefs is tackled by Josh Allen of the Jacksonville Jaguars in the fourth quarter at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Mo (Jason Hanna/Getty Images)

BALTIMORE ORIOLES TAP DRAG QUEEN AS GUEST SPLASHER IN KID-FRIENDLY BIRD BATH ZONE FOR PRIDE NIGHT

But this simple message of faith went absolutely viral for the team.

It also became a curiosity because it's obviously atypical.

It's atypical because, first of all, it was posted by one of the several players who were given access to the team's account as a social media admin gimmick. And it worked.

Jacksonville Jaguars head coach Liam Coen before an AFC Wild Card Round game against the Buffalo Bills at EverBank Stadium on Jan. 11, 2026. (Melina Myers/Imagn Images)

"Rare Jags W, coming from a Texans fan," one fan replied.

A Colts fan agreed – the Jaguars, Colts and Texans are in the same division.

"We're winning the Super Bowl," another offered.

Some fans added the "Jesus is Lord". Some fans asked if the post was referencing God or other gods.

But, as with everything on social media, there were those who did not forget the team's June 1 post on X. That one celebrated the start of Pride month.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Yes, the Jaguars were among the majority of NFL teams that proudly proclaimed their support for the LGBTQ movement on June 1.

That post, by the way, got 301,000 views — or about one-third as many as the one declaring God's goodness.

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

articles.title: Peru's ex-president has 15-year jail sentence for corruption charges overturned
articles.excerpt:
Peru's constitutional court has overturned a 15-year jail sentence handed to the country's former president after he was found guilty of corruption.

Ollanta Humala, who led the country from 2011 to 2...
articles.body_text:
Peru's constitutional court has overturned a 15-year jail sentence handed to the country's former president after he was found guilty of corruption.

Ollanta Humala, who led the country from 2011 to 2016, was convicted in 2025 of accepting illegal funds from the Venezuelan president and Brazilian construction company Odebrecht to fund his election campaigns in 2006 and 2011.

The former president had said he would appeal against the verdict, and now Peru's constitutional court has declared the entire criminal proceedings against him null and void.

Humala is expected to be released from Barbadillo Prison in the capital Lima, according to local media.

After the ruling, Humala's lawyer Julio Espinoza Goyena wrote on social media that the court had decided the contributions his client received on electoral campaigns "do not constitute money laundering".

He said: "The Criminal Chamber currently handling the case must order the definitive dismissal of the proceedings and the FREEDOM of former President Ollanta Humala".

When Humala was convicted, his wife Nadine Heredia was also found guilty of money laundering and sentenced to 15 years in prison.

However, she was granted safe passage to Brazil after seeking asylum in the Brazilian embassy.

Humala was the first of four Peruvian presidents to be investigated in connection with the Odebrecht scandal.

Alejandro Toledo, who governed from 2001 to 2006, was sentenced last year to more than 20 years in prison for taking $35m (£26m) in bribes from the company.

Alan García, president from 1985 to 1990 and 2006 to 2011, killed himself in 2019 as he faced imminent arrest over allegations he was bribed by Odebrecht. He had denied the accusations.

Pedro Pablo Kuczynski, in office from 2016 to 2018, faced impeachment proceedings after it emerged that Odebrecht had paid him millions of dollars in his previous government role.

The investigation is ongoing. Kuczynski has always maintained the payments were not illegal.

Humala's wife Nadine Heredia (right) had also been convicted of money laundering offences, but was granted safe passage to Brazil

At their own trial, Humala and his wife, with whom he cofounded the Nationalist Party, were accused of accepting $3m in illegal contributions from the firm, which they used to finance his 2011 presidential campaign.

They were also accused of taking $200,000 from Venezuelan leader Hugo Chávez to bankroll the 2006 campaign.

But the couple always maintained that they were the victims of political persecution.

Humala, a former army officer, came to national prominence in 2000 when he led a short-live military rebellion against then-president Alberto Fujimori.

In 2006, he ran for president on a platform inspired by the socialist revolution of Venezuela's Chávez.

After an unsuccessful first attempt, Humala ran again in 2011; this time on a more moderate platform emulating the policies of Brazil's then-president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to defeat right-wing rival Keiko Fujimori, the eldest daughter of Alberto Fujimori.

His legal troubles started shortly after his term finished in 2016, when Odebrecht admitted to bribing Latin American government officials and political parties with hundreds of millions of dollars to win business.

Prosecutors accused Humala and his wife of receiving millions from Odebrecht, as well as the illegal funding from Chávez to finance the 2006 presidential campaign.

Humala and Heredia were subsequently placed in pre-trial detention for a year, before they were eventually convicted in 2025.

Peru's ex-president and first lady sentenced to 15 years in prison

articles.title: At least 18 die as 49,000 people cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco
articles.excerpt:
Some drowned and others got caught up in crush, official says, as incident prompts criticism of Spain from France and Italy

At least 18 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta a...
articles.body_text:
Some drowned and others got caught up in crush, official says, as incident prompts criticism of Spain from France and Italy

At least 18 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after approximately 49,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco in a matter of hours, triggering a political crisis for the Madrid government and unleashing a barrage of criticism from other EU countries.

The large influx of people arriving in Ceuta by swimming across from neighbouring Morocco or scaling the high border fence has caught the city of 85,000 off guard and resulted in what one local police association has called a “serious humanitarian crisis”.

Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, who is due to visit Ceuta on Friday with the interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, is under huge pressure from political opponents and other European countries to come up with a swift and comprehensive response.

The latest incident dwarfs the last mass border crossing in May 2021, when 10,000 people entered the territory over the course of two days by taking advantage of a loosening of border controls by Morocco.

That crossing came amid heightened tensions between Madrid and Rabat over Spain’s decision to allow the leader of the Western Sahara independence movement, the Polisario Front, to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. Morocco and the Polisario Front both lay claim to Western Sahara, which was under Spanish rule until 1975, when colonial authorities handed over the territory to Morocco and Mauritania.

That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its longstanding policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara – a move that had caused a diplomatic rift between Madrid and Algiers, which had supported the Polisario group.

Sánchez visited Algiers on 20 July – the first such visit by a Spanish head of government in four years – marking a thaw in relations with Algeria.

Moroccan government sources told the Europa Press news agency that the surge of people entering Ceuta was down to “criminal organisations”, and insisted that Rabat’s cooperation with Spain remained “exemplary”.

On Thursday evening, Spain’s interior ministry announced that 60 members of the armed forces would be deployed to Ceuta, along with an additional 30 Guardia Civil officers. “The armed forces will reinforce the Guardia Civil in the exercise of its powers and any others that may be necessary to maintain security in the city of Ceuta,” the ministry said.

But the situation is evolving rapidly as the city struggles to cope with the massive number of arrivals.

Rachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers association representing Civil Guard officers, described the situation as a “serious humanitarian crisis”. He said: “People are still entering. The reinforcements that have arrived are only helping the injured and other humanitarian efforts.”

Without shelter, thousands of people including unaccompanied children had been left sleeping in parks and on pavements while others roamed the streets aimlessly, Sbihi said. “It’s chaotic,” he added.

Among the 18 who died, many drowned, but some were killed in a crush to cross the breakwater fence at Tarajal beach, Sbihi said.

Video footage on Thursday showed crowds of people walking around the breakwaters at Tarajal beach on to local roads. While most appeared to be young men, there were also families with women and small children.

“Viva España!” some shouted to a freelance photographer working for the Associated Press. It was not immediately clear what had prompted so many people to cross to Ceuta.

Ceuta, along with Melilla, ⁠another Spanish autonomous city in northern ​Morocco, has the E​U’s only land border with ​Africa. ‌Both cities ​periodically ​experience surges in attempted crossings by people seeking to reach Europe.

Juan Jesús Vivas, the mayor-president of Ceuta, demanded the deployment of additional police and troops “to guarantee the inviolability of the frontier” and citizens’ safety. He also called on the central government to declare a national emergency over the crossings.

But the government rejected calls for the declaration of a national emergency, saying such emergencies could not be declared over migration issues, and could be declared only in response to dire meteorological events – such as the current wildfires – or in the face of a volcanic or nuclear threat.

Events in Ceuta have led some other EU countries to issue threats or rebukes.

Spain’s foreign minister, José Manuel Albares, summoned Italy’s ambassador to Madrid on Friday after Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.

Meloni said Italy was prepared to take “extraordinary measures” to defend its borders, claiming that the “shocking” scenes from Ceuta demonstrated that “illegal immigration poses a real threat to the security of Europe’s borders”.

Meloni, whose government has been struggling to regain traction since a failed referendum on judicial reforms in March, appears to be exploiting the incident for political gain before general elections next year in which she faces competition from a new hard-right rival, Roberto Vannacci. She has made security her key political offering.

Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, blamed the situation in Ceuta on the Sánchez government’s decision to offer a now-closed scheme to regularise the status of more than 1 million undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. He said the programme had incentivised human trafficking and was “profoundly wrong”.

Tajani’s remarks prompted a sharp response from Albares, who said the comments were “unbecoming” and accused Italy of “partisan demagoguery”.

The French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said he had given instructions for the strengthening of controls at the Spanish border.

The former French prime minister Michel Barnier was more outspoken, saying France “cannot suffer the consequences of its neighbours’ migration choices”. He also appeared to criticise Spain’s regularisation scheme, saying: “If a member state makes decisions that create a pull factor for migration, we must be able to immediately protect our borders … Mastering immigration is a condition of sovereignty, security and trust between European states.”

In Spain, the opposition People’s party (PP) is calling on Sánchez to come up with a tough response, saying the small military and police reinforcements announced on Thursday night were insufficient.

In a post on X, the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feij, wrote: “People have continued to arrive in Ceuta throughout the night, and those on the ground describe an occupied city, with nothing sufficient being done to prevent it.”

The far-right Vox party, meanwhile, was calling the incident “an invasion”.

articles.title: Andy Burnham to set out devolution plan amid criticism it won’t benefit regions equally – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
Plan set to transform funding so English regions no longer rely on Whitehall handouts for projects

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of UK politics. From 2028 English regional mayors, for...
articles.body_text:
Plan set to transform funding so English regions no longer rely on Whitehall handouts for projects

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of UK politics. From 2028 English regional mayors, for the first time, will be handed a share of income tax receipts instead of central grants and be less beholden to the Treasury by being able to borrow (mainly from private investors) to invest in big projects.

Mayors will also be able to keep a share of business rates totalling tens of millions of pounds by April 2027, and gain greater control over services such as housing and transport, under plans that form part of the government’s devolution agenda.

As my colleague Josh Halliday notes in this story, these will replace existing grants rather than being additional money, but local leaders said no longer relying on ringfenced Treasury handouts would be transformative.

Traditionally, the Treasury in Whitehall has controlled the distribution of local funding, leading to patchy distribution of funds across the country and disempowered local leaders feeling money is not going where it is needed most.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is expected to visit a community centre in the north of England this morning and officially announce what has been described as “the biggest transfer of power from Westminster in a generation”. The government said it would be developing different proposals for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

The plans have been criticised by the Conservatives for being vague, with more details to be released in a white paper and the budget this autumn.

The Conservative shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, said that if faster growing areas get more funding it “could mean those who lose out are precisely those areas which have seen weaker local economies over recent years.”

Some mayors are thought to be considering using their powers to roll out tax reliefs, including the Conservative mayor of Tees Valley and Reform UK’s Greater Lincolnshire mayor, Dame Andrea Jenkyns.

Louise Haigh, who is overseeing No 10 North in her new role as chancellor of the duchy of Lancaster, was asked whether the scheme will enable rich areas to get richer while poorer areas get poorer. Speaking on Times Radio, she acknowledged that London, which already attracts major investment, will be able to retain more money under the government’s tax devolution plans.

double quotation markThere is already a way that the business rates retention is distributed to correspond with central funding formula to correct for that.

Because you wouldn’t want to have it that places like London and Manchester and Bristol were able to retain more of theirs while other areas that weren’t growing at the same rate, were falling behind.

So there will be a formula and funding position set out in the budget that that corrects this, but really, we are the most centralised nation in the G7, and that has held back our growth and our productivity outside London and the south-east for too long.

Asked whether London will be able to retain more money than it has done previously, She added:

double quotation markYes, that’s right, and it will have more powers devolved, 16-19 funding, employment support budgets and the ability to tailor their own vocational routes. This will be an important part of developing their own local regional growth strategy as well.

BP has put its North Sea oil and gas business up for sale as it looks to end six decades of production from the region.

The firm announced on Friday morning that it had launched a formal process to market its North Sea business for a potential sale. The move comes as BP’s new chief executive, Meg O’Neill, tries to simplify the company and cut its debt levels.

O’Neill said in a statement: “The North Sea remains integral to the UK’s energy system. However, as we focus our portfolio and direct capital to our highest-value opportunities, we believe our North Sea business will be better positioned as part of another company.”

She said the UK would “continue to play an important role” in BP’s future. “We’re proud of the jobs we create, the contribution we make to the UK economy, and the work we do to keep energy flowing every day,” she said.

BP’s involvement in the North Sea dates back to 1964, when it was granted its first UK North Sea licence. The company discovered the West Sole gasfield in the winter of 1965, followed by its largest discovery in the area, the giant Forties field, in 1970.

The sale announcement comes a day after Andy Burnham said he would take a “pragmatic” approach to oil and gas drilling in the North Sea, saying the government could not ignore the potential energy resources it held. You can read more here:

In other news, Labour’s former deputy leader Harriet Harman has suggested that men should be banned from running to become the next Labour leader.

“We’ve got to have a woman next time,” the Labour peer told the Electoral Dysfunction podcast.

“And I’ve worked out that the only way we’ll have a woman leader of the Labour party next time, is if we start a conversation now where we say that, actually, men cannot stand for the leadership next time,” Harman, who was Labour’s deputy leader under Gordon Brown, said.

The Conservatives have had three female prime ministers, but Labour has never had a permanent female leader. Margaret Beckett and Harman served only as acting leaders.

Harman added that the Labour party, which has had four female deputy leaders, needed to “start the discussion about male ambition and male allyship”, and that “male ambition should not be to lead themselves, male ambition ought to be to support a woman to lead”.

The domestic abuse commissioner for England and Wales, Dame Nicole Jacobs, has written an op-ed in the New Statesman, in which she says the “epidemic” of domestic abuse and violence against women and girls risks being ignored in the government’s devolution plans – but adds that there is an opportunity there to be taken to improve services across the country as part of a victim-centred system. Here is an extract from her piece:

double quotation markGovernments of all political stripes have made genuine efforts to tackle domestic abuse. Too often, I have seen those attempts fall short because responsibility and accountability is scattered across Whitehall.

It is one of the many reasons why progress on halving violence against women and girls has been slow – the machinery of government is simply not set up to tackle problems that cut across every part of the state.

Take funding for specialist domestic abuse services. Week in and week out, I hear from domestic abuse organisations that are having to reduce the support they offer, let staff go or close entirely. Why? Because money is trapped in short term, centralised budgets, struggling to find its way to those trying to deliver on the ground. This is why Burnham’s drive to devolve power offers opportunity.

By shifting our focus away from individual programmes and isolated funding streams, which local areas tell me inhibit their ability to deliver for victims, we can enable regional leaders to build a system which moves as one around victims. This would see specialist services funded to work in tandem with public services – be that health, housing or social care – to understand what survivors need and adapt their response to ensure they can rebuild and recover away from abuse.

MPs Diane Abbott and Joani Reid have been readmitted into Labour and had the parliamentary whip restored, just under two weeks into Andy Burnham’s premiership.

The party confirmed that this followed separate independent disciplinary processes, although Labour said the leadership played no role in either decision.

Abbott, 72, the mother of the House of Commons, was suspended for a second time last summer after saying she did not regret comments about racism that had led to her initial loss of the whip in 2023.

Reid, the MP for East Kilbride and Strathaven who was elected in 2024, voluntarily relinquished the whip in March this year. Her husband had been arrested on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service in a case linked to China. Reid has never been accused of wrongdoing.

The Guardian understands from Labour party sources that Reid has never been party to the police investigations into alleged Chinese spying.

You can read more on this story by the Guardian’s political correspondent, Aletha Adu, here:

There are 14 regional mayors in England, including the mayor of London, with many areas not represented by one. Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, the first secretary of state, Louise Haigh, defended the devolution plan against accusations that areas with weaker economies and without mayors could lose out on key funding.

double quotation markWe won’t be imposing mayors to areas that don’t want it but we will be creating strategic authorities in every area of England and they will be able to hold these powers and resources as well.

They don’t need to have mayors in order to control them or in order to retain a share of their income tax and business rates.

As we mentioned in the opening post, Ben Houchen, the Conservative Tees Valley mayor, has indicated he would use so-called “fiscal devolution” to lower the tax burden for his voters. According to a report in The Times, Houchen said he wanted to make his region “a more attractive place and a more competitive place to invest in than Manchester and London”.

The Tees Valley Combined Authority comprises five constituent local authorities: Darlington, Hartlepool, Middlesbrough, Redcar and Cleveland, and Stockton-on-Tees. The total population of the area covered is about 700,000.

“Every mayor is backing fiscal devolution because they want more money to spend in their area,” Houchen, England’s only Conservative mayor, said.

“However, if the Tees Valley is handed a slice of local income tax and business rates generated locally, I’ll create a new rebate scheme to put money back into people’s pockets and let families keep more of the money they earn.”

“Fiscal devolution must be about giving places like Teesside the power to do things differently, back growth and reward the people that drive our local economy instead of squeezing every last penny out of them.”

As a reminder, the government has not yet decided the exact portion of taxes mayors will get.

The first secretary of state, Louise Haigh, confirmed this morning that it is “not possible at the moment” for English mayors to give their local residents tax rebates under the devolution plans. Speaking to Times Radio, she said: “We’d have to see the details of that, but it certainly isn’t possible at the moment.”

double quotation markThose kind of schemes necessitate HMRC to set up full schemes, that’s just not possible at the moment. The way that the mayors are set up and work is to reinvest the money into their public services, into their local economies.

Under a new “local first” principle, Andy Burnham will instruct ministers to justify why powers should remain in Whitehall rather than be devolved.

As well as greater control over technical education for teenagers, announced by the government this week, some of those close to the prime minister have called for mayors to oversee schools, GPs and childcare providers through health and education commissioners – a similar role to that played by police and crime commissioners.

No 10 said Britain’s civil service of 520,000 would become “smaller and more strategic” as decision-making moves out of London, where one in five of these officials are based.

England’s directly elected mayors, who control areas spanning three-quarters of the population, would be able to use the revenue generated from business rates and income tax as they wish, including tax breaks for important industries or rebates to residents.

However, experts said one of the most significant consequences was that it would allow combined authorities to take out 30-year loans against their projected income to fund major projects that previously needed Treasury approval.

Mayors said they were currently prevented from funding huge initiatives on housing and transport because they could not take out private loans on the basis of one-year funding settlements from Whitehall. You can read more here:

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of UK politics. From 2028 English regional mayors, for the first time, will be handed a share of income tax receipts instead of central grants and be less beholden to the Treasury by being able to borrow (mainly from private investors) to invest in big projects.

Mayors will also be able to keep a share of business rates totalling tens of millions of pounds by April 2027, and gain greater control over services such as housing and transport, under plans that form part of the government’s devolution agenda.

As my colleague Josh Halliday notes in this story, these will replace existing grants rather than being additional money, but local leaders said no longer relying on ringfenced Treasury handouts would be transformative.

Traditionally, the Treasury in Whitehall has controlled the distribution of local funding, leading to patchy distribution of funds across the country and disempowered local leaders feeling money is not going where it is needed most.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, is expected to visit a community centre in the north of England this morning and officially announce what has been described as “the biggest transfer of power from Westminster in a generation”. The government said it would be developing different proposals for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

The plans have been criticised by the Conservatives for being vague, with more details to be released in a white paper and the budget this autumn.

The Conservative shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, said that if faster growing areas get more funding it “could mean those who lose out are precisely those areas which have seen weaker local economies over recent years.”

Some mayors are thought to be considering using their powers to roll out tax reliefs, including the Conservative mayor of Tees Valley and Reform UK’s Greater Lincolnshire mayor, Dame Andrea Jenkyns.

Louise Haigh, who is overseeing No 10 North in her new role as chancellor of the duchy of Lancaster, was asked whether the scheme will enable rich areas to get richer while poorer areas get poorer. Speaking on Times Radio, she acknowledged that London, which already attracts major investment, will be able to retain more money under the government’s tax devolution plans.

double quotation markThere is already a way that the business rates retention is distributed to correspond with central funding formula to correct for that.

Because you wouldn’t want to have it that places like London and Manchester and Bristol were able to retain more of theirs while other areas that weren’t growing at the same rate, were falling behind.

So there will be a formula and funding position set out in the budget that that corrects this, but really, we are the most centralised nation in the G7, and that has held back our growth and our productivity outside London and the south-east for too long.

Asked whether London will be able to retain more money than it has done previously, She added:

double quotation markYes, that’s right, and it will have more powers devolved, 16-19 funding, employment support budgets and the ability to tailor their own vocational routes. This will be an important part of developing their own local regional growth strategy as well.

articles.title: KFC founder's personal belongings fetch thousands at Kentucky auction
articles.excerpt: Colonel Harland Sanders' personal belongings, including his iconic black bow tie and a 1964 planner that sold for $30,000, were auctioned in Kentucky as his former home and the Claudia Sanders Dinner ...
articles.body_text:
Colonel Harland Sanders' personal belongings, including his iconic black bow tie and a 1964 planner that sold for $30,000, were auctioned in Kentucky as his former home and the Claudia Sanders Dinner House are also up for sale.

SHELBYVILLE, Ky. – More than 70 personal belongings once owned by KFC founder Colonel Harland Sanders sold at auction Tuesday in Shelbyville, Kentucky, drawing collectors from across the country and online bidders eager to own a piece of fast-food history.

The collection included items from Sanders' personal and professional life, from handwritten notes and recipe cards to his signature clip-on bow tie and the 1964 planner that sparked one of the night's biggest bidding wars.

"They had all of this in basements and closets and everything, and decided it was time to let the world, who loves the man, have an opportunity to buy the memorabilia," Bill Menish, owner and lead auctioneer with The Menish Group, told Fox News.

WHY KFC STOPPED CALLING ITSELF KENTUCKY FRIED CHICKEN — AND THE MYTHS THAT STILL WON'T DIE

Colonel Harland Sanders' 1964 executive planner was displayed before auction and ultimately sold for $30,000. (Olivianna Calmes)

Among the night's top-selling items was Sanders' 1964 planner, which sold for $30,000.

A 1955 Kentucky Colonel certificate fetched about $23,000, while his iconic black clip-on bow tie sold for $8,000.

Colonel Harland Sanders' signature clip-on bow tie was among the personal items auctioned in Shelbyville, Kentucky. (Olivianna Calmes)

One collector and former employee of the Colonel said the planner stood out as the most fascinating item in the auction.

"Probably that planner, I would imagine," the buyer said.

Menish said the planner generated additional buzz because of a handwritten note on the back.

"But then on the back, for some unknown reason, there's 11 herbs and spices," he said.

WHY KFC'S FRIED CHICKEN TASTES DIFFERENT FROM THAT OF EVERY OTHER FAST-FOOD CHAIN

Auctioneer Bill Menish discusses several of Colonel Sanders' personal belongings, including memorabilia and kitchen items, before the auction in Shelbyville, Kentucky. (Olivianna Calmes)

While collectors came for the memorabilia, many of the items also documented how Sanders built Kentucky Fried Chicken into one of the world's best-known restaurant brands.

"When he introduced the pressure cooker, which was never intended for fried chicken, he turned it from 30 minutes to 10 minutes," Menish said. "And that's what really revolutionized his ability to service the fast food growing industry."

A vintage Kentucky Fried Chicken operations manual was displayed alongside other memorabilia from Colonel Sanders' career before the auction. (Olivianna Calmes)

Colonel Sanders' family member Elizabeth Pitchford attended the auction to watch pieces of her grandfather's legacy find new owners.

"I really wanted to see the people who were going to be purchasing my grandpa's stuff," Pitchford said. "The items that have been around for so many years, and it's just been overwhelming."

KFC PLANS TO TEST A NEW PROTOTYPE CALLED OPEN HOUSE

The memorabilia auction may be over, but another part of Sanders' legacy is still up for grabs.

Blackwood Hall, the former home of KFC founder Colonel Harland Sanders, is being offered for sale through a sealed bid process in Shelbyville, Kentucky. (Olivianna Calmes)

His former home, Blackwood Hall, and his wife's restaurant, the Claudia Sanders Dinner House, are being offered through a sealed bid process, with offers due Friday at midnight.

The restaurant opened after Sanders sold Kentucky Fried Chicken and remains one of the landmarks tied to the family's history.

The properties have been owned by the Settle family since 1974.

Olivianna Calmes joined Fox News in 2024 as a Multimedia Reporter based in St. Louis, Missouri.

articles.title: Kate Middleton is 'indispensable' to royal family as slimmed-down monarchy faces mounting pressure: expert
articles.excerpt:
Katie Nicholl, Vanity Fair royal correspondent and co-host of "The Royals Uncensored," says the Princess of Wales won public respect through duty and resilience after health challenges.

Kate Middleto...
articles.body_text:
Katie Nicholl, Vanity Fair royal correspondent and co-host of "The Royals Uncensored," says the Princess of Wales won public respect through duty and resilience after health challenges.

Kate Middleton has become one of King Charles' most beloved family members, with one royal expert calling her the "monarchy's greatest asset."

The claim came from Vanity Fair royal correspondent Katie Nicholl, co-host of "The Royals Uncensored." After more than 20 years covering the royal family on tours and engagements, Nicholl said she has spoken to countless palace insiders, many of whom are enchanted by the Princess of Wales.

"I think Catherine, the Princess of Wales, has always been a very valuable asset to the royal family," Nicholl told Fox News Digital. "She is the commoner who married into the royal family ... [She has made] a seamless transition into that unique world of royalty. It's not easy ... There's a huge amount of sacrifice that goes into being a member of the royal family."

PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON FINALLY FEEL FREE TO SHOW AFFECTION IN PUBLIC: EXPERTS

King Charles III kisses Catherine, Princess of Wales, after the Requiem Mass for the Duchess of Kent at Westminster Cathedral in London on Sept. 16, 2025. Royal experts told Fox News Digital the touching moment reflects the increasingly close relationship the monarch shares with his daughter-in-law. (Jordan Pettitt - Pool/Getty Images)

"Catherine's had to give up a huge amount, and yet she does it all with a great deal of grace and dignity, always with a smile," Nicholl said. "So she is absolutely the monarchy's greatest asset."

Nicholl also noted that "the king adores her, and the queen adores her."

Catherine, Princess of Wales speaks with children during an official welcome at the Town Hall on the first day of her visit to Reggio Emilia on May 13, 2026, in Reggio Emilia, Italy. (UK Press via Getty Images)

Royal experts told Fox News Digital that Charles and Kate have forged an even deeper bond since both were diagnosed with cancer. Buckingham Palace announced the king's diagnosis in 2024. In December 2025, Charles shared the "good news" that his treatment would be scaled back in 2026.

WATCH: KATE MIDDLETON IS 'THE MONARCHY'S GREATEST ASSET: EXPERT'

Just weeks after the king's announcement, Kate revealed in March 2024 that she was undergoing treatment for an undisclosed form of cancer. She completed chemotherapy that September and announced in January 2025 that she was in remission.

British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard told Fox News Digital that the king, 77, had been greatly inspired by the Princess of Wales' strength.

Catherine, Princess of Wales, Princess Charlotte of Wales and King Charles III during Trooping the Colour on June 15, 2024, in London. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)

"King Charles sees enormous value in Princess Catherine," Chard said. "Not just as the wife of his heir, but as the cornerstone of the monarchy itself. He genuinely loves his 'darling' daughter-in-law. His face lights up when he is with her. They share similar interests, and they have shared a similar cancer journey, one that has created a deep bond and understanding that goes beyond duty."

King Charles III and Catherine, Princess of Wales, are seen here at the state banquet for German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier and his wife, Elke Budenbender, at Windsor Castle in Windsor, England, on Dec. 3, 2025. (Aaron Chown - Pool/Getty Images)

Chard argued that it hasn't just been Charles who quickly realized that Kate represented the monarchy's future.

"The late queen saw it too," Chard said. "She recognized Catherine's superpowers early on — her ability to listen, find solutions and bring calm to difficult situations."

Queen Elizabeth II, England's longest-reigning monarch, died in 2022 at age 96. (Geoff Pugh)

"King Charles fundamentally views his time on the throne as stewardship," she said. "He sees himself as the caretaker of the institution and is acutely conscious of preparing the next generation. Collaborative preparation between the king and his heir is essential. Having Princess Catherine as the wife of his heir, Charles has struck gold."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Prince William, Prince of Wales, Catherine, Princess of Wales, Princess Charlotte, Prince George and Prince Louis watch an RAF flypast from the balcony of Buckingham Palace after attending Trooping the Colour 2026 on June 13, 2026, in London. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

Royal author Sally Bedell Smith previously told People magazine that Kate is "like the daughter he never had."

"He has always had a very strong bond with her," Smith told the outlet. "He shares with William an impulse to protect her. They are in this together, Kate and the king."

Kate Middleton and the former Prince Charles examine artwork produced on silk during a visit to the Dulwich Picture Gallery on March 15, 2012, in Dulwich, south London, England. (John Stillwell - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

When Kate made her diagnosis public, Buckingham Palace said Charles was "so proud of Catherine for her courage in speaking as he did."

Catherine, Princess of Wales congratulates patient Claire Lorente and her partner, Pablo, as she rings the end-of-treatment bell at the Christie cancer care hospital in Manchester, England, on June 4, 2026. (Andy Stenning - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

Author Christopher Andersen previously wrote in his book "Kate!" that the king was by Kate's side "to lend his cherished daughter-in-law moral support" during her health battle.

Kate's advocacy work following her cancer diagnosis continues, Nicholl told Fox News Digital.

Catherine, Princess of Wales curtseys to King Charles III on Sept. 16, 2025, in London. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"Thankfully, despite a serious health issue, she has overcome that," Nicholl said. "We've just seen her climb the three highest peaks in the United Kingdom to raise money for the Royal Marsden. She's turning her experience into something positive, and I think that's earned her a great deal of respect among the British public, along with a lot of love and affection. People are very much behind her and William."

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Catherine, Princess of Wales, is seen visiting Evelina London Children's Hospital in London, on July 6, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

"Princess Catherine connects with people in a way that restores faith in the monarchy," Chard said. "She has learned every aspect of the institution over many years and has blended in carefully without fuss. Princess Catherine is central to the institution's success, and King Charles knows this."

With a slimmed down monarchy, Charles needs key allies now more than ever. His younger brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, stepped back as a working royal in 2019 following his controversial ties to late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Charles has since formally removed Andrew’s princely title and HRH style.

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on Feb. 19, 2026, and released after about 11 hours under investigation. He was detained on suspicion of misconduct in public office over allegations that he shared confidential trade reports with Jeffrey Epstein while serving as the U.K.'s trade envoy. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

In 2020, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, stepped back as senior working royals and later settled in California.

From left: Prince William, Kate Middleton, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle attend a ceremony to mark the centenary of the Royal Air Force on the forecourt of Buckingham Palace on July 10, 2018, in London. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped back as senior royals in 2020. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"Princess Anne and other senior working royals are all stretched thin — and none of them are young," author Catherine Mayer previously told People magazine. "William and Catherine carry the whole thing."

Sources told the outlet there had been "even greater attention and expectation on the Waleses." Still, royal experts told Fox News Digital that Kate is well-positioned to support the king.

Queen Camilla, Prince William, King Charles and Kate Middleton are seen at the "No Time To Die" world premiere at the Royal Albert Hall in London, on Sept. 28, 2021. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"Naturally, King Charles recognizes the value of Kate, who is indeed the monarchy's greatest asset," Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital. "We should add, 'together with her partnership with William and their family.' While we praise Catherine's many strengths, William is the future king. She will one day be queen consort. They see themselves as a close-knit couple."

"William is currently at the center of reports that he and the king differ over how to handle Prince Harry, in particular," Fitzwilliams said. "As she showed when the Sussexes met with the king and Queen Camilla, she fully supports William's approach."

Catherine, Princess of Wales, speaks to guests during a Cancer Research UK reception marking the charity's 125th anniversary at St. James's Palace on June 2, 2026, in London. (Jonathan Brady - Pool/Getty Images)

As William and Kate prepare for their future roles, they are likely to remain under close public scrutiny. With Charles' support, royal experts believe the couple is well-positioned for the years ahead.

Prince William is heir to the British throne. (Aaron Chown - Pool/Getty Images)

"It’s not at all surprising King Charles and Princess Catherine have bonded," British royals expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital. "One can tangibly feel the public also values her wonderful assets from the reception she always receives when in public, as well as in opinion polls. She has become indispensable and has won the public’s trust."

"Charles can depend on Catherine because she is consistent, steady and modern in her approach to family, shaped by her upbringing and dedication to duty," Fordwich said. "She handled the strain of her cancer battle with dignity, without any indication of self-pity."

Catherine, Princess of Wales cools down with a fan as she attends Day 14 of the 2026 Wimbledon Tennis Championships at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club on July 12, 2026, in London. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)

"One can observe from the body language between Charles and Catherine that they are so comfortable together, derived from the time they spent together during their cancer battles."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Bombshell voting scandal adds to pattern of noncitizen voters as Trump warns of threat to ‘heart' of democracy
articles.excerpt:
America First Legal President Gene Hamilton posits that there are ways to fix ongoing problems with U.S. voting systems.

New Jersey Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s recent announcement of 6,600 ineli...
articles.body_text:
America First Legal President Gene Hamilton posits that there are ways to fix ongoing problems with U.S. voting systems.

New Jersey Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s recent announcement of 6,600 ineligible voters found on the state’s rolls is only the latest in a decades-long string of cases involving noncitizens registered to vote in U.S. elections, records show.

Sherrill said that the ineligible voters were registered due to a "serious software error" in New Jersey’s Motor Vehicle System. Her announcement came within a week of a major address from President Donald Trump in which he warned that digital election interference posed a "cyber threat aimed at the very heart of our democracy."

While New Jersey is the latest documented failure, it is not an isolated anomaly. New Jersey's error adds to a 25-year record of state reviews, software failures and prosecutions that found noncitizens on voter rolls and, in some documented cases, casting ballots. Experts say the episodes establish a recurring vulnerability. However, due to the lack of a national standard for identifying and reporting errors, reviews are sporadic and use different methods, making it impossible to determine how widespread the problem truly is.

"It's a major vulnerability," Jason Snead, executive director of the conservative think tank the Honest Elections Project, told Fox News Digital. "And we have seen just within the last couple of years many states that have checked their voter rolls and found non-citizens on them … So, this is a big problem."

NEW JERSEY REMOVES 6,600 PEOPLE FROM VOTER ROLLS WHO WERE ELIGIBLE TO CAST A BALLOT FOR 2024 ELECTION

Mikie Sherrill, governor of New Jersey, speaks in the Assembly Chamber of the New Jersey State House in Trenton, New Jersey, US, on Tuesday, March 10, 2026. (Heather Khalifa/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

According to New Jersey’s preliminary findings, fewer than 400 individuals who were improperly registered ended up voting. Sherrill said they lived all across the state and mostly lacked a party affiliation, though there were some registered as Democrats or Republicans.

Fox News Digital reached out to the New Jersey Secretary of State Division of Elections, state Attorney General Dale Caldwell and the chairs of several key legislative elections oversight committees for clarification on which elections the 400 ineligible voters participated in and to request details on the state’s auditing protocols. Fox News Digital did not receive a response from any of the state officials mentioned above.

Snead explained that though states are required by law to ensure their voter rolls are up to date and accurate, there is no uniform federal requirement for a state to disclose its findings. He said that this has led to differences across states in how the law is enforced and how errors are reported.

"There are federal requirements to maintain clean and accurate voter rolls. And of course, it is a federal crime for a noncitizen to register and to vote, but there's no requirement that a state report how many non-citizens that they have found up to the federal government. That's entirely a state law question," he explained.

He argued that problems involving noncitizen voting are greater in blue states due to policies he said make it easier to cheat.

LEAVITT RIPS BLUE STATE’S EXPLOSIVE NONCITIZEN VOTER-ROLL ADMISSION: ‘NOT A COINCIDENCE’

"When you look at the policies that are pushed in blue states by the left, things like automatic voter registration, giving drivers licenses to illegal aliens, banning voter identification laws, no proof of citizenship to vote on and on and, this is the inevitable outcome of all of those policies," said Snead, adding, "This is not the first time that we've seen a state with automatic voter registration add potential non-citizens to the rolls."

After the president’s speech, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin released a statement announcing that preliminary DHS reviews of state records found "as many as" 250,000 noncitizens registered to vote in four states: 35,152 in New Jersey, 190,832 in California, 15,903 in Nevada and 14,576 in Pennsylvania.

Fox News Digital reached out to DHS for clarification on its preliminary findings. However, DHS did not answer Fox News Digital’s questions and instead sent a statement from Mullin reiterating the number.

In the statement, Mullin emphasized to Fox News Digital that "this shouldn’t be a red or blue state issue: ONLY Americans should elect American leaders." He added that "we’ve put these governors on notice. States must work with us to ensure free, fair, and honest elections."

Charles Stewart III, a professor of political science specializing in elections at MIT, explained that the controlling federal law governing voter registration, the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA), is "silent on the issue of noncitizens on the roll."

He told Fox News Digital that because "this was not an issue in the early 1990s … one of the ambiguities right now and controversies is over precisely what sort of obligations states have to audit their rolls for noncitizens."

"This is really at the crux of the matter and two of President Trump's executive orders. It's the crux of the matter in the Save America Act. It is the crux to the matter in the current efforts, well, back to the executive orders and a lot of the lawsuits. And the states are pointing out, when being pressed by the federal government, that yes, it is illegal for noncitizens to vote, for sure, and states should have an obligation to make sure noncitizens are not registering, but there is no federal law that compels states to do investigations, nor is there a federal law to compel them to report.

Meanwhile, states that have published review results have reported concerning findings. Besides New Jersey, state reviews conducted since 2020 have found evidence of significant numbers of noncitizens registered to vote in Louisiana, Iowa, Michigan, Ohio and Illinois, a Fox News Digital review found.

Earlier this year, Louisiana Secretary of State said that using the federal Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) database, which was rolled out by the Trump administration last year, the state identified 403 noncitizens on its voter rolls, 83 of whom had voted in elections, American Press reported.

In 2025, an audit by the Iowa secretary of state confirmed that 277 noncitizens were registered to vote and that 35 successfully voted in the 2024 election while five attempted to vote but were rejected.

TRUMP RELEASES DECLASSIFIED ELECTION INTELLIGENCE, SAYS IT REVEALS 'SHOCKING VULNERABILITIES'

The same year, the Michigan Department of State published its findings from a review of the 2024 election, which it said proved that "credible cases of noncitizens casting a ballot in Michigan elections are extremely rare." The review found that 15 people, who it said "appear to be non-U.S. citizens," cast a ballot in the election. Additionally, the department identified a Chinese national who allegedly voted illegally.

The Ohio Secretary of State's Office announced in 2024 and 2021 that it had identified 597 and 117 apparent noncitizen voter registrations, respectively, and referred the cases for further investigation.

According to findings cited in Illinois legislation and testimony by secretary of state officials before the general assembly, a programming error in the state's automatic voter registration system allowed the records of 574 people who identified themselves as noncitizens to be transmitted to election officials between 2018 and 2019.

Further, officials in Pennsylvania, Texas, Maryland, Colorado, Florida and North Carolina have also reported cases of noncitizens being registered to vote as far back as 2000.

In testimony given to the Pennsylvania House State Government Committee in 2017, then elections commissioner Jonathan Marks revealed that the state had found 1,160 records of apparent noncitizens who self-reported and canceled. Marks said that a deeper analysis of the years 2000 through 2017 found 544 ballots were cast by the identified registrants.

In Texas, authorities discovered a resident alien named Rosa Ortega registered in 2002 and voted five times from 2004 through 2014, according to Attorney General Ken Paxton.

In another case, a Ghanaian national named Michael Nana Baako registered to vote in Maryland, swearing that he was a U.S. citizen in 2005 and subsequently voted in 10 federal elections between 2006 and 2018, according to the DOJ.

A 2012 report by the Colorado Department of State revealed that the state identified 3,903 registered voters whose citizenship status was "in question." An additional 430 Colorado voters were found to have identified themselves as ineligible to vote because of citizenship requirements.

The report noted that in Colorado "no proof is required to validate the status indicated on a registration form." It said that individuals can register to vote at a driver’s license office, state public assistance office, county office, private voter registration drive, or even online, none of which verify citizenship.

Three reviews conducted by the Florida Department of State for the years between 2013 and 2017 identified 821 noncitizen registrations and 126 people with voting histories.

Meanwhile, a 2017 state audit in North Carolina concluded that 41 legal-status noncitizens cast ballots.

NJ REPUBLICAN SAYS MOTOR VOTER SCANDAL VINDICATES YEARS OF ELECTION INTEGRITY WARNINGS, PUSHES FOR LEGISLATIVE PROBE

(Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images) (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Fox News Digital also reached out to the Justice Department to ask how many individuals the agency has charged with noncitizen voting or unlawful voter registration since 2000. However, a spokesperson for the DOJ did not offer specifics. Instead, the spokesperson sent Fox News Digital a statement assuring that the department’s Civil Rights Division "is investigating and will keep pressing states to clean their rolls" and is "prosecuting cases where the law and evidence support it."

The DOJ spokesperson reiterated that "it is illegal for any noncitizen to vote in a federal election" and that "every unlawful vote dilutes the voice of American citizens."

"Whether or not a case is prosecutable doesn't change the fact that the wrongful vote happened — DHS found over 250,000 likely noncitizens on voter rolls nationwide, and New Jersey's own Governor confirmed 400 noncitizens voted there," the spokesperson said.

"The fact of the matter is that election after election after election after election happened and no one did anything about it," remarked Gene Hamilton, president of America First Legal.

He pointed to a letter sent by the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division to election officials in all 50 states which he said, "reminded them of their obligations and the possibility of legal consequences for not taking action."

Since President Donald Trump's return to office, the Civil Rights Division has filed lawsuits against 30 states and the District of Columbia seeking to compel the production of full voter registration lists under the NVRA, according to the Brennan Center for Justice.

"There are ways to fix it," said Hamilton. "It's just a matter of desire."

Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.
