articles.body_text:
The U.S. Embassy in the Bahamas is urging Americans to avoid jet ski rentals, citing deaths, injuries and reported sexual assaults linked to unlicensed operators.

The family of Tyler Wilkin, is exhaustively trying to track down the person responsible for killing him in what was described as an execution-style shooting.

The 35-year-old Ohio native was found shot dead with a gunshot wound to the back of his head while on a camping trip on Playa La Selva in Luquillo, Puerto Rico.

Tyler Wilkin, 35, was allegedly shot in the head, execution style, when he was on a camping trip with friends in Puerto Rico. (Lilly Wright, GoFundMe)

OHIO MAN FOUND SHOT DEAD IN EXECUTION-STYLE KILLING WHILE CAMPING ON PUERTO RICO BEACH: REPORTS

Wilkin was born and raised in Ohio, but moved to Puerto Rico in 2024 with his girlfriend.

A fundraiser has been started to raise $30,000 to hire a private investigator to take over Wilkin's case. A statement posted to the fundraiser said the "funds will help us [Wilkin's family and friends] cover any and all expenses that may arise during the private investigation. Tyler deserved a full life, and he deserves for every possible avenue to be explored."

📩 Send me a story idea: kelsie.cairns@fox.com

Luquillo, where Wilkin was found dead, is a city with a significant amount of unsolved violent crime, according to Jamie Copenhaver, a former sheriff's investigator and private investigator. He has investigated cases in Puerto Rico in his capacity as a law enforcement officer and as a PI.

MICHIGAN ATHLETE LURED BY SNAPCHAT MESSAGE BEFORE BEING SHOT, DUMPED IN LAKE WHILE STILL ALIVE

Tyler Wilkin's body was reportedly discovered by authorities on Playa La Selva in Luquillo, Puerto Rico on July 10. (Getty Images: Swathi Chirra)

Wilkin reportedly sent text messages to his friends concerned about a "howling" noise and what sounded like "fireworks" outside of his tent, FOX 19 reported.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"The howling struck me as possible stalking behavior," Copenhaver told Fox News Digital. "If you're camping and hear those noises in the middle of the night, you're naturally going to grab a flashlight and investigate. I think it's possible someone intentionally lured him away from his campsite."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

He is concerned that investigative efforts of local police may lack essential training and resources required to take on this homicide case.

LISTEN: DISPATCH AUDIO CAPTURES FRANTIC HUNT FOR SUSPECT IN PENN STATE SENIOR'S FATAL SHOOTING

A fundraiser was created to hire a private investigator to find out how American Tyler Wilkin ended up shot to death in Puerto Rico. (Alba Cuebas-Fantauzzi)

"Unlike many police departments in the mainland U.S., agencies there are often overwhelmed by the number of violent crimes they're investigating. They're doing their best, but it's a tremendous workload," Copenhaver said.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Tyler Wilkin is survived by his parents and four other siblings. (Lilly Wright, GoFundMe)

Copenhaver said Wilkin's loved ones' decision to hire a private investigator just makes sense.

In addition to hiring a PI, he said the family should also contact the FBI in San Juan if they have not done so already.

He said, "I'd ask them to take an interest in the case to make sure every avenue is explored and whoever murdered this young man is brought to justice."

"At this time, the SJFO is providing technical assistance to PRPD, but this case remains an ongoing local investigative matter," the FBI said in a statement to Fox News Digital, referring to its San Juan Field Office and the Puerto Rico Police Department. "We will defer to PRPD for any statements or comments but encourage the local public to call in tips and information, through Tips.FBI.Gov , 1-800-CALL-FBI, or calling the SJFO at 787-987-6500."

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Puerto Rico Police Bureau.

articles.title: Taco Bell offers $1 Mexican pizza, other lettuce-free deals to win back customers after outbreak
articles.excerpt:
Dr. Janette Nesheiwat joins 'Saturday in America' to discuss the ongoing cyclospora outbreak across the U.S.

Taco Bell is offering steep discounts on lettuce-free menu items as the fast-food chain wo...
articles.body_text:
Dr. Janette Nesheiwat joins 'Saturday in America' to discuss the ongoing cyclospora outbreak across the U.S.

Taco Bell is offering steep discounts on lettuce-free menu items as the fast-food chain works to recover from the business impact of the cyclospora outbreak.

Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite known to cause cyclosporiasis, the hallmark symptom of which is diarrhea, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Cases linked to the multistate cyclospora outbreak began surfacing in May.

The FDA said its traceback investigation identified shredded iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms and sourced from central Mexico as the likely source of the outbreak.

CYCLOSPORA OUTBREAK: IS IT STILL SAFE TO EAT AT RESTAURANTS? HERE'S WHAT TO KNOW

Although the FDA later said a laboratory test on one lettuce sample was a false positive, the agency said its epidemiological evidence continues to support the recall of Taylor Farms iceberg lettuce.

Nine states reported cases of cyclosporiasis linked to Taco Bell.

Taylor Farms announced that it was "voluntarily removing all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico from the U.S. market," the FDA reported, and Taco Bell announced in mid-July that it completed the removal of affected Taylor Farms lettuce from its restaurants.

Taco Bell announced it completed removal of iceberg lettuce connected to a foodborne illness outbreak from its restaurants. (iStock)

Foot traffic at Taco Bell has dropped each day since July 13, Reuters reported.

Shares of parent company Yum! Brands have fallen nearly 10% since July 10, according to reports.

In the wake of the outbreak, Taco Bell has been offering discounted items that exclude shredded lettuce, the ingredient tied to the outbreak investigation.

Earlier this week, Taco Bell announced on Instagram that it would be offering its fan-favorite Mexican pizza, which is lettuce-free, for $1 for one day at participating locations. The promotion followed a $1 deal on Enchiritos and $1 regular nacho fries (for rewards members using the app), both lettuce-free menu items.

A Mexican pizza typically costs about $5.69 and contains seasoned beef, refried beans, two crispy flour tortilla shells, Mexican pizza sauce, diced tomatoes and a blend of mozzarella, pepper jack and cheddar cheese, according to Taco Bell's website.

The Mexican pizza is one of the lettuce-free items Taco Bell has offered for $1 in the wake of the cyclospora outbreak. (Joshua Blanchard/Getty Images for Taco Bell)

An Enchirito is priced at $4.29, though prices vary by location. The item is made with a warm flour tortilla filled with seasoned beef, refried beans and diced onions and is smothered in a red sauce and melted shredded cheddar cheese, according to Taco Bell.

Taco Bell has been using social media to communicate with customers about the outbreak. Taco Bell CEO Sean Tresvant wrote a letter posted on LinkedIn "to every Taco Bell fan."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"You have always stood by us, and we will always stand by you," he wrote. "We felt the love. Through the posts. The comments. The stories. We saw them all. The community that said, 'We've got you.' The fans who said they 'can't quit us.' We appreciate every bit of that energy. Thank you."

Taco Bell also posted a collage of supportive messages from customers on social media.

Since the cyclospora outbreak was linked to shredded lettuce at some Taco Bell locations, the chain has been offering deals on lettuce-free menu items. (iStock)

Reactions to Taco Bell's Mexican pizza promotion were generally positive on Instagram, and several people noted the menu item's lack of lettuce.

"You're just gonna keep me coming in daily aren't you," wrote one user. "I basically can't afford not to at this point!"

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"I'll risk cyclospora for this any day," wrote another.

"Considering the fact lettuce already tastes like diarrhea, I've never left you," another commented, along with a heart emoji.

"You have always stood by us, and we will always stand by you," Taco Bell's CEO wrote on LinkedIn amid the cyclospora outbreak. (Marvin Joseph/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

Another enthusiastic customer chimed in, "Taco Bell, just wanted to let y'all know I got my cheesy beefy burrito and avocado chicken stacker and 30 Diablo hot sauce packets regardless of any lettuce issue because I'll go to the ends of the Earth for you guys. My love is unconditional and nothing will separate me from your cheesy beefy burrito and avocado chicken stacker. Yes this is my love letter to you."

Fox News Digital reached out to Taco Bell for comment.

Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Moreno unloads on Fauci after Senate hearing, calls him Democrats' 'hero' over pandemic policies
articles.excerpt:
Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, reflects on Dr. Anthony Fauci’s testimony on ‘Hannity.’

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, doubled down Thursday on his criticism of Dr. Anthony Fauci after the former top health...
articles.body_text:
Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, reflects on Dr. Anthony Fauci’s testimony on ‘Hannity.’

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, doubled down Thursday on his criticism of Dr. Anthony Fauci after the former top health official declined to answer questions during a Senate hearing, calling him Democrats' "hero."

Appearing on "Hannity" Thursday evening, Moreno argued Fauci's handling of the COVID-19 pandemic was driven by a desire for power rather than public health.

"This is about controlling American people," Moreno said. "He treated us like lab rats."

Moreno said Fauci's approach to the pandemic reflected what he believes Democrats ultimately want from government.

TOP 5 MOMENTS FROM FAUCI'S HEARING: PAUL BOOTS LAWYER, MORENO ERUPTS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, criticized Dr. Anthony Fauci's handling of the COVID-19 pandemic during an appearance on Fox News' "Hannity." (Anna Moneymaker / Getty Images)

"You want to give power to Democrats, socialists and communists in this country? They will take away your freedoms, they will take away your liberties, they'll control you, they'll replace you," he said. "They want to systematically destroy this country, and that's why Fauci is their hero. He got to do what they only fantasize about, which is total and complete control of the American people."

Moreno and Fauci clashed during Wednesday's Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing after Fauci, on the advice of counsel, invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination and declined to answer questions from committee members.

RAND PAUL SEEKS CONTEMPT CHARGES AFTER FAUCI INVOKES FIFTH AMENDMENT MORE THAN 100 TIMES

Former NIH Director Anthony Fauci testifies before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in Washington, D.C., on July 29, 2026. Fauci was expected to be questioned about his diary entries during his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. (Getty Images)

A frustrated Moreno told Fauci that the former White House chief medical advisor had inspired him to run for the Senate because of his influence over COVID-19 policies.

"Here I am sitting in front of you six years later saying, 'Who the f--- do you think you were for doing that? It is a total disgrace what you did to this country,'" Moreno said.

Asked Thursday whether he stood by those remarks, Moreno argued Fauci's influence set back children's health for decades and devastated small businesses.

"The reality is this guy damaged a lot of things in this country," he said.

FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

Senator Bernie Moreno, a Republican from Ohio, during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee confirmation hearing in Washington, DC on Wednesday, June 17. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Moreno also pointed to more than 1,000 pages of internal notes released by committee Chairman Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., ahead of the hearing. According to Paul, the notes suggest Fauci privately expressed views about COVID-19 that differed from some of his public statements.

"This is one of the most depraved bureaucrats," Moreno said, adding that Fauci should face prosecution over his handling of the pandemic.

Although Fauci received a pardon from former President Joe Biden, Moreno noted that state investigations remain possible. On Thursday, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced his office would open an investigation after Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right during Wednesday's hearing.

"We know what he was actually thinking," Moreno said. "We know he lied to the American people. State attorneys general, like the one in Florida—I hope the one in Ohio does the same thing. We got to pursue this guy."

Former NIH Director Anthony Fauci listens during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on July 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Fauci declined to answer questions, asserting his Fifth Amendment right. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Moreno said the moment that bothered him most during the hearing came when he asked Fauci to apologize to audience members who said they were harmed by or disagreed with pandemic policies.

"He wouldn't even look at them," Moreno said. "That's how despicable this guy is."

Fox News Digital's Alex Miller, Adam Pack and Robert McGreevy contributed to this report.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Fauci's attorney for comment.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

articles.title: Italy World Cup winner and AC Milan legend Franco Baresi dies aged 66
articles.excerpt:
Franco Baresi, the former AC Milan captain who was one of Italy’s most acclaimed defenders, has died. He was 66.

His death was announced on Friday by Milan, the football club where he spent his entir...
articles.body_text:
Franco Baresi, the former AC Milan captain who was one of Italy’s most acclaimed defenders, has died. He was 66.

His death was announced on Friday by Milan, the football club where he spent his entire 20-year playing career. No cause of death was given.

“The entire history of AC Milan is in tears,” Milan said.

In August 2025, Baresi underwent surgery to remove a pulmonary nodule and subsequently began a course of immunotherapy.

His last public appearance was at the opening ceremony for the Milano Cortina Winter Olympics in February, when, along with former Inter Milan defender Giuseppe Bergomi, he carried the torch into the San Siro — the stadium he formerly played in.

“His example and integrity will be forever etched into the Club’s DNA, just as his iconic number 6 shirt is,” Milan added. “The condolences AC Milan extends to Franco Baresi’s family at such a difficult time are shared by every Rossonero, who feels this loss as their own.”

Baresi was on Italy’s team that won the World Cup in 1982.

“With the passing of Franco Baresi, Italy loses not only one of the greatest champions in its sports history, but also an example of loyalty, professionalism, and dedication,” Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni said on X.

Baresi, who was widely regarded as one of the best defenders of all time, was a true one-club player. He progressed through the ranks at Milan and made his first team debut at the age of 17, in April 1978.

He chose to stay with Milan even after it was relegated to Serie B — for the second time in three seasons — in 1982, just before he helped Italy win the World Cup that summer, and was given the captaincy at the age of just 22.

Baresi made more than 700 appearances for the Rossoneri, captaining the team to global dominance in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

With Milan, Baresi won three Champions League trophies, six Serie A titles, two Intercontinental Cups, three European Supercups and four Italian Supercups.

“For generations, Franco embodied the values, character and excellence that define this club,” Milan owner Gerry Cardinale said. “Even as he battled his greatest challenge over the last year, he was always there for the club, quietly reminding us all what it means to wear these colours.

“Franco’s legacy is profound and will endure forever. Our thoughts are with his family and all those whose lives he touched.”

In his final interview with La Gazzetta dello Sport last year, Baresi said he recalled being a “Milanista” (Milan fan) as a child.

“When I arrived at Milanello (Milan’s training centre) for the first time as a 14-year-old, it seemed like entering paradise,” Baresi said.

As well as the 1982 World Cup, Baresi also helped Italy finish runners-up in the 1994 competition — although he was one of three Azzurri players to miss a penalty in the shootout defeat to Brazil in the final.

Baresi finished runner-up to teammate Marco van Basten in the Ballon d’Or awards in 1989.

When Baresi retired in 1997, Milan also retired his No 6 jersey — which was a first for Italian football. The club also held a celebration match in his honour, featuring many football stars Baresi had played with and against.

Baresi was made honorary president of Milan in 2020.

“Italian soccer has lost one of its legends,” Italian football federation president Giovanni Malago said, labelling Baresi “an extraordinary champion who wore only two shirts for his entire career: those of Milan and Italy”.

“We will have a tribute to remember him the next time the national team plays,” Malago added.

It could have all been so different for Baresi and Milan, however. Baresi had trials at Inter when he was younger but he was rejected by the Nerazzurri, who opted to sign his older brother Giuseppe Baresi, with Franco going on to join the youth team of their fierce city rivals.

Giuseppe also captained his team and the image of the two Baresi brothers exchanging pennants before kickoff became the symbol of the Milan derby throughout the late 80s.

“On November 19, 1995, I made my Serie A debut against Milan. I was 17 years old, and on the other side was the captain of that team: Franco Baresi,” former Italy captain Gianluigi Buffon said on X, referring to his Italian league debut with Parma.

“For a boy my age, finding myself on the field against champions like him was something incredible,” Buffon added. “From that day on, I had an even clearer understanding of what it meant to represent football with class, leadership, and respect. Ciao Franco. Rest in peace.”

articles.title: AFC backs UEFA and CONCACAF who plan boycott over FIFA World Cup proposals
articles.excerpt: The ‌Asian Football Confederation has said it “stands in solidarity” with regional ⁠bodies UEFA and ⁠CONCACAF in opposing plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors but stopped short ...
articles.body_text:
The ‌Asian Football Confederation has said it “stands in solidarity” with regional ⁠bodies UEFA and ⁠CONCACAF in opposing plans to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors but stopped short of threatening ⁠to boycott events run by FIFA, global football’s governing body.

The confederation in a statement on Friday expressed “deep concern” over the proposed establishment of a $20bn commercial ⁠subsidiary, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the World Cup and FIFA’s other events.

“The fact that the situation has reached the point where the real possibility of a FIFA World Cup boycott has entered public discourse should concern everyone ‌who cares about the future of our game,” the statement said.

“Football should never have been placed in such a position.”

UEFA, European football’s governing body, voted unanimously on Thursday to boycott all FIFA events unless the plans were dropped. CONCACAF, the regional federation for North America, Central America and the Caribbean, has also rejected ⁠FIFA’s proposal.

On Thursday, AFC President Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa had said the way the proposal had been made was “totally unacceptable”, in a letter to member associations.

The AFC said “the proposed FFE cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus and ⁠unity required to move forward.

“The FIFA World Cup ⁠is the pinnacle of global football and derives its strength from the participation of all confederations and the world’s leading football nations.”

The AFC also made a thinly veiled attack on the ⁠governing body’s president, Gianni Infantino, saying the plan “has exposed fundamental weaknesses in FIFA’s consultation and decision-making processes that ⁠must now be addressed”.

Even after FIFA issued ⁠a new statement on Friday, saying each national association “should be allowed to review the proposal and have a say in shaping their own future”, the AFC said “central concerns surrounding governance, ‌institutional process and meaningful consultation remain unanswered”.

It said the furore must become a catalyst for institutional reform at FIFA, and that “meaningful democracy is not ‌measured ‌solely by the opportunity to vote.

“It begins with transparent governance, timely consultation, informed deliberation and genuine participation throughout the decision-making process.”

articles.title: About 49,000 migrants enter Spanish territory of Ceuta, officials say
articles.excerpt:
About 49,000 migrants have crossed into Spain's North African territory of Ceuta from Morocco in the last 24 hours via land and sea, officials estimate.

Videos and images showed thousands of people s...
articles.body_text:
About 49,000 migrants have crossed into Spain's North African territory of Ceuta from Morocco in the last 24 hours via land and sea, officials estimate.

Videos and images showed thousands of people swimming into the city on Thursday, while local media reported crossings continuing overnight.

Officials say at least 18 people have died while trying to reach the territory in recent days.

This comes after Spain's Supreme Court ruled this month that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla, another Spanish exclave, cannot be summarily returned to Morocco.

Spain sending troops as thousands enter enclave of Ceuta from Morocco

Ceuta, on Morocco's northern coast, is separated from mainland Spain by the Strait of Gibraltar and has long been a focal point for migrants attempting to reach Europe.

Local officials had appealed to Madrid for help after a recent rise in attempted crossings, but there were chaotic scenes on Thursday as border controls apparently broke down.

The astonishing estimation by Spanish officials suggests the number of migrants who entered into Ceuta in the last day or so could be more than half of the population of the city - which sits at around 83,600, according to the latest local figures.

Spain later deployed its armed forces to bolster security in Ceuta and at its sister city of Melilla, where between 300 to 400 crossings were also reported overnight.

Coveted by Morocco, both cities have long been a flashpoint in diplomatic relations with Spain. Madrid asserts that both territories are integral parts of Spain and have the same status as the semi-autonomous regions on its mainland.

They form the European Union's only land borders with Africa.

Crowds gathered at the border between Morocco and Spain overnight

Many of those crossing the border from Morocco have been young, mainly men, although there are also women and children in the crowds and even babies.

Officials estimate at least 7,000 of those who crossed illegally into the territory in the last 24 hours are minors.

Usually, to try to enter Ceuta, migrants swim several kilometres from further up the coast. This time they appear to have been able to get close to the border fence itself with ease. At the start, some even walked along the rocks on the jetty and around the end of it, but most had to swim out and around to reach the beaches on the other side.

It's not clear where the Moroccan border guards were at this point and why the groups of migrants were not dispersed or stopped.

Many young men were seen swimming into Ceuta or crossing the land border

The sudden influx of people on Thursday followed several days with an increase in arrivals swimming into Ceuta. It appears that word of their success spread quickly.

The last time there was a surge in arrivals - though on nowhere near this scale - was in 2021. At that point, the Moroccan authorities allowed some 8,000 people to cross the border following a dispute with Madrid over the sovereignty of the Western Sahara.

That diplomatic dispute has flared again recently, after Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez travelled to Algeria which backs independence for the region.

Spain's interior ministry said it was working with Morocco to ensure the return of all who crossed illegally into its territory "as soon as possible".

Sánchez is set to visit Ceuta later on Friday.

Overnight into Friday, crossings continued as did clashes between migrants and police along the border, local media reported.

It is not yet clear what prompted this surge in illegal crossings from Morocco, or how hard the authorities there tried to prevent it. At one point, a Spanish official said the border was in total collapse.

Italy's prime minister was very quick to comment on events in Ceuta, calling the images from there "shocking" and writing on social media that such "uncontrolled immigration" was a security threat to Europe.

She said Italy would consider suspending the Schengen zone agreement with Spain on free movement, although it's unclear what that means in practice given that the two countries are not neighbours and undocumented migrants are unlikely to board flights.

In any case, the migrants who have arrived in Ceuta are now stuck there - not on the Spanish mainland.

Spain has now set up a large military presence at the border

Her comments echoed similar remarks made by foreign minister Antonio Tajani, who was accused of weaponising immigration for political ends by his Spanish counterpart, José Manuel Albares.

The Spanish foreign minister said such remarks were "improper" for "a partner and friendly country from which we expect European solidarity and not partisan demagoguery".

He also summoned the Italian ambassador to Madrid on Friday.

The Schengen Area is a system of open borders spanning 29 European countries that have officially abolished controls at their common borders.

articles.title: FIFA World Cup plan fallout: Infantino’s senior adviser, Cordeiro, resigns
articles.excerpt:
Carlos Cordeiro, senior adviser to FIFA President Gianni Infantino, has resigned following the proposal by football’s governing body to sell a stake in its World Cups and events.

Cordeiro said on Fri...
articles.body_text:
Carlos Cordeiro, senior adviser to FIFA President Gianni Infantino, has resigned following the proposal by football’s governing body to sell a stake in its World Cups and events.

Cordeiro said on Friday that he is stepping down with immediate effect in ⁠protest at proposals to seek private investment in a newly formed FIFA Forward Enterprise venture, ‌calling the plan “a bad deal for football”.

In FIFA’s plan, the FFE would create a $20bn subsidiary to run the World Cup and its other events, with a stake of up to 20 percent to be offered to external investors. It would be bankrolled by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner.

“Let me be clear: I had no involvement in this proposal ⁠and I oppose ⁠it unequivocally,” Cordeiro said in a statement.

“It is ⁠a bad deal for ⁠FIFA’s Member Associations, ⁠a bad deal for football and a bad deal ‌for the long-term future of the game.”

Cordeiro had represented football’s global governing body on the White House Task Force for the 2026 World Cup, held in the United States, Canada and Mexico.

A former banker and ex-US Soccer Federation vice president, Cordeiro was hand-picked to ⁠help grow world football for FIFA.

In his statement, Cordeiro questioned why FIFA would consider raising $4.2bn by selling part of its “most valuable asset” when the organisation sits on billions of dollars in reserves and has no debt.

His resignation comes as FIFA’s 211 member associations face pressure to decide on the controversial proposal by September 19, with Infantino ⁠saying they “risk being left behind” if they do not accept it.

“The ⁠FIFA President himself has highlighted the $15bn in revenue generated between 2022 and 2026,” Cordeiro added, saying FIFA already had the financial capacity to provide additional support to member associations from its existing resources.

“Against that backdrop, selling ⁠a permanent stake in football’s most valuable asset to raise $4.2bn makes little sense.”

As senior adviser to Infantino, Cordeiro’s remit ⁠was to “advise FIFA on new strategic initiatives to grow the ⁠game at all levels”.

Announcing the appointment in 2021, Infantino had said: “Carlos is the right person to advise us as we modernise our regulatory framework and grow the sport in ways that advance football for men, women and youth ‌across the globe.”

Cordeiro built a long career in business and global investment banking in Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA) and across Asia, advising governments and some of the world’s ‌largest ‌international companies.

Prior to joining US Soccer, he was a vice chairman at Goldman Sachs and earned an MBA from Harvard Business School.

articles.title: Trump admin cannot refuse detained illegal immigrants a chance for release on bond, appeals court rules
articles.excerpt: A federal judge in Boston ruled against the Trump administration's $100,000 fee for H-1B visas, deeming it an unauthorized tax. The fee, which was significantly increased from a typical $2,000-$5,000,...
articles.body_text:
A federal judge in Boston ruled against the Trump administration's $100,000 fee for H-1B visas, deeming it an unauthorized tax. The fee, which was significantly increased from a typical $2,000-$5,000, aimed to prioritize US citizens in the workforce. The administration is appealing the decision.

A federal appeals court on Thursday ruled that the Trump administration cannot deny migrants detained inside the U.S. a chance for release on bond as part of its expanded mandatory detention policy.

In a 2-1 decision, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals in San Francisco ruled against the administration.

Four other appeals courts have also rejected the policy, although the Fifth Circuit in New Orleans and Eighth Circuit in St. Louis have ruled in favor of the federal government.

The deepening circuit split raises the chance that the U.S. Supreme Court will eventually take up the case. The administration asked the high court last month to consider the case.

APPEALS COURT BLOCKS TRUMP ADMIN FROM HOLDING MIGRANTS WITHOUT BOND FOR 90 DAYS

A federal appeals court ruled that the Trump administration cannot deny migrants detained inside the U.S. a chance for release on bond. (Jim WATSON / AFP via Getty Images)

The Department of Homeland Security said it "strongly disagrees with the Ninth Circuit panel and is confident in its legal position regarding mandatory detention."

"President Donald Trump and Secretary Mullin are now enforcing the law as it was actually written to keep America safe," the department said in a statement.

Under previous administrations, most illegal immigrants with no criminal record who were arrested inside the U.S. were allowed to seek a bond hearing while their immigration cases were pending, and mandatory detention was typically reserved for those detained at the border.

But last year, the government issued guidance expanding mandatory detention to include illegal immigrants inside the U.S. The move was part of the president's mass deportation plan, leading to several lawsuits by immigrants pursuing a release from custody.

The Department of Homeland Security said it "strongly disagrees with the Ninth Circuit panel and is confident in its legal position regarding mandatory detention." (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

Some federal judges who ordered bond hearings criticized the administration for repeatedly violating their orders.

The administration has said that Congress changed immigration law in 1996 to allow mandatory detention past the border and that previous administrations failed to enforce that measure.

But Ninth Circuit Judge Daniel Bress, who was appointed by President Donald Trump, rejected that argument.

"Although no reading of the complicated and interrelated textual provisions at issue here is without some shortcomings, the historical understanding of the statute is the better one," said Bress, writing for the majority.

DEMOCRAT COMPARES ICE TO 'DOMESTIC TERRORISTS' AS 111 HOUSE DEMS DEMAND TEXAS DETENTION CENTER CLOSE

Some federal judges who ordered bond hearings criticized the administration for repeatedly violating their orders. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

Bress was joined by Judge M. Margaret McKeown, who was appointed by former President Bill Clinton.

Judge Carlos Bea, who was appointed by President George W. Bush, dissented, arguing that the amendment Congress passed 30 years ago supports the administration's position.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Suffolk wildfire near Sizewell nuclear plant ‘stabilising’ after 24 hours
articles.excerpt:
More than 100 firefighters remain at scene after Dunwich Heath blaze spread across 150 hectares and forced evacuations

Fire crews tackling a large wildfire burning for more than 24 hours near Britain...
articles.body_text:
More than 100 firefighters remain at scene after Dunwich Heath blaze spread across 150 hectares and forced evacuations

Fire crews tackling a large wildfire burning for more than 24 hours near Britain’s biggest nuclear power station have said the situation is “stabilising”.

More than 100 firefighters have been battling the blaze in Dunwich Heath, near Leiston on the Suffolk coast, since Wednesday evening.

By late Thursday, while the incident remained “dynamic”, Suffolk fire and rescue service said the blaze appeared to be stablising.

At least 12 fire appliances remained at the scene overnight to tackle smaller fires breaking out, while crews monitored identified hotspots.

A fire service spokesperson said: “Although the fire is dynamic, it remains stable and Suffolk fire and rescue service is making good progress.”

Firefighting efforts include a helicopter capable of dropping 100 litres of seawater on each pass. Six London fire brigade appliances will support the response.

The “unprecedented” wildfire, which broke out at about 5pm on Wednesday, grew approximately 150 hectares – roughly the size of 210 football pitches.

The blaze is a few miles from Sizewell B nuclear power station and the construction site for the new Sizewell C plant.

Freddie Gulliver, an emergency manager at the Suffolk Joint Emergency Planning Unit, said there was no immediate concern about the fire spreading towards Sizewell B.

A spokesperson for the energy supplier EDF said the wildfire was “not affecting operations” at Sizewell B, adding that the company was closely monitoring the situation. The spokesperson said the site had emergency plans covering a range of scenarios, including a fire on the premises.

About 50 people have been evacuated from their homes and a nearby holiday park to Westleton, where the village hall has been turned into a rest centre.

Conservationists have raised concerns for rare birds and wildlife on the heath and nearby RSPB Minsmere, including Dartford warblers, nightjars and stonechats, as well as reptiles such as adders, common lizards and slow worms.

The fire service has released a video showing blackened trees and scorched ground across parts of the nature reserve.

Gulliver praised the local community for opening their homes to evacuees, saying only a small number of people had needed to stay in the rest centre overnight.

He thanked the people running the village hall: “They’ve been absolutely brilliant at looking after everyone, so I want to stress my thanks and gratitude to everyone involved.”

Speaking to residents, Gulliver said firefighters were containing the blaze by flooding trenches with water and using helicopters to drop thousands of litres of seawater.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said Suffolk’s fire service would have “all of the support” it needed to tackle the wildfire.

The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, called for Burnham to host an emergency Cobra meeting to discuss wildfires across Britain, including the Suffolk blaze.

According to the Met Office, Suffolk has received only 2% of its average July rainfall so far. Other counties have recorded as little as 1% – or even none – of their typical rainfall for the month.

articles.title: At least 18 die as thousands of migrants reach Spain’s African enclave of Cueta – Europe live
articles.excerpt:
PM Pedro Sánchez expected to visit territory today as Italy demands Spain be suspended from the Schengen area amid concerns over fresh migration crisis

The opposition People’s party (PP) is calling o...
articles.body_text:
PM Pedro Sánchez expected to visit territory today as Italy demands Spain be suspended from the Schengen area amid concerns over fresh migration crisis

The opposition People’s party (PP) is calling on Sánchez to produce a swift and tough response, saying the small military and police reinforcements announced last night are insufficient.

The PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, is not dialling down his language.

“People have continued to arrive in Ceuta throughout the night, and those on the ground describe an occupied city, with nothing sufficient being done to prevent it,” he’s just posted on X.

“In Melilla, too, around 400 irregulars have entered. I insist that Sánchez must defend our national security, our territorial integrity, and our coexistence.

As prime minister, he has instruments and means at his disposal, and all that remains is for him to give the orders.

As serious as what is happening is the fact that the Government is reacting with this weakness. All of Spain stands with Ceuta and Melilla.”

The far-right Vox party, meanwhile, is calling the influx “an invasion”.

The Spanish interior ministry has just said that more than 49,000 people are believed to have swum or walked into Ceuta over the past 24 hours.

That, obviously is a huge number, and dwarves the 10,000 people who entered the territory during the border crisis in 2021.

That mass crossing came amid heightened tensions between Madrid and Rabat over Spain’s decision to allow a western Sahara independence leader to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain.

To give some perspective, the population of Ceuta is around 85,000.

The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, is en route to Ceuta, where he is expected to visit the Tarajal border and speak to the media some time after midday local time.

At least 18 people died as thousands of migrants breached the Spanish-Moroccan border in Cueta yesterday, prompting concerns about a fresh migration crisis and questions over the implications for the European Union.

A spokesperson for the Guardia Civil force, which polices Spain’s borders, said ⁠the migrants were “massively entering from the sea” through the Tarajal breakwater, but could not provide an estimate of the numbers.

Spain’s interior minister said on Friday that it estimated some 49,000 migrants crossed into Cueta over the past 24 hours.

More people were reported crossing into the enclave over night, with Spanish media reporting “passivity” from the Moroccan police.

In response, the Spanish government is deploying extra troops and police officers to protect the border between the tiny African enclave and neighbouring Morocco. Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez is expected to visit the territory later today.

But the fresh migration crisis sparked also a conflict within the European Union as Italian authorities demanded Spain to be suspended from open border Schengen area until they restore control.

In a rare direct clash between two EU countries, Italy’s far-right prime minister Giorgia Meloni angrily said that pictures coming from Cueta demonstrated that “uncontrolled illegal immigration poses a concrete threat to the security of Europe’s borders.”

“Italy will not stand by and watch. … We are prepared to intervene with extraordinary measures to defend the borders and the safety of citizens, including the suspension of the Schengen Area with Spain,” she said.

Italian foreign minister Antonio Tajani backed her calls, saying he was in favour of Spain’s suspension, and linking the migration crisis with a recent decision with the Spanish government’s decision to regularise over 500,000 undocumented migrants resident in Spain.

In response, Spanish foreign minister José Manuel Albares said the Italian comments were “unbecoming of a foreign minister of a partner and friendly country” dismissing them as “partisan demagoguery,” and said he would summon the Italian ambassador to Madrid on Friday.

Instead, he linked the influx of migrants with a recent decision by Spain’s supreme court saying that migrants intercepted at sea while attempting to reach Ceuta or Melilla could not be summarily returned under the enclaves’ special border rejection regime.

I will bring you all the updates as the day progresses.

It’s Friday, 31 July 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: Middle East crisis live: Trump claims Gaza deal reached; Iran targets US bases in Kuwait

Response from Hamas and Israeli officials suggest Gaza deal still faces obstacles; Tehran launches drone strikes at Kuwait in retaliation for recent US attacks

Trump claims agreement for ‘complete di...
articles.body_text:
Response from Hamas and Israeli officials suggest Gaza deal still faces obstacles; Tehran launches drone strikes at Kuwait in retaliation for recent US attacks

Trump claims agreement for ‘complete disarmament’ of Hamas in Gaza but support uncertain

Saudi Arabia prepares sea and possible land offensive against Houthis

Donald Trump claims a deal has been reached for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its forces from Gaza, but many hurdles and conditions remained in the Palestinian territory.

“The agreement will be carried out in carefully structured phases,” the US president said on social media. “As disarmament is completed, Israeli forces will withdraw, and the International Stabilization Force will work with a new Palestinian police force to take responsibility for Gaza being safe for its residents and its neighbors.”

Senior Hamas officials have reportedly agreed to the plan, but the question of whether the group disarms before or after Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza has already emerged as a point of contention. “We will not take any action regarding disarmament prior to Israel’s withdrawal from the Strip,” Ghazi Hamad, a member of the Hamas negotiating team, told ​Al Jazeera.

Earlier an Israeli official told the Reuters news agency that the proposed terms were not satisfactory.

“Israel demands the complete disarmament of Hamas, including ​the removal of weapons from Gaza and the complete demilitarisation of the Strip as a precondition for ‌any process,” the official said, adding that the plan under discussion did not “provide a satisfactory response to these demands and Israel conveyed its objections”.

The announcement comes nine months after a US-brokered ceasefire was signed. Negotiations between Israel and Hamas had largely deadlocked over the implementation of its second phase, including the disarmament of Hamas and the reconstruction of Gaza.

In the US-Israeli war on Iran, which is showing signs of escalating across the region, Iran’s army on Friday launched drone strikes at US military facilities at the Ahmad Al Jaber airbase in Kuwait. The strikes were in response to recent US attacks on Iran including a strike on a home in Qeshm, Iran’s state media reported.

And Saudi Arabia is preparing for a major military offensive against the Houthis by sea and possibly by land in central Yemen, Yemeni sources believe, in a move to break the chokehold on its oil exports through the southern Red Sea.

Twenty-five commodities vessels passed through the ⁠Bab el-Mandeb strait on Thursday, while traffic through the strait ⁠of Hormuz ⁠remained ​low with only two tankers transiting, according to Kpler shipping ⁠data.

Analysts are expecting major oil companies to report large profits while fighting between Iran and the US impeded petroleum shipments. Six of Europe’s largest oil companies have posted first-quarter profits of $22bn altogether, a total 43% higher than the same time last year, according to Global Witness.

Saudi Arabia on Thursday said it had set up a maritime defence alliance of 14 regional countries to secure navigation around the Bab al-Mandab strait.

An Iranian strike hit a Chinese firm’s building in Kuwait on Thursday, severely damaging the structure and killing a worker, Kuwait’s military said, hours after Jordan’s air defences shot down five missiles launched from Iran.

Egypt’s government said on Thursday authorities were analysing drone fragments from an unprecedented strike on one of its ports, after President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi warned of regional escalation. His government had earlier confirmed that a fire on two gas vessels in the Damietta port – one of which was US-owned – was a result of a drone strike, the first to target the country since the outbreak of the Middle East war.

Reuters has issued some news alerts after speaking to a Hamas official about the next phase of the Gaza ceasefire, including disarmament.

The news agency reported the official saying Israel must withdraw its forces from Gaza, and that if it does not approve the accord then Hamas will not implement it. Israel has yet to publicly say anything about the deal.

We are getting some of the first international reactions of the supposed Gaza deal announced by Donald Trump.

In the UK, Louise Haigh, who runs the new office of the prime minister, said any progress in peace negotiations is “extremely welcome” while the government awaits Israel’s response.

“It’s extremely welcome news if there has been any progress in the peace negotiations and any step forward to disarming Hamas,” she told BBC Breakfast.

“Obviously, we will need to await the Israeli government’s response and its commitment to the ceasefire and a way forward and a withdrawal from Gaza, and to cease its activities of settler violence and taking action against such settler violence in the West Bank.

“But if progress has been made, then it’s extremely welcome news, because the suffering in Gaza and the wider region has been too extreme for far too long, and the human cost of the war has been absolutely obscene and intolerable.”

She added: “We’re awaiting the response from the Israeli government, so we’ll set out the details in due course of our wider government response.”

Meanwhile, in Lebanon, local media reported “massive explosions” overnight in the southern parts of the country, where Israeli forces say they have blasted an underground tunnel network belonging to Hezbollah.

Lebanon’s official National News Agency (NNA) reported explosions in Yahmar al-Shaqif, Arnoun and Kfar Tebnit, all areas close to the Beaufort Ridge that is occupied by the Israeli military.

The explosions began at about midnight and “reverberated with tremendous and unprecedented force throughout the entire south”, NNA reported.

A correspondent for the news agency said the blasts near Beaufort Castle, the 900-year-old castle and strategic ridge captured by Israeli troops in May, had “caused the windows of a number of houses in the town of al-Qlailah to shatter, due to the force of the blasts and the tremors felt by residents across the region”.

The report added: “The explosions caused damage to some homes, while residents reported that the sound of the blasts was intense, accompanied by a powerful shock wave that shook the town, as well as the smell of gunpowder in the air.”

In a post on X, the Israel Defense Force (IDF) said it “destroyed several key features in the underground tunnel network” in the Beaufort Ridge area. It claimed that the tunnel network, located about 6km (just under 4 miles) from the Israeli town of Metula across the border, was built over 20 years and consisted of several levels, serving as a “central terror headquarters for [Hezbollah’s] “Badir” unit in southern Lebanon, which was funded and planned by the Iranian terror regime”.

“The existence of the infrastructure posed a threat to the residents of the north [of Israel] and to our forces,” the IDF said.

“Over the past weeks, IDF forces have completed their hold on the Beaufort Ridge area, while controlling and clearing the underground infrastructures and preparing them for destruction.”

More now on Iran’s military saying it launched drone strikes targeting US military facilities in Kuwait on Friday, as fighting between Washington and Tehran resumed after a nearly week-long lull.

The army said it targeted “fighter aircraft shelters, satellite communications systems and equipment storage facilities at Ahmad al-Jaber air base in Kuwait”.

There was no immediate comment from the US military’s Central Command.

The Iranian army said in a statement the strikes came in response to US military’s recent aggression and “brutal attack” on a residential home on Qeshm Island, Agence France-Presse reports.

Local media reported on Thursday that three members of a family were killed in US strikes on the island in the strait of Hormuz.

The US military earlier said it had carried out a “heavy wave of strikes” against Iran.

Qeshm Island is a storage site for Iranian attack craft, drones, sea mines and other materials used to disrupt shipping through the Hormuz strait and has come under frequent American attack.

articles.title: BP to sell North Sea business; AI companies lead record surge on Korea’s stock market – business live
articles.excerpt:
Live, rolling coverage as British oil company looks for buyer amid political dispute over future drilling licences

The FTSE 100 has gained 0.7% in the first half hour of trading, which means… drum ro...
articles.body_text:
Live, rolling coverage as British oil company looks for buyer amid political dispute over future drilling licences

The FTSE 100 has gained 0.7% in the first half hour of trading, which means… drum roll… its latest record high.

The new high-water mark is 10,981.83 this morning. We shall see if the index can reach the “psychologically important” (i.e., meaningless) 11,000 mark today.

Up there among the winners this morning is NatWest Group. The bank is up 3.6% after upgrading its financial outlook and share buyback plans after revealing a jump in profits. The Polar Capital investment trust, which has exposure to AI companies, is the top gainer, up 4.3%.

Those chemical leak costs and paused share buyback have put Melrose Industries at the bottom of the index this morning.

Melrose shares are down 6.3%, making it the biggest faller on London’s blue-chip index. Spreadbetting platform IG Group is down 5% after publishing financial results and revealing a plan to buy US fantasy sports business Underdog.

Aerospace company Melrose Industries has paused its share buybacks as it waits for potential legal and regulatory action over a leaking chemical tank in California.

The company’s GKN Aerospace business said the tank at its Garden Grove facility was leaking methyl methacrylate, a flammable chemical used in the acrylic for windows for the F-35 fighter jet and passenger cabin windows on commercial aircraft, because it was overheating. The local area had to be evacuated in case the tank exploded (which it did not).

Melrose on Friday said the was “back to partial production” after the chemical tank incident at the end of May, and that it was “working closely with relevant authorities and customers to safely resume full production”.

However, the company paused its £175m share buyback, “pending clarification of financial impact of the Garden Grove incident, including from ongoing regulatory and legal processes”.

Peter Dilnot, chief executive of Melrose Industries, said:

double quotation markWe are managing the situation at our Garden Grove transparencies site following the incident in May. Partial production has since resumed, and we will continue to work closely with customers, regulators and other authorities to safely restore the site to full production in the second half.

The incident has already cost the company £16m in lost revenues, plus another £13m in exceptional costs. It will have another £25m to £30m in costs in the second half of the year.

Economic uncertainty dampened UK house price growth in July as prospective house buyers remained cautious about interest rates amid the ongoing US war with Iran in what should be peak housebuying season.

House prices rose by just 0.1% in July from a month earlier, according to lender Nationwide, while annual price growth slowed to 1.8% this month, down from 2.2% in June.

The UK’s biggest building society said the price of an average home edged slightly higher in July to £277,542, up from £277,484 the previous month. However, this is still lower than the average price recorded in May, when it rose above £278,000.

Robert Gardner, chief economist at Nationwide, said:

double quotation markMarket activity and house prices have remained soft in recent months, in part reflecting the uncertain economic backdrop. Geopolitical tensions remain high, with the conflict between Iran and the US again exerting upward pressure on energy prices and market interest rates in recent weeks.

Financial market expectations for the future path of Bank Rate have been volatile, reflecting shifting views about the inflationary implications of events at home and abroad.

The owner of British Airways has reported a steep fall in profits and said it expects no growth in passenger capacity this year as the US-Israeli war in Iran takes its toll.

International Airlines Group (IAG) said it expected demand to stay strong, but added that its “disciplined cost control” could only partly mitigate the impact of “a significant fuel price increase” caused by the attacks on Iran. Iran closed the strait of Hormuz in response to the attacks, a key export route for oil from the Gulf.

The company, which also owns Iberia and Aer Lingus, among others, said that it was a “resilient revenue performance despite lower capacity than planned”.

Revenue increased in the first half of 2026 by 1% to €16bn, while profit after tax fell 21% to €1bn.

Luis Gallego, IAG’s chief executive, said:

double quotation markWith these results IAG has again demonstrated that its excellent fundamentals are supporting continued value creation for our shareholders, despite the impact of the crisis in the Middle East and wider geopolitical events.

Good morning, and welcome to our live coverage of business, economics and financial markets.

BP has put its North Sea oil business up for sale, saying it will try to find a buyer amid a political dispute over whether the UK government should allow more drilling.

Prime minister Andy Burnham on Thursday signalled that he would be open to more extraction in the North Sea, although he did not make clear if that would mean new licences or allowing expanded use of existing wells.

BP, one of the biggest companies on the FTSE 100, said it was selling the North Sea business as part of an ongoing portfolio review under American chief executive Meg O’Neill. The American was appointed in December with a remit to refocus the company after a tumultuous period of three chief executives in three years.

The company said it wanted to direct the spending required on the North Sea to other places which could offer higher financial returns.

double quotation markThe UK has been our home for more than 100 years and will continue to play an important role in our future. We’re proud of the jobs we create, the contribution we make to the UK economy, and the work we do to keep energy flowing every day.

The North Sea remains integral to the UK’s energy system. However, as we focus our portfolio and direct capital to our highest-value opportunities, we believe our North Sea business will be better positioned as part of another company. It has world-class people, resilient assets and a proud heritage, and it is precisely these qualities that can attract an owner ready to back its next chapter. We are seeking an outcome that recognises that value.

The question of whether to allow more North Sea drilling has become politically contentious in recent months. Environmental campaigners are aghast that Labour is considering allowing more drilling for planet-heating fossil fuels, but Burnham appears to have decided it would be more useful to drill at a time of high energy prices.

Donald Trump revealed Burnham’s plans after a first phone call between the US president and the new prime minister. Burnham later told reporters:

double quotation markI indicated in the phone call that we had, a week last Monday, that I would take a pragmatic approach when it comes to the North Sea, and that is my intention as we go forward from here.

There is a resource there. When people are struggling, we can’t ignore that. Hence, me indicating that to the president.

South Korea’s stock market has been going through a period of turbulence for the ages thanks to the AI boom – and fears it will bust. It continued on Friday, with the largest single-day increase in the benchmark Kospi index’s history.

Korea’s Kospi is up an astonishing 17.91% today. It fell 11% on Tuesday – just shy of the record 12.06% decline hit in early March in the first days of the Iran war – and 6% on Wednesday.

Global stock markets have been dominated in recent months by artificial intelligence companies. But Korea’s stock market does not have the depth of the US, meaning its AI-exposed chip companies are even more dominant. The share price of chipmaker SK Hynix soared 30% on Friday, while Samsung Electronics was up 28%.

Over the last 12 months the index is up 104%, but over the last one month it is down 20%. In this wild week it has dropped a mere 1.1% – all that sound and fury, signifying nearly nothing. These are not normal moves.

Sergi Lanau, director of emerging markets strategy at Oxford Economics, said that “We believe sentiment is still frothy in Korea”, citing the size of assets in leveraged exchange-traded funds (ETFs), which use debt to pump up returns. He said:

double quotation markAlthough we believe the AI buildout still has legs, we expect burned leveraged traders in Korea to continue to exit the market, keeping it under pressure. That’s sufficient reason to lower our weight on the broader emerging market complex to neutral.

Korea’s authorities have this week sought to tighten restrictions on leveraged ETFs, although given the wild swings some investors will already be ruing the day they bought them.

10am BST: Eurozone inflation rate (July; previous: 2.8%; consensus: 2.9%)

articles.title: ‘Rob has the bucks cash’: NSW Liberals used Reformers funds to pay for ‘personal expenditure’, Icac hears
articles.excerpt:
Robert Assaf separately tells anti-corruption inquiry money funnelled through lobbying firm to create ‘maximum benefit from a tax perspective’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

...
articles.body_text:
Robert Assaf separately tells anti-corruption inquiry money funnelled through lobbying firm to create ‘maximum benefit from a tax perspective’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A group of young conservative Liberal power brokers accused of soliciting illegal donations used some of the funds to pay for a bucks night, one of its members has told a corruption inquiry.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday heard again from Robert Assaf, who this week was the first witness from the conservative right Liberal factional group the Reformers to give evidence.

The inquiry is investigating allegations that the Reformers solicited or accepted illegal donations to recruit or renew members to the party – a practice known as “branch stacking”. The group wanted more conservative policies on same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia.

The counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC asked Assaf about a decision to move alleged payments from prohibited donor Michael O’Hara from a bank account in the Reformers’ name to Beckington, a registered lobbying firm set up by the group and run by member Christian Ellis.

O’Hara earlier this week admitted to a fake arrangement in which he paid Beckington for “strategic wealth strategy investment advice”. He disputed whether the payments to the Reformers were to the NSW Liberals or should be considered political donations.

On Friday, Assaf said funnelling money through Beckington rather than the Reformers account was to create “the maximum benefit from a tax perspective”.

Dwyer replied: “That’s an explanation that you thought of overnight. Is that right?”

Asked if he was aware that it was illegal to minimise tax by creating fake invoices, Assaf said he knew that now, but not at the time. Asked if he thought the arrangement was “dishonest”, he said: “I would have thought it was tricky.”

Assaf admitted to temporarily using funds from the Reformers account to pay for a bucks night.

In a WhatsApp message to the group in August 2020, Reformer Jean-Claude Perrottet, the brother of former premier Dominic Perrottet, wrote: “Rob has the bucks cash coming back.”

Asked what this meant, Assaf said: “I think you recall I referred to us being immature and young, using the account as an advance on our personal expenditure.”

“This was one of those moments where we, I think, we had booked a venue for either my bucks or Christian [Ellis’s] bucks. It required an upfront payment.”

“I think it was cancelled, maybe because of Covid, one of them, so it was waiting for it to get reimbursed.”

He also said he had make fake invoices to Beckington in the name of his wife, Carmel Assaf, but did not agree that this was to reimburse him for Reformers work. He said he had done so to claim a 10% fee promised to him for finding new clients for Ellis.

The commission heard Assaf was employed in communications at Catholic Schools NSW, the governing body for 600 schools in the state, in 2019, alongside Reformers associate Dylan Whitelaw, who gave evidence earlier in the week.

The Catholic Schools NSW chief executive, Dallas McInerney, is alleged to have arranged and approved payments to the group to support branch stacking efforts through Beckington, where Whitelaw later came to be employed.

Assaf disputed an earlier claim made by Whitelaw that he spent 60% of his time at Catholic Schools NSW on factional work, saying it was more like 10 to 20%. But he said he would sometimes “chuck a sickie” to do Reformers work.

Under questioning from Dwyer, Assaf admitted that he knew that money being paid to Beckington was to fund work that Whitelaw was doing for the Reformers. “I knew that, yes,” Assaf told the hearing.

The inquiry heard that Assaf’s friendship with Ellis later broke down.

The inquiry heard that when McInerney allegedly wanted to end the relationship with Beckington in 2021, Assaf provided the former with advice about it on “multiple” occasions.

“[That advice] would have been something like: ‘Christian’s a liar. He’s greedy. I don’t trust him, and I’m not sure he’s doing much for you at the moment,” he said.

The inquiry on Friday returned to whether the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, had knowledge of and supported the Reformers.

Assaf said he recalled sending a screenshot of a message from McInerney in which he said he wanted to “shake down Angus for 10K”, and reading a message sent by Whitelaw in which he claimed McInerney had received “the commitment from Angus, the 15k injection plus a 3k monthly donation”, but denied any donation had taken place.

“I don’t think Angus worked out,” Assaf said. Taylor, who is not accused of wrongdoing, on Friday again denied making payments to the group.

The Icac presiding commissioner, Fabian Gleeson, intervened on multiple occasions during Assaf’s evidence. Before the lunch break, Gleeson told Assaf he had become “a bit argumentative in your response”.

“I believe they call that hangry commissioner,” Assaf said.

Gleeson said: “I’m not aware of what young people’s speak is these days, Mr Assaf. What I’d like you to do is to sit there, concentrate, and answer a further question which council assisting has, and then we’ll adjourn. Understand?”

Assaf was expected to appear again on Monday, before the commission is scheduled to hear from the NSW shadow attorney general and Liberal leader in the upper house, Damien Tudehope.

Many of the Reformers worked as staffers in Tudehope’s office, and Tudehope gave frequent talks at Reformers recruitment events. O’Hara is his former business partner.

Tudehope, who has stood aside from his shadow cabinet roles during the inquiry, is not accused of wrongdoing.

The inquiry will also hear from Jean-Claude Perrottet and Jeremy Greenwood, both named in Icac’s allegations. The watchdog heard on Thursday that Jean-Claude Perrottet allegedly paid for memberships as part of branch-stacking efforts, forbidden under Liberal party rules.

He has previously denied any wrongdoing, while Dominic Perrottet is not accused of wrongdoing.

articles.title: AC Milan and Italy great Baresi dies aged 66
articles.excerpt:
Franco Baresi became captain of AC Milan at the age of 22

Franco Baresi has died at the age of 66, with AC Milan saying their former captain's "example and integrity will be forever etched into the c...
articles.body_text:
Franco Baresi became captain of AC Milan at the age of 22

Franco Baresi has died at the age of 66, with AC Milan saying their former captain's "example and integrity will be forever etched into the club's DNA".

Baresi spent his entire 20-year playing career with the club from 1977 until he retired in 1997, winning six Serie A titles and three European Cups/Champions Leagues.

Regarded as one of the greatest defenders to play the game, Baresi captained Milan for 15 seasons, making 719 appearances and scoring 33 goals.

He was capped 81 times by Italy and was part of the squad which won the 1982 World Cup. He played in the 1994 final, which Italy lost to Brazil.

In 2020, Baresi became honorary vice-president of AC Milan, with the club retiring his number six shirt four years later.

Baresi formed part of one of European football's most celebrated defences alongside Paolo Maldini, Alessandro Costacurta and Mauro Tassotti.

He also lifted four Supercoppa Italianas, two European Super Cups and the Intercontinental Cup twice.

In the 1994 World Cup, he returned from a knee injury to play in the final and largely nullified the threat of Brazil's Romario and Bebeto in a 0-0 draw.

It was the first World Cup final to be decided by a shootout and Baresi missed the first penalty, with Brazil eventually winning it 3-2.

Baresi had surgery in August 2025 to remove a lung nodule, and his last public appearance was at the San Siro Stadium for the Winter Olympics opening ceremony in February.

In a statement on X, AC Milan wrote: "Milan is in tears following the passing of Franco Baresi. His example and integrity will be forever etched into the club's DNA, just as his iconic number 6 shirt is."

In a further post on the club's website,, external they added: "Announcing the loss of someone who embodied the heart and soul of AC Milan is incredibly difficult. But everyone at the club and all the Milanisti must live up to Franco Baresi's memory.

"In memory of Franco, we stand united, knowing he'll guide and push us throughout our Rossoneri journey. Forever. Because Baresi is forever."

Listen to the latest Football Daily podcast
