articles.body_text:
Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd arrested a Washington, D.C.-based basketball coach and five teen players after they allegedly shoplifted from a Florida 7-Eleven in the middle of the night. The coach, Malik Harvey, also faces charges for lying to deputies about the players' identities. A mother of one of the players cooperated with authorities.

Ten members of a Pennsylvania high school football team, including several coaches, face charges after a player was allegedly stomped with cleats, and jabbed in the buttocks with a broomstick.

According to the Montgomery County District Attorney's Office, a 15-year-old player was allegedly assaulted on two separate occasions in 2025 by teammates from Cheltenham High School.

Prosecutors said the first incident happened on Aug. 15, 2025, and was recorded by two juvenile players, then shared with students and other teammates over the following semester.

RITZY PRIVATE ACADEMY ATTENDED BY KARDASHIAN KIDS FACES TRIAL IN BIZARRE 'KISSING CLUB' SCANDAL

Isaiah Simpson, 18, was charged with conspiracy to commit aggravated assault, simple assault, recklessly endangering another person and related charges. (CSD Cheltenham High School)

During the alleged Aug. 15 incident, prosecutors said that the video recording showed several football players using a broomstick to poke the victim's buttocks, and also showed other juvenile teammates holding him down. No coaches were present during the Aug. 15 incident.

Several witnesses allegedly saw Isaiah Simpson, 18, kicking or stomping on the victim during the second incident on Sept. 3, 2025.

The same juvenile from the Aug. 15 incident used a broomstick to poke at the victim's butt, according to the grand jury filing.

SJSU VOLLEYBALL COACH'S ALLEGED ASSAULT VICTIM SPEAKS OUT FOR THE FIRST TIME SINCE ALLEGATIONS SURFACED

The victim told investigators that during the Sept. 3 incident, he curled into a ball in his football equipment to shield his head while others allegedly kicked, stomped and punched him in the head and groin with cleats.

The coaches, again, weren't involved in the Sept. 3 incident but four coaches would later learn about it, according to authorities.

Simpson was charged with conspiracy to commit aggravated assault, simple assault, recklessly endangering another person and related charges. Another football player, Josiah Peeler, 18, was charged with false swearing. Four other football players were charged, but their names weren't released as they're juveniles.

SJSU DIDN'T PENALIZE VOLLEYBALL COACH DURING TRANS SCANDAL AMID TITLE IX COMPLAINTS, FEDERAL FINDINGS ALLEGE

Cheltenham High School head football coach Terence Tolbert, 55, faces charges of conspiracy to endanger the welfare of a child and endangering the welfare of a child. (Facebook/Terence Tolbert)

Volunteer coach Ralph Burnley, 60, gave the victim a ride home after practice when he learned that the player was "jumped" and injured in his genital area. Burnley then called head coach Terence Tolbert, 55, and told him what happened.

Text messages between coaches followed that call, leading to a group call with the victim. Assistant coach Darian "DJ" McFadden, 42, and Tolbert allegedly told the victim the matter would be handled and asked him not to tell his mother about the incident.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Assistant coach Benjamin Johnson III, 45, allegedly joined other coaches in a decision to keep the matter in-house rather than alert the school or the boy's mother, fearing it could jeopardize the team.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Josiah Peeler, 18, was charged with false swearing in connection with the Cheltenham High School football hazing case. (CSD Cheltenham High School)

The coaches were hit with charges of conspiracy to endanger the welfare of a child and endangering the welfare of a child.

The victim's mother learned of the second alleged attack shortly afterward from a relative who had heard about it from other parents. She then took the victim to the hospital, where he was diagnosed with a contusion to his penis.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

High school administrators learned of the alleged hazing through an anonymous reporting app, called police and then canceled the football team's season.

Montgomery County District Attorney Kevin Steele said, "These assaults on a football player were not the typical goofing around by teammates. These were crimes."

"Numerous witnesses, many reluctant to share what they saw and knew, testified about what occurred in the Cheltenham High School locker room on these two occasions and testified about actions taken by some of the football coaches after the assaults," he said. "After carefully considering all of the testimony and evidence, including reviewing the recovered videos of one of the assaults, the Grand Jury recommended charges against the four juveniles, two other football players and four coaches."

Adam Sabes is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Adam.Sabes@fox.com and on Twitter @asabes10.

articles.title: 'Hot seat rankings' for all 16 SEC coaches as beginning of 2026 college football season draws nearer
articles.excerpt:
Trey Wallace explains why Lane Kiffin has such lofty expectations put on him for his first year of coaching at LSU.

At the beginning of every college football season, there are always a few questions...
articles.body_text:
Trey Wallace explains why Lane Kiffin has such lofty expectations put on him for his first year of coaching at LSU.

At the beginning of every college football season, there are always a few questions that are on every fan's mind.

One of which is "who looks like they can win it all every season," but since I already addressed that earlier this week, I'm here to tackle the second most popular question: which coaches are on the hot seat heading into fall?

More specifically, I wanted to look at every coach from the SEC and give them a "hot seat ranking" based on their job security in 2026.

PERCEPTION IS REALITY, AND THE SEC NEEDS TO START WINNING AGAIN BEFORE IT CONTINUES TO PUFF OUT ITS CHEST

I will be lumping all 16 SEC coaches into one of five categories that should give everyone an idea of where these guys stand before the start of the season.

We have a lot to get to, so let's get this hot seat party started.

Head coach Pete Golding of the Ole Miss Rebels looks on in the first half against the Miami Hurricanes during the College Football Playoff Semifinal at the VRBO Fiesta Bowl at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Ariz., on Jan. 8, 2026. (Getty Images)

The SEC has six "new" coaches among its ranks in 2026, and the reason I put a heavy set of quotations around that word is because some of these guys have already been coaches in the conference.

Obviously, Lane Kiffin was previously at Ole Miss for six years and even had an infamous stop in Knoxville for one season to coach the Tennessee Vols, but if we want to get technical, the Rebels have a "returning" SEC coach of their own in Pete Golding.

The colorful successor to Kiffin in Oxford guided Ole Miss to the College Football Playoff semifinals in 2025, but 2026 will be his first full season, so I'm including him here.

None of these guys are getting fired in their first season, so they earned themselves a ranking almost completely removed from the rest of the guys on this list.

THREE SEC WIN TOTALS YOU SHOULD ABSOLUTELY POUNCE ON BEFORE THE 2026 COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON BEGINS

Sure, if Kiffin has a first-year implosion and finishes 6-6, he will certainly be sitting on a blazing hot seat coming into 2027, but no one else is even close to that talk right now.

Enjoy it, men. Odds are you will never feel this secure in your job again.

Georgia coach Kirby Smart reacts to a play during the first half of the team's NCAA college football game against South Carolina on Saturday, Sept. 18, 2021, in Athens, Ga. (AP Photo/Butch Dill)

The seat can't get much colder than this, and ironically enough, these two coaches sit on opposite ends of the royalty spectrum in the SEC.

Kirby Smart has earned every bit of the job security he has going for him, as the Georgia Bulldogs head coach enters year 11 of his storied career in Athens.

In 2021, the man delivered a national championship 40 years in the making to a starving fanbase then followed it up with another the very next year just for good measure.

Though Georgia fans aren't thrilled with their recent lack of CFP success, the Dawgs are still reigning SEC champs and look like the favorites to win the league again in 2026, so Kirby's seat is ice cold.

For Clark Lea, just the fact that he had Vandy of all programs knocking on the door of the Playoff last season means his seat couldn't get any colder.

For crying out loud, the man won ten games at Vanderbilt, something no coach has ever done in program history.

When you couple that with the fact that guys like Diego Pavia, Eli Stowers, and a smattering of offensive linemen aren't in Nashville anymore, fans rightly expect the Commodores to take a step back in '26, cooling the seat even more for Lea.

Vandy could go 2-10 this year and I still don't think Clark Lea will be packing his bags. Now THAT'S job security.

Texas Longhorns head coach Steve Sarkisian walks into Camping World Stadium ahead of the Citrus Bowl against the Michigan Wolverines in Orlando, Fla., on Dec. 31, 2025. (aAustin American-Statesman via Getty Images)

These three coaches are sitting on some pretty cool seats, all things considered.

While the situations aren't perfect, they can't get much better for at least two of the three names in this category.

Mike Elko led the Texas A&M Aggies to an 11-win season and a Playoff berth, and for a fanbase desperate to shed those pre-World War II championship taunts, it feels like a step in the right direction.

When you pair the winning with A&M's historic recruiting class that is brewing for 2027, Elko is as cool as a cucumber.

The same goes for Eli Drinkwitz, who experienced a bit of a step back in 2025, but still won eight games and has things trending up in Columbia.

Drinkwitz earned a massive extension after being courted by a few big boy job openings like Florida and Penn State, and while that doesn't always guarantee job security (as I'll explain later), it is a nice bonus to help keep the seat cool.

Steve Sarkisian is the outlier here, as I almost put him in the next category.

I don't believe Sark is in any danger of losing his job, hence the cool seat, but the expectations for this season are so high that, should he fail to deliver, we could be having an entirely different conversation 365 days from now.

But that hasn't happened yet, so for now, Sark and Texas are rolling and 2025 should be considered just a minor blip on the radar.

Tennessee head coach Josh Heupel yells to an official during the first half of an NCAA college football game against Georgia , Saturday, Nov. 16, 2024, in Athens, Ga. (AP Photo/John Bazemore)

Things start warming up in this category; perhaps these coaches are starting to sweat through their team-issued polos.

No coach in this category is in any immediate danger of being fired during the 2026 season, but a bad start could really raise those temperatures in a hurry.

For three of the four coaches here, it's all about expectations.

DeBoer, Heupel, and Venables have all been solid to very good throughout most of their tenures at their respective schools.

The problem is that all three are at programs that demand excellence.

DeBoer in particular is standing in the shadow of perhaps the biggest giant to ever coach in the Southeastern Conference, and although he just signed an extension to stay in Tuscaloosa, having an empty trophy case with regard to SEC and national championships is starting to make the natives very restless.

Another season without a deep Playoff run could send DeBoer packing.

Heupel's rope is a touch longer than Venables', given that this year is supposed to be a ramp-up for what should be a loaded 2027 roster in Knoxville, but the Vols have zero Playoff wins entering year six of his tenure.

Finally, Jeff Lebby probably deserves to be in the tier above this one, especially since the Bulldogs were a barren wasteland of talent when he came to town and they were a few plays away from potentially being an eight or nine-win team last year.

But another sub-.500 season will almost certainly give even the most patient fans and boosters in Starkville a reason to start looking for the exit door of the Lebby era.

South Carolina Gamecocks head coach Shane Beamer takes the field with his team before a game against the Wofford Terriers at Williams-Brice Stadium on Nov. 23, 2024. (Jeff Blake/ Imagn Images)

I wrote an article last month about how you could make the argument that Shane Beamer's seat is the hottest in the country, and that includes a man by the name of Mike Norvell.

Beamer's seat is radioactive heading into the 2026 season, and much of that has to do with that dirty word, "expectations," again.

South Carolina was a dark-horse candidate to make the College Football Playoff last season and ended up face-planting to the tune of a 4-8 campaign.

A similar 4-8 season for a CFP hopeful in Florida cost Billy Napier his job, so another subpar record in 2026 could spell doom for Beamer and co.

The Gamecocks have an incendiary talent at quarterback in LaNorris Sellers, a freak athlete at wide receiver in Nyck Harbor, and an all-conference selection and future first-round draft pick at edge rusher in Dylan Stewart, so the pieces are in place, at least in theory, to have a good bounce-back year.

Anything less than 8-4 is probably a massive disappointment in Columbia, and I could honestly see Beamer being shown the door if South Carolina isn't at least 4-2 by the time their bye week rolls around.

The SEC is a cutthroat league, and Beamer could end up being the latest casualty before the season is even over.

articles.title: ‘To play God’: Cuba’s healthcare system collapses under US pressure
articles.excerpt:
As President Donald Trump tightens US sanctions against Cuba, the island's healthcare providers warn of medical shortages and rising death rates.

Havana, Cuba – It used to be a point of pride. At the...
articles.body_text:
As President Donald Trump tightens US sanctions against Cuba, the island's healthcare providers warn of medical shortages and rising death rates.

Havana, Cuba – It used to be a point of pride. At the William Soler Pediatric Hospital in Havana, more than 90 percent of the newborns who needed neonatal surgery survived their procedures.

But in recent months, Alioth Fernandez, the head of the hospital's surgical unit and anaesthesiology department, has witnessed an alarming decline.

“Now, that figure has plummeted,” Fernandez said. “In the first half of this year, we have seen very high mortality among newborns needing surgery, with more than half of the cases resulting in death.”

Fernandez is among a growing number of doctors and patients in Cuba expressing alarm over the deteriorating healthcare conditions across the island.

Six months ago, on January 29, United States President Donald Trump announced a fuel blockade against Cuba, threatening any country that exports fuel to the island with punishing tariffs.

The aim was to weaken Cuba's government, which Trump labelled a national security threat. Only one foreign oil tanker has reached Cuba in the months since.

The result has been nearly daily blackouts that last up to 20 hours, as well as shortages of essential items.

The pressure has exacerbated strains on Cuba's healthcare system, once considered the flagship achievement of the country's 1959 revolution.

Although healthcare in Cuba remains free, public and universal, experts say its reach and quality have diminished significantly. That has translated to a cost in human lives. Fernandez is seeing the toll of the political conflict firsthand in his young patients.

“Children are the least to blame,” Fernandez said. “Because children certainly have no ideology, nor did they ask to be born in a ‘communist’ country.”

For Fernandez, the most distressing part has been how avoidable some of the deaths have been.

Many did not occur as the result of surgical complications but rather from infections, driven by diminished hygiene standards, malnutrition and the limited availability of antibiotics.

In the past, Fernandez explained, patients were added to a waiting list for procedures, based on their medical conditions and the date of their arrival for treatment. Names rarely stayed on the list for more than a month. Backlogs were systematically cleared.

But with limited resources – from electricity outages to increasingly rare shipments of medicines and supplies – healthcare professionals say they are now forced to pick and choose whom to treat.

“Now, we have to play God. When you secure the resources for a single surgery, we have to decide who gets to be operated on,” Fernandez said.

“It’s an impossible situation because, ultimately, they are all just children.”

Cuba has long struggled under the economic restrictions imposed by the US. But experts say the Trump administration has heightened those pressures, pushing Cuba's healthcare system to the brink.

“Children are dying because doctors lack access to essential medical supplies and medicines," United Nations human rights commissioner Volker Turk said last month as he called for sanctions relief. "This is unacceptable."

For more than 60 years, Cuba has operated under a comprehensive US trade embargo, the longest in modern history.

Rooted in Cold War political rivalries, the embargo has hindered Cuba from accessing medicines and equipment available to much of the world.

Cuba is banned, for example, from buying advanced US-made pharmaceuticals and technology in which more than 10 percent of the components originate in the US.

According to Cuban officials, European medical suppliers frequently refuse to trade with the island out of fear of US sanctions.

That risk has been amplified since Trump took office, first in 2017 and again in 2025.

With the aim of exerting "maximum pressure" on Cuba's economy, Trump has imposed sanctions and designated the country a "state sponsor of terrorism".

Under that designation, international banking institutions could face massive fines for processing transactions involving Cuban entities.

January, however, marked a turning point. Trump threatened the island with military intervention, and in the months since, he has moved to make international trade with Cuba more arduous.

In addition to January's fuel blockade, Trump issued an executive order in May that bars companies from providing support to the Cuban government.

Participating in several key sectors – from energy to financial services and mining – is also prohibited under Trump's order. Failure to comply could result in the US-based assets of international firms being seized.

In the wake of Trump's order, two of the world’s biggest shipping companies – Hapag-Lloyd and CMA CGM – abandoned their operations in Cuba.

The tightening restrictions have forced the Cuban government to effectively ration care.

In February, Havana announced a package of emergency energy-saving measures. Among them was the suspension of all non-essential medical services across the island.

But non-essential does not mean unimportant. Fernandez, the paediatric anaesthesiologist, explained that preventive healthcare plays a major role in saving lives.

Under normal conditions, he said, preventive healthcare helps doctors catch potentially fatal conditions like appendicitis sooner.

But in recent months, Fernandez has observed patients arriving at his hospital in a "worsened" condition than they might otherwise have had.

“All the appendicitis cases we treat now present complications," he said. "They demand more resources and antibiotics – supplies we don’t have.”

Deaths in Cuba have also escalated as years of increasing restrictions take effect.

Just last month, the Cuban Ministry of Public Health (MINSAP) reported that survival rates for childhood cancer dropped from 85 percent to 65 percent amid the oil blockade.

Infant mortality has also steadily climbed. In 2017, at the start of Trump's first term, Cuba had an infant mortality rate of four for every 1,000 live births. That figure climbed to 7.7 in 2024, just before Trump's second term, and reached 9.9 in 2025.

The maternal mortality rate similarly rose to 44.1 deaths for every 100,000 live births by the end of 2025, up from 40.6 the previous year.

Lilian Delgado, an obstetrician and gynaecologist at Cuba’s main maternity hospital, explained that the escalating humanitarian crisis has triggered a sharp rise in premature births and severe morbidity among pregnant women.

“Conditions are far from ideal at all the levels of the system,” Delgado noted. “There are shortages everywhere.”

The decision to prioritise emergency care can be deceptive. A wide range of medical procedures are considered "elective". But just because they do not rise to the level of an emergency does not mean they are optional.

Typically, in Cuba, emergency surgeries are those that need to be urgently completed within 48 hours. Other necessary surgeries often fall into the "elective" category.

Mastectomies – a common breast cancer treatment – are among the surgeries often categorised as elective. So too are some organ transplants.

Healthcare advocates point out that, if certain elective surgeries are postponed too long, they too can result in deadly conditions.

More than 100,000 Cubans are currently on waiting lists for elective or reconstructive surgeries, a backlog MINSAP credited to the US sanctions.

Among those waiting are 5,152 cancer patients and approximately 12,000 children. Delgado said some of her patients have been languishing on such lists for months.

“Our surgical services are severely hampered by a lack of supplies,” she explained. “We have more women suffering from serious complications, and our operating rooms have become tied up with emergency cases, making it impossible to perform elective surgeries.”

Hospitals in Cuba largely have backup generators to weather the increasingly frequent power outages. But accessing even emergency medical care is tough when the fuel blockade is affecting basic services like transportation.

“Ultimately, if you have a cancer patient and cannot operate due to a number of factors – such as a nationwide blackout forcing the suspension of surgeries – then, whether you intend to or not, you are directly condemning that patient to death,” Delgado said.

The oil embargo has cost “human lives, both directly and indirectly”, she added.

The William Soler Pediatric Hospital alone used to perform 10,000 surgeries annually, ranging from routine procedures to complex operations such as liver transplants.

But surgical activity came to a near-standstill during the COVID-19 pandemic. "All resources plummeted," Fernandez recalled.

The number of annual surgeries fell to barely 1,000. That downward trend has continued in recent months, according to the surgeon.

Currently, the hospital performs only one or two elective surgeries per day – or three or four operations daily when emergency cases are included.

"At this pace, we will have performed around 700 operations by the end of the year," said Fernandez.

The elective surgeries still being performed are those that “cannot be postponed", like cancer cases, critical spinal deformities or other conditions that "can be fatal if delayed".

“We have been trying to handle as many cases as possible with the limited resources we have,” Fernandez added.

Erenia Carrillo, 57, is among the 100,000 Cubans waiting for surgery. She suffers from kidney failure.

Every other day, a vehicle funded by Cuba's public health system picks her up and takes her to the hospital. There, an artificial kidney filters her blood for four hours, removing the toxins and excess fluid that her body can no longer clear.

Carrillo began her dialysis treatment more than a year ago, in March 2025. But she has noticed her quality of care decline.

According to government data released last month, 2,888 Cubans undergoing dialysis for chronic kidney failure have seen their treatment disrupted by the worsening energy crisis.

"The hospital used to supply all kinds of medications,” Carrillo said. “Now, with the tightening of the embargo, even the staff coming to care for us arrive late because they have no transport to get here.”

Sometimes the machines break down, and the clinic must ration the functioning ones.

When a single artificial kidney has to be shared among multiple patients, Carrillo’s four-hour dialysis session is cut down to just two or three hours.

Hospital shortages mean that many dialysis patients are forced to source their own medications. Carrillo receives hers from her son in Mexico.

Out of the 395 medicines produced domestically in Cuba, 300 were out of stock due to the inability to secure raw materials, according to a statement from MINSAP last month.

Deliveries to Cuba's state-run pharmacies, meanwhile, have grown more and more infrequent.

For much of last year, shipments to the municipality of Cerro – one of 15 boroughs in the capital, Havana – came roughly once every 10 days.

But a pharmacy clerk, who spoke to Al Jazeera in June on condition of anonymity, said that deliveries have become scarce.

Since the oil blockade began, shipments come months at a time. The last time Cerro's pharmacies were stocked was on June 16, the clerk said. Before that, the last shipment was on February 23.

“This is the longest an order has ever taken to arrive,” the clerk said, estimating that the boxes only covered 30 percent of her community's needs.

With shipments so scarce, medication can run out on the first day after it arrives, she added.

The clerk herself suffers from hypertension, or dangerously high blood pressure. She takes medication to treat the condition every morning and every night.

But like her customers, she said she has no choice but to turn to the black market to meet her needs.

Prices there are often higher than they otherwise should be. The average monthly wage is roughly $11 for those working for the state, the country's largest employer.

"I buy enalapril on the street, whatever the cost. What else can I do?” the clerk said. “When I can't find it, I take something else. It’s not a proper treatment, and it puts my health at risk, but what choice do I have?"

Roxana Martinez, a community doctor serving the Havana neighbourhood of Cayo Hueso, has had to face patients knowing she had no medication to give them.

“There are practically no medicines in the pharmacy,” Martinez said. “We used to have options to substitute one medication for another, but not any more.”

Some patients arrive with dangerous conditions, she added, “and I don't have a single pill to give them”.

She has been forced to recommend herbal infusions and natural medicine instead. To manage hypertension, for instance, she suggests lemongrass brew or tamarind juice.

“Natural medicine has been used forever, but it is becoming more important now because sometimes it is the only option available,” said Martinez.

Only on Wednesday did Cuba loosen restrictions to allow the creation of private pharmacies, as part of a slate of economic reforms designed to lessen pressure on the island.

But the strain of the oil blockade continues to make jobs like hers even more difficult.

Cuba's state-run healthcare system boasts 10,000 neighbourhood clinics, 149 hospitals and 451 polyclinics, which combine general and specialist care.

But Martinez explained that, even with so many facilities, the country struggles to keep up with the needs of its 9.4 million inhabitants.

The country's medical guidelines dictate that primary care physicians like her should care for a maximum of 700 patients. Martinez used to see 1,875 at her clinic.

This year, however, that figure skyrocketed to more than 3,000. She explained she was forced to absorb a second clinic into her practice due to a shortage of doctors.

Wave after wave of humanitarian crises have prompted a mass exodus from Cuba in recent years. The oil blockade is only the latest to hit the island.

Cuba's population has shrunk by more 10 percent since 2020, according to conservative estimates.

While doctors can earn thousands of dollars per month abroad, Martinez said her salary is only about $20 a month. Still, she remains devoted to her patients, no matter what the oil blockade may bring.

“The workload is overwhelming, but I take it on because the patients need it,” Martinez said.

articles.title: Travelers clash after TSA shares surprising guidance about airport etiquette
articles.excerpt:
A college student, Nick Ruiz, shared this video of airport personnel handling instrument cases rather roughly at Los Angeles International Airport.

The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) ha...
articles.body_text:
A college student, Nick Ruiz, shared this video of airport personnel handling instrument cases rather roughly at Los Angeles International Airport.

The Transportation Security Administration (TSA) has sparked debate about airport etiquette after recommending that travelers bring hammocks to airports so they can relax during long layovers.

In a recent post marking National Hammock Day, the agency wrote, "Nobody said you couldn't bring a hammock to the airport."

It added, "To reduce tension, or to avoid having a falling out with the airport, check with them about where you can and can't hang your napping apparatus."

FLIGHT ATTENDANTS BEG TRAVELERS TO STOP DOING THE ONE THING THAT ANNOYS CREWS MOST

The post included photos of travelers relaxing in hammocks strung up inside airport terminals.

July 22 marked "National Hammock Day, so we highlighted the occasion on our social media channels," the TSA told Fox News Digital.

Diane Gottsman, an etiquette expert based in San Antonio and founder of The Protocol School of Texas, said most travelers understand that delays and layovers can be exhausting — but that doesn't mean personal comfort should come at the expense of others.

The TSA is drawing attention after suggesting travelers could bring hammocks to the airport with them.  (Daniel Bockwoldt/picture alliance via Getty Images)

"Bringing your own hammock through security for the specific reason of setting up camp is not considerate of others in a tight public space," Gottsman told Fox News Digital.

She noted that each airport has its own rules and safety policies.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Before you get caught stringing up your suspended apparatus between two poles, ask airport staff if there is a safe, out-of-the-way place to hang within the rules of the airport," Gottsman said.

Permission to use hammocks inside terminals usually depends on individual airport rules and applicable local rules.

She said most travelers will likely continue choosing an uncomfortable airport chair over turning a terminal into a campsite.

Travelers understand that delays and layovers can be exhausting, but that doesn't mean personal comfort should come at the expense of others, etiquette experts say. (AFP via Getty Images)

The post sparked debate online, with some social media users arguing that airports have become too casual.

"Airports used to be a civilized place," one user wrote on X.

Others pointed out that the TSA only determines what passengers can bring through security checkpoints.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"TSA doesn't control the airport," one Reddit user wrote. "Every airport will have its own rules."

The TSA post sparked debate online, with some social media users arguing that airports have become too casual these days. (iStock)

Others argued that hanging a hammock inside an airport could create safety concerns or obstruct other travelers.

"I love my hammock, but this would be obnoxious," one Reddit user wrote.

Some travelers, however, fully embraced the idea.

"I vowed to myself to always travel with my hammock," one Reddit user wrote after describing using one during a long layover before eventually being asked by airport police to take it down.

Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Conservatives mock Talarico for gushing over Fauci doll in resurfaced Christmas post
articles.excerpt:
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico has embraced his

On Christmas Day 2021, Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico celebrated receiving a Dr. Anthony Fauci doll — a decision he i...
articles.body_text:
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico has embraced his

On Christmas Day 2021, Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico celebrated receiving a Dr. Anthony Fauci doll — a decision he is now being mocked for.

"​​I got the coolest action figure for Christmas!" Talarico wrote on social media at the time. "​​Thank you to all the health care superheroes working today. Let’s help by getting vaxxed and boosted!"

Republican lawmakers and conservative pundits were quick to poke fun at Talarico when his nearly five-year-old post began recirculating on X earlier in the week.

TEXAS DEM NOMINEE JAMES TALARICO INVOKES FAITH TO DEFEND ABORTION RIGHTS, ‘THE BIBLE IS SILENT ON ABORTION'

Dr. Anthony Fauci returned to the news cycle following his repeated refusal to answer questions under oath before Congress, invoking his Fifth Amendment right to avoid making self-incriminating statements. (Alex Wroblewski / AFP via Getty Images)

"Do you think James Talarico still plays with his Fauci action figure?" Rep. Brandon Gill, a Texas Republican, wrote Wednesday.

Republicans, facing a well-funded challenger in Talarico, have sought to portray him as effeminate in an effort to harm his image among Texas voters. His opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, branded him as "too low-T for Texas," and an AI ad produced by a conservative group portrayed the Democratic hopeful prancing around in a dress.

"It comes as no surprise that James Talarico has a Dr. Fauci action figure," commentator Benny Johnson quipped on X.

The National Rifle Association, along similar lines, cautioned its X followers to "Never trust a grown man that plays with dolls."

RAND PAUL SEEKS CONTEMPT CHARGES AFTER FAUCI INVOKES FIFTH AMENDMENT MORE THAN 100 TIMES

On Christmas Day 2021, Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico celebrated receiving a Dr. Anthony Fauci doll — a decision he is now being mocked for. (Kamil Krzaczynski /AFP via Getty Images) (Abigail Dollins/Fort Worth Star-Telegram/Tribune News Service via Getty Images))

Talarico’s post resurfaced Wednesday as Fauci returned to the news cycle following his repeated refusal to answer questions under oath before Congress, invoking his Fifth Amendment right to avoid making self-incriminating statements.

At the time of his post, Talarico was serving as a member of the Texas House of Representatives, a post he still holds today. Even when he first posted the image of his toy, conservatives attacked the Texas lawmaker for attaching himself to what they believed to be unpopular lockdown policies.

"James Talarico called Fauci a superhero," Republican Texas Sen. Ted Cruz wrote on X Wednesday. "Today, Fauci took the Fifth 111 times. Apparently accountability was sold separately."

"If you push the lever, it pleads the Fifth," the senator later added.

TOP 5 MOMENTS FROM FAUCI'S HEARING: PAUL BOOTS LAWYER, MORENO ERUPTS AS CONTEMPT VOTE LOOMS

Texas State Rep. James Talarico, D-Travis, and Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, shake hands. (Bob Daemmrich/Getty Images)

Fauci suggested that the hearing was the result of Sen. Rand Paul’s "unhinged obsession" with him.

Republicans appear to view Talarico’s admiration for Fauci as something that will hurt his electoral prospects, with Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s campaign account posting "Christmas in July" alongside a Christmas tree and mask emoji in response to Talarico’s post.

The figurine, which features a "removable mask" and can be purchased online for around $25, is part of a line of toys called "real life action figures" manufactured by a company called FCTRY. Other figures in the series include Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

The Talarico campaign did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital Thursday.

articles.title: More prisoners in England and Wales are recalled than released for first time
articles.excerpt:
Returns for breaches of licence conditions rose 31% in the first quarter of 2026, adding to pressure on prison places

More people were recalled to prison than were released during the first three mon...
articles.body_text:
Returns for breaches of licence conditions rose 31% in the first quarter of 2026, adding to pressure on prison places

More people were recalled to prison than were released during the first three months of 2026, the first time on record the “recall rate” has surpassed 100% in England and Wales.

Between January and March 2026, 12,977 people were released from prison while 13,193 people were returned to prison for breaching their licence conditions, up 31% from last year, new Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data showed.

This means that for every 100 people released, 101 people were recalled to custody, creating a “recall rate” of over 100%.

This rate has increased rapidly from about 30% a decade ago. Between January and March 2016, 17,923 people were released and 5,185 were recalled, meaning about 30 people were recalled for every 100 prisoners released.

Prisons in England and Wales are close to capacity, and the government has recently paused its plans to release about 6,000 prisoners early to ease the crisis.

Andy Keen-Downs, the chief executive of the Prison Advice and Care Trust, said: “The prison population crisis will not be solved if as many people are being sent back to prison as are leaving it.”

He warned that if current circumstances don’t change, prison places may run out by Christmas.

“Hundreds of people are recalled every month not because they have committed new offences, but because they have fallen foul of licence conditions,” he said. “This makes little sense at a time when the government is doing everything it can to reduce pressure on the prison system.”

In total, 51,419 prisoners were recalled to jail in the year to March 2026 after breaching the terms of their licence, up 28% from the previous 12 months and the highest number since current records began in 2015.

Of all recalls, 22% involved a further charge of offending, while the vast majority were for breaches of licence conditions, which have risen sharply over the past decade.

Breaches include failing to keep in touch with probation services or failing to reside at an approved address.

The figures also showed 70,066 prisoners have been freed early since September 2024, when the government brought in emergency measures in response to the overcrowding crisis.

Enver Solomon, the chief executive of the social justice charity Nacro, said the number of recalls were “piling further pressure on an already overcrowded prison estate” and showed “a system that simply isn’t working”.

“Thousands of people are being sent back to custody each year for licence breaches rather than new crimes, and we know from our work that many of these recalls are linked to homelessness after leaving prison, addiction to drugs and alcohol, and mental health issues,” he said.

Almost 13,000 people left prison homeless or as rough sleepers in the year to April 2025, a 39% rise from the previous year.

Pavan Dhaliwal, the chief executive of the charity Revolving Doors, which works with people who are in repeat contact with the justice system, said the system needs reform so recall becomes a “genuine last resort”.

“Sending people back to prison when they are struggling to rebuild their lives is costly, counterproductive and keeps the revolving door turning,” she said.

The MoJ said the increase was probably due in part to early release schemes, under which more prisoners have been released on licence earlier in their sentences.

Alex Hewson from the Prison Reform Trust said more people on short sentences being released on licence was creating “more opportunities for recall”.

“We are now using recall far more frequently than in the recent past, and it is reasonable to ask whether every return to custody is necessary and proportionate,” he said. “Given the pressure on both prisons and probation, that question deserves serious attention.”

articles.title: In Their Own Hands: Ghana’s Drug Vigilantes

Citizen vigilantes patrol Ghana's streets, fighting an opioid crisis. We meet those taking the law into their own hands.

Ghana is facing an opioid addiction crisis, with a flood of cheap, synthetic d...
articles.body_text:
Citizen vigilantes patrol Ghana's streets, fighting an opioid crisis. We meet those taking the law into their own hands.

Ghana is facing an opioid addiction crisis, with a flood of cheap, synthetic drugs destroying lives and communities. In the northern city of Tamale, a group of civilians, frustrated by what they see as the inaction of local authorities, are taking the law into their own hands. The ‘anti-drug task force’ patrols the streets, seeking out dealers and users and meting out its own brand of justice. Some government officials condemn the vigilantes, while others embrace them as a useful tool in the fight against illegal drugs. As word spreads about the success of Tamale’s task force, some question whether civilians can properly replace state services – and warn about the dangers of vigilante justice.

articles.title: NATO jets scramble as Russian missile detonates in Poland
articles.excerpt:
NATO fighter planes have been scrambled as a Russian missile entered Polish airspace and crashed.

The missile, which entered Polish airspace early on Thursday, was part of a barrage of ballistic miss...
articles.body_text:
NATO fighter planes have been scrambled as a Russian missile entered Polish airspace and crashed.

The missile, which entered Polish airspace early on Thursday, was part of a barrage of ballistic missiles and drones launched by Russia against Ukraine overnight, killing at least eight civilians, including children, and injuring more than 50.

Concern that Russia’s war on Ukraine risks entangling neighbouring NATO states is on the rise. Poland is just one of several alliance members to have confronted repeated stray drones and missiles. Such incidents have become increasingly common in recent months as Russia and Ukraine have launched hundreds of projectiles at one another.

NATO members, including Poland, launched F-16 jets in response to the sighting of the missile, as well as an aerial refuelling aircraft and an airborne early warning plane, a spokesperson for the alliance said.

NATO will continue to take all necessary measures to defend its territory, the spokesperson added.

Polish authorities said the explosion had created a wide crater in the eastern village of Tarnawa-Kolonia. While the incident caused no injuries or damage, it will deepen tensions between NATO and Russia as European countries fear the four-year-old war could spill into their territory.

“Poland and NATO activated their air and ground defences,” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on social media.

“This incident is yet another reckless act by Russia and a dangerous consequence of its war against Ukraine,” he said.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk rushed to the site of the incident. “Everything indicates” that it was a Russian missile, he said.

Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X that it was “a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile” that violated NATO airspace.

“This is yet another clear demonstration that strengthening Ukraine’s air defense now is urgent and serves as a guarantee for the protection of the entire Euro-Atlantic community,” he said.

Stray drones and missiles have become a core focus for European countries, especially for those on NATO’s eastern flank.

Romania has reported repeated incursions by stray drones into its airspace. On Monday, following the latest incursion of three drones, Bucharest summoned Russia’s ambassador to complain about the “repeated violations”.

In May, Estonia and Latvia reported drones entering their airspace from Russia. The government in Riga then collapsed over an argument on how to handle the projectiles.

Last year Poland added deployments to its air defences in response to the threat. It has also regularly detected violations of its airspace by Russian missiles and drones.

Drone incursions have, meanwhile, also led to discussions in the European Union about building a possible “drone wall” to shield its eastern flank.

articles.title: Trump admin's push to scrap DEI in federal government takes landmark step with new hiring rule
articles.excerpt: Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor outlines how the Trump administration is transforming the federal government by prioritizing merit over DEI. He details the elimination of self-atte...
articles.body_text:
Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor outlines how the Trump administration is transforming the federal government by prioritizing merit over DEI. He details the elimination of self-attestation, implementation of skills-based assessments and efforts to boost accountability for underperforming employees. These reforms aim to cut waste and restore performance across the 2.2 million-strong federal workforce.

FIRST ON FOX: The Trump administration on Wednesday took another step in its sweeping campaign to eliminate DEI policies from the federal government, removing decades-old hiring guidelines that officials say encouraged race-conscious employment decisions in favor of a renewed emphasis on merit-based hiring.

The U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) issued a final interim rule on Thursday that removes references to the 1978 Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures, which govern employee selection standards, citing a recent Justice Department legal opinion that found the guidelines unconstitutional in the way they encouraged race-conscious decision-making.

The move affects how federal agencies approach hiring by eliminating references to long-standing guidance centered on "disparate impact," the idea that hiring practices that could produce unequal outcomes among racial groups can be legally problematic even absent intentional discrimination.

Administration officials argue those guidelines pressured employers to focus on racial outcomes rather than qualifications, while supporters of the guidelines contend they help guard against subtle forms of discrimination.

DEI HIRING BOOST FOR ONE BLUE STATE'S MUSLIM COMMISSION INITIATIVE FLIES IN FACE OF TRUMP'S ANTI-WOKE PUSH

President Donald Trump takes questions from the media during a meeting in the Oval Office of the White House on July 21, 2026. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"Federal hiring should be based on merit, qualifications, and the ability to perform the job," OPM Director Scott Kupor said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"This rule ensures OPM's regulations reflect legal guidance while preserving the rigorous, job-related standards that help agencies recruit and hire the most qualified workforce in service to the American people."

The rule took effect immediately after it was published in the Federal Register on Thursday but will remain open for public comment for 60 days before OPM decides whether to make it permanent.

COAST GUARD ENDING RACE-BASED ADMISSIONS FOR OFFICER COMMISSIONING PROGRAM UNDER TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN

Hundreds protest outside a rally held by President Donald Trump at Macomb County Community College in Warren, Mich., on April 29, 2025. (Getty Images/Dominic Gwinn)

OPM serves as the federal government's human resources agency, setting hiring, personnel and workforce policies for roughly 2 million civilian federal employees across executive branch agencies. It oversees the rules governing how federal agencies recruit, hire, promote and manage their workforces.

This move serves as the latest example of the administration moving beyond simply shutting down DEI offices or ending diversity training and now targeting the legal and regulatory framework that critics argue enabled DEI policies in the first place.

KEY TRUMP AGENCY PUTS TOP UNIVERSITIES IN CROSSHAIRS OVER ALLEGED RACE-BASED DORM PROGRAMS

The U.S. Office of Personnel Management building in Washington June 5, 2015. (Reuters/Gary Cameron)

Since the beginning of President Donald Trump's second term, the administration has highlighted hundreds of colleges that have rolled back DEI initiatives, along with policy changes involving transgender athletic participation, parental rights, race-conscious programs and merit-based admissions.

They also dismantled federal DEI programs, terminated DEI-related grants and contracts, cut ties with companies embracing DEI policies, required federal contractors to comply with the administration's requirements, and warned schools they could lose federal funding over certain DEI practices.

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.

articles.title: Iran’s war with the US is not its only conflict as internal crises mount
articles.excerpt:
Government fears social discontent on ‘most important battlefield’ of economy and livelihoods as war takes its toll amid anti-state dissent

Iran, in the midst of an escalating five-month war with the...
articles.body_text:
Government fears social discontent on ‘most important battlefield’ of economy and livelihoods as war takes its toll amid anti-state dissent

Iran, in the midst of an escalating five-month war with the US, continues to stumble from one internal crisis to another – whether it is over public executions, the rising cost of living, the alleged bias of the state broadcaster or even the post-midnight destruction of pavements outside liberal-leaning Tehran cafes. Very little that happens in Iran, cultural or political, momentous or trivial, does so uncontested.

But there is now a growing threat of a long diplomatic deadlock, forged by mutual distrust in which neither side believes the other will stick to any agreement. That impasse has occurred as the war broadens, drawing in Yemen, Iraq and now Egypt. In Iran, at least, the advocates of escalation are winning. As a result, a convergence of Iran’s conflicts, internal and external, becomes more likely.

Parts of the Trump administration and the Iranian opposition – including Reza Pahlavi, the son of the former deposed Shah – have never abandoned the belief that the Iranian government is on the brink of collapse.

What is true is that the picture of cohesive if brittle society presented by the millions attending the funeral of the supreme leader Ali Khamenei earlier this month revealed only one side of the public mood.

Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, rarely tires of warning that the conditions that led to the bloody protests in January remain.

At a recent meeting of the supreme judicial council he argued: “Iran is engaged in a full-scale war. Today’s war is not just a war of missiles; the enemy has come to the conclusion that it cannot force the Iranian nation to surrender through military attacks. The most important battlefield today is the economy and livelihood of the people. If economic pressures cause social discontent to form and this discontent spreads, the enormous social capital that the people have created in support of the system will be lost.”

Undoubtedly dissent, in the form of despair, exists.

Golshan Fathi, a Tehran human rights activist, recently wrote on her social media page: “The same sick cycle repeats … morning … the call to prayer, news of an execution … noon with power cuts, afternoon the water stops … dusk, the anxiety of war and renewed attacks on cities, and at midnight, the earth trembles.

“And tomorrow, the same story again. Caught between natural disasters, management failures, and man-made crises … every day we don’t live, we just practice enduring. Repetition, repetition, repetition … until a weary land no longer asks, ‘What will tomorrow bring?’ It just waits to see, ‘When will the next crisis arrive?’”

Dissent in the form of political protest also exists, whether it is those inside jails or citizens in the squares of Isfahan protesting against the current wave of intimidatory public executions. Many critics ask why the punishment of the accused takes place in public gallows, yet their trials are held in secret courts.

On Monday the political bureau of the Nation’s Union party warned that ignoring the protests over the wave of executions could have “devastating consequences”, and urged academics and religious scholars to intervene to end this state violence.

Azar Mansouri, once a close reformist ally of Pezeshkian, warned last week at the annual meeting of the Iranian reformist front about a small but vocal group that seemed determined to portray negotiated agreements with the US as retreats or defeat. War, she warned, “is not just a confrontation between military forces and armies. It is the destruction of the economy, the erosion of social capital, the spread of despair, the emigration of elites, the increase in poverty and the loss of opportunities for development. Ultimately, it threatens the future of the nation.”

Similarly a “we do not want war” statement signed by 268 political activists this month said they believed the overwhelming majority opposed war, and this should be tested in a public vote. Another letter from 1,000 activists linked with the former president Mohammad Khatami warned “the contemporary experience of Iran is that war has no winners. Those who advocate negotiations should not be slandered.”

What unites these initiatives is a fear that diplomats are losing, and Iran is being edged into a forever war that can be portrayed as an Iranian-Arab war, a war that would be to Israel’s advantage.

Yet opposition to the whole principle of negotiation with America – fuelled by Donald Trump’s own erratic behaviour – is being voiced by hardliners, in street rallies and more recently on unofficial billboards.

The sway of the hardliners lies less in their strength in parliament – many were elected on low turnouts and anyway have been deposed from key committees in parliament – but in the belief a network of deep-state support exists in the military and in the office of the supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei. The absence of Khamenei from public view makes it harder to resolve the controversy about whether the family see any purpose in negotiations with America.

The closure of cafes, or the destruction of the sidewalks around them, is also seen as a crude attempt to shape debate. Last year the prominent hardliner Saeed Jalili described the cafes as an anti-Islamic “third space” beyond the dormitory or the office where people go to escape loneliness. “In this concept the family loses any meaning. This stands in opposition to Islam’s philosophy of marriage.”

Despite being a conservative newspaper, Jomhouri-e Eslami complained “an addiction to violating the dignity of one’s political opponents is increasing every day”. That in turn is, in part, a reference to the criticism of negotiators meted out by the publicly funded national broadcaster IRIB, long seen as a preserve of those opposed to talks with the west. Many see IRIB as an exclusive platform for the hardliners rather than a mirror of a diverse society.

The crisis between the government and the broadcaster is now out in the open after interventions by Pezeshkian and Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, the chief negotiator, were censored.

The government in a statement complained: “Censorship of the president’s speech, unilateral destruction of the government’s performance, and efforts to destroy the memorandum of understanding that was formed to get the country through the crisis and protect national interests are no longer media criticism; they are a stand against national cohesion, empathy, and unity.

“The question is clear: is the Iranian broadcasting system with the people, government, and interests of Iran or with those who benefit from division, tension, and polarisation? The national media should be the voice of Iranian unity, not a platform for destroying the government and disrupting national understanding.”

There are calls for a complete overhaul of the organisation’s accountability when a new head is appointed this September. At one level the politics of the national broadcaster should not matter, since surveys suggest less than 12% of the country watch it. The difficulty for the government is that this leaves audiences watching hostile foreign satellite channels instead.

This tension over the national broadcaster coincides with a period of unprecedented economic pressure. In the next six months food rationing might become necessary, Majid-Reza Hariri, the head of the Iran-China chamber of commerce, warned this week. Gholamhossein Mohammadi, the deputy minister of labour, said more than a million jobs had been lost as a result of the war.

In a way rationing – through food price inflation – has already started as Iranians are being forced to change their diets due to the cost of fruit, eggs and chicken. Year-on-year food inflation reached 134% in July, meaning the average household’s monthly food budget has more than doubled in a year. Overall inflation is at 84%. In a further sign of the long-term pressure on living standards, figures released this week showed the real value of the mimimum wage had plummeted.

Azadeh Mokhtari, one of the best chroniclers of the impact of the economy on everyday lives, wrote this week: “Society has reached a point where ‘I don’t have the patience’ and ‘I don’t have the energy’ have become everyday phrases. No one asks ‘how are you?’ any more because everyone knows the answer.”

The toll of the war on the economy has spread everywhere from the internet to tourism. All 400 hotels on Kish Island in the strait of Hormuz – the site of US bombing on Thursday – have shut. As many as 30,000 Iranians visited medical centres during the two wars in 2025 and 2026. Civilian facilities such as the Bushehr meteorological centre have been almost destroyed and the Bushehr airport has become unusable. The Chabahar maritime watchtower has been completely destroyed; 12 bridges and two tunnel openings have been damaged. This will take decades to repair.

Yet one of the biggest bombshells was detonated on national television when Zabihullah Khodayian, the head of the General Inspection Organisation, a national audit office, revealed the scale of foreign-exchange corruption among so-called trusts, highly secretive government-sponsored bodies set up to evade US sanctions.

These trusts, embedded in the Iranian political system for years, are entities set up to transfer Iranian oil income outside the network of sanctions. It is self-evident that they act in an untransparent way, and siphon off public money. Khodayian confirmed as much, saying one trust was given $200m (£149m), had not returned the money, and had also left the country. He said a further 229 individuals owed the state a total of €23.5bn (£20.2bn), while the judiciary said cases were being opened against nearly 50 individuals.

It is still unclear on what basis these trusts were selected, how much they charge, what guarantees they have provided to preserve the country’s resources, and how they are held accountable. But there is a growing chance that a major scandal is about to be revealed that could involve Iran’s elite. If so, all the talk of social cohesion across the classes will start to look very hollow.

articles.title: At least five members of same family killed in Russian missile attack, Zelensky says
articles.excerpt:
Five members if the Voronov family were killed, Zelensky said, with others missing

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has branded a Russian missile attack that killed five members of the same fam...
articles.body_text:
Five members if the Voronov family were killed, Zelensky said, with others missing

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has branded a Russian missile attack that killed five members of the same family a "horrific crime".

Zelensky shared a picture of the Voronov family on social media, writing that parents Artem and Olena and three of their children - Mark, Azariah Ilay, and Emilia - had all been killed after a missile decimated their home.

Their other children - Zakhar, Dominika, Viorika, Federica, and a grandson Artem - are also still missing after Russia launched more than 70 missiles and over 280 drones overnight.

The worst attack was near Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih.

Missile that left crater deep inside Poland was probably Russian - Polish PM

The attack - which officials said had killed eight people - comes after Zelensky met US President Donald Trump in Washington DC this week to urge the US to grant Ukraine a licence to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.

"Today, the Russians destroyed an ordinary home of an ordinary family in Radushne near Kryvyi Rih in our Dnipropetrovsk region with a strike from their ballistic missile," Zelensky wrote on X on Thursday.

"It is definitively known that the parents and three children perished. The Russian missile strike was so powerful that almost nothing remained of the house… Under the rubble, fragments of human bodies were found, and only forensic examinations can determine to whom exactly in the family those bodies belong.

"This Russian evil can only be stopped by the entire world. No one in the world can be left alone against such terror. And when we say that Ukraine needs missiles for 'Patriots', when we seek capabilities to defend against Russian ballistics, we are not talking about abstractions."

Local defence council chief Oleksandr Vilkul said two private homes had been destroyed in the attacks.

Another eight people were wounded, including an 84-year-old woman who was taken to hospital, and two children who were pulled from the rubble alive, officials added.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said an object that crashed into a field in eastern Poland in the early hours of Thursday was probably a Russian missile.

Ukraine's acting Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha had earlier said a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile had "crossed into Poland as part of Russia's massive strike against Ukraine, violating Nato airspace".

Watch: Aftermath of Radushne strike, as Kyiv residents seek shelter

Ukraine had been expecting a Russian offensive, with Zelensky warning just hours before the strikes that Moscow was preparing for a "massive attack".

In Kyiv, one person died and fires broke out in three non-residential buildings overnight, the capital's mayor Vitali Klitschko wrote on Telegram.

The mayor of Poltava also reported a death, which came after he said a Nova Poshta postal terminal had been attacked.

There were also explosions in Lviv and mayor Andriy Sadovyi said residential buildings had been damaged.

Multiple people were injured with some trapped under a building, he added, saying residents were helping rescuers to clear the rubble.

A building damaged by a Russian missile strike on Lviv, Ukraine, 30 July 2026

In neighbouring Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk was heading to the site of a 10m-crater (33ft), after "a violation of Polish airspace occurred" during Russia's attack on Lviv.

Polish armed forces said they had mobilised on-duty fighter jets during the strikes, after detecting at least a dozen missiles over western Ukraine that could have posed a threat to Polish airspace.

The closest one was observed about 5km from the Polish border at 03:29, after which it changed direction and headed eastwards.

The military said they had subsequently located the crater with scattered debris on Polish soil - in a field about 2km away from the village of Tarnawa-Kolonia, Lublin province, in the south. The site has been secured, they said.

Police said they had received a report of a powerful explosion in the area.

Poland's prime minister said the crater was likely caused by a Russian missile, but investigations were still ongoing.

"All the indications are that it was a Russian Kh-101 ballistic missile, but we want to be 100% certain about the type of missile and who launched it," Donald Tusk said at a specially convened meeting in Lublin.

Meanwhile in Russia, a regional official reported an overnight attack on the warehouse of a retailer in the city of Penza.

One person was injured at a Wildberries facility, Regional Governor Oleg Melnichenko posted on Telegram.

Wildberries is often described as "Russia's Amazon" and its sites have been the target of recent Ukrainian attacks.

The military action follows repeated calls by Ukraine's president to bolster Kyiv's anti-ballistic missile defences.

"The protection of people's lives depends directly on their willingness, or lack of willingness, to provide air defence missiles," he wrote on X on Wednesday.

The Patriot is one of the few air defence systems able to intercept ballistic missiles, which Russia has increasingly used to bombard Ukrainian cities.

Russia's businesses under strain from Ukraine's attacks on Wildberries

Why is Ukraine rolling out the red carpet for a US far-right influencer?

Zelensky and Netanyahu meet Trump as wars in Ukraine and Iran drag on

articles.title: New York City immigrant business owners are planning to sue Mamdani over taxpayer-funded supermarkets
articles.excerpt: Economist David Bahnsen criticizes NYC Mayor Mamdanis plan for city-run grocery stores, arguing that government intervention in markets historically leads to inflation and reduced standards of living....
articles.body_text:
Economist David Bahnsen criticizes NYC Mayor Mamdanis plan for city-run grocery stores, arguing that government intervention in markets historically leads to inflation and reduced standards of living.

Several immigrant business owners are preparing to sue New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani over his plan for city-owned grocery stores, Fox News Digital confirmed on Wednesday.

The New York Post first reported on Tuesday that the Multicultural Business Coalition’s (MBC) board voted to file a lawsuit against the city over Mamdani's plan to open five taxpayer-funded grocery stores that will sell food at prices up to 30% below traditional retailers.

According to MBC Chairman Frank Garcia, the MBC is now planning to send a letter to Mamdani's office in the coming days detailing its upcoming legal plans to protect competing stores, bodegas and other small businesses. If Mamdani does not respond or meet with the organization within the next three weeks, the group plans to take further legal action.

MAMDANI CONFRONTED ON FAILED CITY-RUN GROCERY STORE ATTEMPT IN KANSAS CITY, CLAIMS HIS PLAN WILL WORK

The Multicultural Business Coalition announced efforts to take legal action against New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's taxpayer-funded grocery stores. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

"The [New York City] commissioner said this administration is open to speak to everybody, and they want to hear from everybody," Garcia said. "So I've been waiting for a meeting for a couple of months. Why aren't they having me?"

He added, "We are ready to file the lawsuit if the mayor doesn't meet with us."

Garcia also emphasized that the lawsuit is a nonpartisan initiative and is primarily focused on raising awareness for small business owners struggling with rising costs in New York City. Though the lawsuit has not yet been filed, he said that his lawyers will be "ready to go" after the three-week deadline thanks to broad support from other organizations.

STEPHEN A SMITH SLAMS MAMDANI'S POLICIES, SAYS HIS BIGGEST FANS 'ARE NOT PEOPLE WHO PAY BILLS EVERY DAY'

New York City bodega and business owners expressed concerns over New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's grocery store initiative. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images ; Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images)

"We're nonpartisan. So we're going to meet everybody, Republican or Democrat. There was a Democratic Jewish organization. There were others that we're gonna meet with [along with] civil rights organizations. We're gonna be with all the different civil rights organizations that are willing to support this and have the funding already to fund this," Garcia said.

Fox News Digital reached out to the mayor's office for comment.

The MBC, which was founded earlier this year to oppose Mamdani's grocery store initiative, is composed of members from African, Asian, Caribbean, Hispanic, Jewish and Middle Eastern business communities. The organization has also received widespread support from city and state lawmakers such as New York State Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins.

NYC MAYOR MAMDANI CALLS THREAT OF RICH PEOPLE LEAVING NYC OVER TAXES 'IMAGINED'

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani also faced legal backlash from landlords over his endorsed rent freeze. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)

The announcement of a lawsuit came after Mamdani unveiled more details about his city-backed grocery stores, which faced renewed criticism as a "communist fantasy."

Mamdani also faces a lawsuit from New York City landlords hoping to overturn the city's rent freeze.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

articles.title: Labour asks Electoral Commission to investigate Reform UK over donations
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Reform’s Robert Jenrick says party confident it followed all rules at the time, after latest Guardian revelations

The Electoral Commission has been asked to investigate whether Reform UK h...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Reform’s Robert Jenrick says party confident it followed all rules at the time, after latest Guardian revelations

The Electoral Commission has been asked to investigate whether Reform UK has broken donations rules, after the Guardian revealed that the convicted fraudster George Cottrell transferred more than $2m to his mother in the days before her donations to the party in 2024.

Labour’s new chair, Bridget Phillipson, wrote to the commission on Thursday asking for it to examine the donations and whether they had been recorded correctly.

The commission has already made a referral to the Metropolitan police, who are looking into whether Reform may have been concealing or disguising donations derived from an “impermissible” donor.

The Guardian has since reported that Cottrell’s mother, Fiona Cottrell, received several tranches of money adding up to more than $2m, which she attributed to her son, according to financial industry sources. Her son is a close ally and adviser to Nigel Farage.

Transfers were then made either directly to Reform or via Britain Means Business, a fundraising vehicle for the political party, according to sources.

In her letter, Phillipson said the Guardian’s new revelations “may be relevant to the question of whether the true source of political donations made to Reform UK has been correctly identified and whether the statutory requirements governing permissible donors have been complied with”.

At a press conference on Thursday, Reform’s economics spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, said the story “has been going on for a long time”, but he did not engage with the substance of the allegations.

He told the BBC: “We are entirely confident that Reform followed all electoral rules at the time when the donations were made. Of course, we’ll participate with any inquiries. To the best of my knowledge, we haven’t even been contacted by the police, so I don’t think we have anything more to add to that.”

Jenrick suggested that journalists should be questioning George Cottrell, and he said they should return to the intended subject matter of the press conference, which was social care. “Reform is certain that all the electoral rules were followed,” he told ITV. “If you’ve got a question for Mr Cotrrell then I think you have to direct that to him.”

The Met’s investigation is examining donations to Reform, including those from Britain Means Business, a fundraising vehicle whose director is the party’s deputy leader, Richard Tice. The firm gave Reform two donations of £250,000 in the run-up to the 2024 general election. These were first revealed by the Guardian.

Cottrell, who was convicted for fraud in the US, now lives in Montenegro but is seen often alongside Farage. He has previously been described as Farage’s chief of staff but Reform UK has maintained that he is only a volunteer.

Asked about the transfers, lawyers for Cottrell said their client had no further comment.

In previous legal correspondence, Cottrell has not denied giving his mother – who is understood to be of relatively modest means – large sums of money. Instead, he said via lawyers that “any political donations his mother has made have been entirely her own decision, and are a matter for her”.

Fiona Cottrell has not responded to several attempts by the Guardian to contact her.

Asked on Wednesday for a response to the story, a Reform spokesperson said: “Reform takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations and always ensures that the Electoral Commission guidelines on donations, as set out in the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, are strictly followed, as has been the case with all donations.”

Farage is fighting a byelection after resigning his seat of Clacton. All other mainstream parties have declined to stand a candidate against him, though there are 34 independents on the ballot paper, including novelty candidates such as Count Binface.
