articles.title: Washington's grizzly bear power grab is finally coming to a long-overdue end
articles.excerpt:
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum discusses President Donald Trump honoring veterans and American exceptionalism during celebrations for America's 250th birthday on ‘One Nation.’ (Courtesy: Freedom 250)
...
articles.body_text:
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum discusses President Donald Trump honoring veterans and American exceptionalism during celebrations for America's 250th birthday on ‘One Nation.’ (Courtesy: Freedom 250)

For far too long, federal bureaucrats who have never set foot on Wyoming lands have controlled decisions about our wildlife. That era is finally ending, thanks to the Trump administration. Last week, Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum announced a new rule giving Wyoming and our neighboring states the flexibility to manage grizzly bear populations that have thrived in recent decades.

The Greater Yellowstone grizzly bear population tells one of America's greatest conservation success stories. When these bears were listed under the Endangered Species Act (ESA) in 1975, we had roughly 136 bears in the ecosystem. Today, that population has grown to an estimated 1,000 bears — more than a seven-fold increase that far exceeds every recovery target ever established. The science is unambiguous: this population is not only recovered but thriving and expanding beyond the boundaries of the Yellowstone region. Yet the grizzly bear remains listed. This defies logic, science, and frankly, the very purpose of the ESA.

Grizzly bears in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem have cleared federal recovery benchmarks since 2004. For two decades, Wyoming has spent tens of millions of dollars building the biologists, conflict response teams, and monitoring programs behind this recovery. Wyoming people know these bears and have earned the right to manage them. Wyoming's Bear Wise program has spent years teaching ranchers and recreationists how to live alongside a growing grizzly population, and it works. Wyoming Game and Fish biologists relocate dozens of bears every year to resolve conflicts before they escalate, including one moved out of Sublette County this summer after a cattle conflict.

HIDDEN DANGER AT POPULAR US NATIONAL PARK FORCES TRAIL CLOSURES AS BEAR SIGHTINGS CLIMB

Glacier National Park authorities said the hiker's "injuries are consistent with those sustained by a bear encounter," adding that the individual was found "approximately 50 feet off the trail in a densely wooded area with downed timber."  (Juan Giribet/VWPics/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

The grizzly was briefly delisted in 2007, only to be relisted by the Obama administration's Fish and Wildlife Service in 2009 after activist litigation. The pattern repeated itself under Biden. When the state petitioned again for delisting, the Biden administration slow-walked the review for years and ultimately rejected it in 2023, again citing the same activist lawsuits and manufactured uncertainty rather than the recovery data Biden’s own agency had collected.

The Biden administration's final word came on January 8, 2025, just twelve days before he left office. With one foot out the door, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service rejected Wyoming's and Montana's delisting petitions yet again, leaning on the same tired excuses as always. In their place, they offered an almost laughable substitute: letting landowners kill a bear without a permit, but only once livestock were already in imminent danger. Ranchers could act only after the damage was already being done. It was bureaucratic sleight of hand dressed up as compromise, and nobody in Wyoming was fooled. After sixteen years of activist litigation and manufactured uncertainty, this was Biden's final parting shot at a region he had spent years

working against, one last slap at the people who had asked Washington, again and again, simply to be trusted with their own land and wildlife.

COUNTRY STAR JOHN RICH JOINS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ADVOCATING FOR LANDOWNERS' RIGHTS

Coastal brown bear, also known as Grizzly Bear, Ursus Arcos, female and cubs. South Central Alaska. United States of America. (Photo by: Education Images/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)  (Education Images/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Biden’s bureaucrats knew the population had recovered. They knew the law required returning management to the states. Instead, they hid behind litigation and let special left-leaning interests dictate wildlife policy for a species they will only ever encounter in a nature documentary.

The ESA was written to recover imperiled species and then return their management to the states once recovery is achieved. When we refuse to delist recovered species, we send a dangerous message: that the ESA is not really about conservation at all, but about permanent federal control.

Wyoming's ranchers, hunters, and wildlife managers live with grizzly bears every day. We understand the balance between conservation and coexistence better than anyone behind a desk in Washington, and that experience is exactly why our folks in Wyoming should be making these management calls.

There are about 60 grizzly bears living in Banff National Park, according to Reuters. (George Rose/Getty Images)

That is why, every Congress, Senator Barrasso, Rep. Hageman, my Senate Western Caucus colleagues, and I introduce legislation to delist the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem population of the grizzly bear. Keeping them listed indefinitely does not help the species; it hurts it and undermines good-faith conservation efforts by eroding public trust in the ESA. When the law loses credibility by refusing to acknowledge its own successes, it becomes harder to build support for protecting species that truly are endangered. It is time to delist the grizzly in our area and let science, not politics, dictate our wildlife policy.

This proposed rule by the Trump administration is a good first step, and I will keep working with Secretary Burgum and my colleagues to see it through to full delisting. Wyoming has earned the right to manage what we helped recover. The science has said so for years. Now, finally, we have a federal government willing to admit it.

President Trump promised to return power to the states. Once again, he is keeping his promises.

U.S. Sen. Cynthia Lummis is a Republican from Wyoming who sits on the Senate Banking, Commerce, and Environment and Public Works committees.

articles.title: Europe burns: a visual guide to the wildfires
articles.excerpt:
Ferocious flames continue to rage in parts of France and Spain, with no sign of abating. We chart the destruction in graphics and pictures

The hellish infernos that have torn through parts of France ...
articles.body_text:
Ferocious flames continue to rage in parts of France and Spain, with no sign of abating. We chart the destruction in graphics and pictures

The hellish infernos that have torn through parts of France and Spain have caused deaths, the evacuation of 330,000 people from their homes, widespread destruction and clouds of toxic smoke. Records have already been smashed and with the fourth heatwave of the European summer setting in, there are few signs of the waves of wildfires ending.

France has already surpassed the worst previous year for the size of the area burned, with August, usually the hottest month, yet to come.

In Spain, the cumulative number of fires in 2026 has also set a new record for this time of year, and the cumulative burnt area remains just below the level reached by late July during a devastating fire season in 2022.

The extreme severity of the blazes is the result of “whiplash” wet-then-dry weather this year, supercharged by the climate crisis. Last winter and much of spring in western Europe was very wet, encouraging heavy growth of trees, shrubs and other vegetation.

However, by May the first of a series of heatwaves had hit Europe. All heatwaves are made more intense and more likely by the global heating caused by fossil fuel burning. The heatwave at the end of June was the most severe ever recorded in Europe and would have been impossible without the added heat from more than a century of carbon pollution.

The high temperatures meant the hot atmosphere strongly evaporated water from rivers and lakes and sucked plants and soil dry, with the conditions made 80 times more likely by global heating. As a result of the drought conditions, vegetation became tinder and the risk of wildfires soared, leading to a series of wildfires scientists have described as “firewaves”.

The situation has been worsened by the unprecedented development of enormous “fire clouds” – pyrocumulonimbus – in France. These form from the heat from huge fires and become a self-feeding firestorm, spitting lightning bolts and sparking further blazes.

The severity of the fires has been extremely challenging for the fire-fighting authorities, who in the past would have expected to extinguish the fires. One firefighter, Javier García, told Associated Press he had never faced anything like it in his two decades in the job.

“The evolution is alarming,” he said, adding that they were now prioritising evacuations and property protection because fast-moving walls of flames were too ferocious.

Many thousands of residents and holidaymakers have had to evacuate, often prompted by urgent alerts sent to their phones. Emergency shelters have been set up, including 78 by the Red Cross in Spain. “This is a pattern we are seeing more and more across Europe: heatwaves, drought and wildfires feeding into one another, and communities bearing the consequences,” said Maria Alcazar Castilla, from the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.

The longer-term damage to homes and livelihoods is yet to be reckoned with, but will be large. The wildfires around Bordeaux have claimed some of the region’s famous vineyards, while the tourism and manufacturing industries around Valencia have been hard hit.

A further longer-term impact will be the damage to health caused by the toxic smoke from the fires. About 1.5 million people a year are estimated to have their lives shortened by wildfire smoke.

Emmanuel Macron, the French president, has described the wildfire emergency as the “toughest” situation the country had dealt with since the second world war. In Spain, Pedro Sánchez, the prime minister, said his country was suffering the effects of the climate crisis.

Europe is the fastest-warming of all continents, owing to an increase in heat dome conditions and the proximity of the Arctic, where reflective ice is melting rapidly.

Simon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, said: “The science on the cause is unequivocal: global heating, driven by humanity burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, is making protracted heatwaves, severe floods and violent mega-storms more frequent, more intense and more costly.

“The awful costs of this climate crisis – both human and economic – are now reaching national emergency levels. What needs to be done is equally clear: leave coal, oil and gas behind faster, scale up renewables and protect people where the impacts are already hitting hardest.”

The EU has watered down a series of green measures in the past year in the face of political opposition and corporate lobbying. Hadja Lahbib, the European commissioner for crisis preparedness, told the Financial Times: “The commission can only be as ambitious as the member states want it to be. When member states drag their feet [on the climate crisis] … there is a real danger and an incalculable price.”

articles.title: ‘Slap in the face’: LA mayor decries bid to rebuild burnt-out warehouse before cleanup is done
articles.excerpt:
Spoilt food smelling like ‘dead body’ plagues residents after weeklong fire, yet company asks permission to rebuild

One month after a huge fire ravaged a Los Angeles warehouse and doomed neighbors to...
articles.body_text:
Spoilt food smelling like ‘dead body’ plagues residents after weeklong fire, yet company asks permission to rebuild

One month after a huge fire ravaged a Los Angeles warehouse and doomed neighbors to a persistent, thick stench of rotting food, the facility’s owners have filed applications to rebuild.

That request to restore the warehouse – which residents called a “ticking bomb” after a similar fire at the building in 2024 – was publicly criticized by the Los Angeles mayor, Karen Bass, in a post on social media earlier this week.

“I can’t believe they would even think about starting the rebuilding process while they haven’t cleaned up the mess they’ve created,” Bass said. “It’s a slap in the face to the families that are forced to live with the consequences of an irresponsible corporation’s actions every single day.”

Applications filed earlier this week with the Los Angeles department of building and safety ask for permission to “repair and rebuild” the building to its “original, pre-fire condition”. The city has not yet approved or denied the permits.

The mess left by a weeklong fire in June remains. Rats, flies and odors have shrouded the area, and local residents have equated the smell of 85m pounds of spoiled food to that of a “dead body”. A recent NBC investigation found that conditions at the warehouse could lead to the rapid population growth of a fly breed known to infect people.

Lineage Logistics, the cold-storage company that operates the warehouse and is managing cleanup efforts, said on 25 July that food waste in the burned-out area of the warehouse had been cleared and is being moved offsite. Demolition of the remaining warehouse would begin this week, Lineage said.

But the city, and the warehouse’s neighbors, say Lineage is not moving fast enough.

The Los Angeles county department of public health said on Wednesday it would begin fining Lineage up to $2,000 a day if it did not resolve “underlying” problems at its facility.

The department has already issued six separate citations in the last week over unsanitary conditions and pest control issues, amounting to $4,500 in fines against Lineage. In a 28 July inspection report, the city reported observing an “accumulation of decaying organic waste, sludge, and food residue” across the property and nearly 200 living or dead flies in that waste.

“Our top priority right now is completing the cleanup as quickly and safely as possible,” a representative for Lineage said in a statement. “The application is for a permit to repair the damage from the fire, which was not caused by the cold storage operations at the facility. This is normal course in the repair process and will not impact or distract us from the important work of cleanup.”

articles.title: Ella Langley's faith and authenticity fuel record-breaking rise, experts say
articles.excerpt:
Country music superstar Ella Langley encouraged fans to not to measure themselves against social media or other people’s expectations during a concert performance.

Ella Langley is making music histor...
articles.body_text:
Country music superstar Ella Langley encouraged fans to not to measure themselves against social media or other people’s expectations during a concert performance.

Ella Langley is making music history without leaving behind the faith, values and traditional sound that first won over fans.

The 27-year-old country star's song "Choosin' Texas" has hit the No. 1 spot on the Billboard Hot 100 chart for the 15th nonconsecutive week, surpassing Mariah Carey's 2005 R&B classic "We Belong Together" and Whitney Houston's iconic 1992 power ballad "I Will Always Love You," both of which spent 14 weeks atop the chart, according to a report published by Billboard on Monday.

Langley became the first solo female artist to top the Billboard Hot 100 for that long with a non-holiday song. Mariah Carey's perennial 1994 holiday hit, "All I Want for Christmas Is You," is the only song by a solo female singer to spend more time at No. 1, with 22 weeks atop the chart.

ELLA LANGLEY'S 'CHOOSIN' TEXAS' SPENDS 15 WEEKS AT NUMBER ONE ON THE BILLBOARD HOT 100

The milestone is the latest achievement in a breakout year that has transformed Langley into one of country music's biggest success stories.

Ella Langley is making music history without abandoning her roots. (SXSW Conference & Festivals via Getty Images)

Beyond the charts, Langley won major industry awards and has expanded her mainstream profile through high-profile brand partnerships, television appearances and recognition from some of country music's most influential artists.

Born in Hope Hull, Alabama, Langley left her hometown in 2019 to move to Nashville, Tennessee, where she spent years writing songs, touring and building a loyal following online.

Langley made her breakthrough with her Riley Green duet "You Look Like You Love Me," which went viral on TikTok, amassed millions of streams on Spotify and Apple Music and introduced her to a wider audience.

The country star's song "Choosin' Texxas" has topped the Billboard Hot 100 for 15 nonconsecutive weeks.  (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

COUNTRY MUSIC STAR RILEY GREEN FIRES UP FANS WITH EPIC NEW SUMMER JAM 'THINK AS YOU DRUNK'

Since then, Langley has emerged as one of country music's most recognizable faces, pairing record-setting commercial success with growing mainstream visibility. The singer recently launched an American Eagle campaign and earned praise from icons including Shania Twain.

Throughout her rise, Langley has continued to publicly discuss her Christian faith and Alabama upbringing while releasing music firmly rooted in traditional country.

She has frequently thanked God during award speeches, and last month went viral for passionate remarks about faith, Christianity and love during a concert in Lexington, Kentucky.

Langley recently landed a campaign with American Eagle.  (Getty Images for American Eagle Outfitters)

While speaking with Rolling Stone last week, Twain described Langley as an "authentic songwriter."

SHANIA TWAIN CALLS ELLA LANGLEY AN 'AUTHENTIC SONGWRITER' WITH A UNIQUE SOUND IN NEW INTERVIEW

"She sounds original," Twain said. "She really does seem very unapologetic."

"That commands respect," Twain added. "I believe what she's saying."

Music and branding experts say those qualities may help explain why Langley has resonated with audiences far beyond country music and why her rise comes at a time when country has become one of America's dominant musical genres.

Shania Twain praised Langley as an "authentic songwriter" and "unapologetic." (Matthew Baker/Getty Images for ABA)

Veteran country music journalist Marcus K. Dowling told Fox News Digital that Langley's appeal isn't a departure from country music's traditions but rather an extension of them.

"Country music has proven that, more often than not, when music, above all else, is rooted in a strong sense of faith, family, and fun, it appeals to a lowest and middle common denominator of Americans better than most any other stereotypical American thing," Dowling said.

"Look at the back to back to back moment for Langley," he continued. "It's a tale of how to break a star in on country that's as old as the genre is: A duet with a more established male performer. A discovery, by the genre's fanbase, that her authentically rooted musicality is real, and pairs well with her spotlight-ready cosmetic appeal."

"Then, a song that ties a female performer to an emotive core defined by lovestruck universal yearnings," he added. "From Patsy Cline singing ‘Crazy’ through to Dolly and "Jolene," Gretchen. Wilson's "Redneck Woman" and more, what Ella's doing has a long lineage of always working when executed with intentionality, honesty, and precision."

Langley made her breakthrough with her Riley Green duet ""You Look Like You Love Me." (Theo Wargo/Getty Images)

Doug Eldridge, founder of Achilles PR, said Langley's success also reflects what audiences are increasingly looking for in entertainers.

"Humility and self-deprecation go a long way, when it comes to connecting with fans," Eldridge said. "In the end, authenticity is a lot like humidity — you can’t see it, but you can feel it; when you do, it’s undeniable."

"Langley has humidity and people embrace that," he added. "At this point, that’s what most of us want: real."

Dowling told Fox News Digital that he believes Langley's rise is emblematic of a broader resurgence that has propelled country music to its greatest level of mainstream popularity in decades.

"We haven't seen country be this pop-dominant in 40 years, dating back to Dolly Parton, Kenny Rogers and the like achieving initial mainstream moments that were almost entirely couched in a very stereotypical brand of blending the Appalachian and Western aesthetics with what, ultimately, country had become as a repository for really great, crossover-friendly pop music," he said.

Langley has continued to frequently speak out about her faith.  (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

Eldridge argued that country's recent dominance is not surprising because its songs often center on universal experiences.

"Most of the artists are singing about topics that the majority of Americans can relate to: loving your family, being proud of your country, first love, lost love, struggling with bills, trying to be a better person, and giving thanks to Jesus," he said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"This has been the foundational basis for American vision, values and virtues for a long time," Eldridge added. "Others are just waking up to that reality."

Langley's growing mainstream appeal has drawn comparisons to Taylor Swift's crossover from her country music beginnings to global pop stardom.

However, Eldridge pointed to what he views as a key difference between the two artists.

The singer's rise has drawn comparisons to Taylor Swift's early career crossover. (Andre Dias Nobre/AFP via Getty Images)

"Langley is more true to country music, than Swift ever was in her early days," Eldridge said. "That said, Swift built an audience — and later, an empire — so she knew what she was doing all along."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Eldridge told Fox News Digital that it is too early to know whether Langley will ultimately follow Swift's trajectory or reach the same level of commercial success. He also pointed out that Swift is far from the first country-pop crossover star.

"Swift deserves all the credit for her self-built, billion-dollar empire, but assigning her sole attribution for the country-pop cross-over is looking past all those artists who successfully built that model and passed down the blueprint," he said.

PR expert Doug Eldridge said Langley should stick to her roots rather than pursue a full pop crossover. (Ethan Miller/Reuters)

Eldridge argued Langley may be better served by continuing to lean into the country sound and faith-based identity that have defined her career rather than pursuing a full-fledged pop crossover.

"Langley has both commercial appeal and a sense of authenticity — it’s hard to maintain both once you fully commit to the pop cross-over," he said.

"Historically speaking, country artists have careers; pop artists have a moment."

Ashley Hume is an entertainment journalist for Fox News Digital and Fox Business who covers breaking news, celebrity culture, major industry events and the business of entertainment.

articles.title: Fifteen elephant deaths at Kenya park may be due to cyanide poisoning
articles.excerpt:
Analysis of samples collected from carcasses found traces of toxic chemical compound, says Kenya Wildlife Service

The recent deaths of 15 elephants near a park in southern Kenya in the past month wer...
articles.body_text:
Analysis of samples collected from carcasses found traces of toxic chemical compound, says Kenya Wildlife Service

The recent deaths of 15 elephants near a park in southern Kenya in the past month were likely caused by the animals ingesting pesticides used on nearby tomato farms, the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) has said.

Erustus Kanga, the agency’s director general, told Citizen TV that analysis of samples collected from the carcasses had found traces of cyanide, a chemical compound used in farming as a predator control poison and a pest fumigant, also used by poachers.

“Cyanide is a highly toxic chemical,” he said. “If elephants consume cyanide, they cannot survive a day or two.”

The deaths occurred in the Kimana sanctuary and Kuku Group ranch areas around Amboseli national park, an area covering 392 sq km (96,865 acres) and that, together with other neighbouring conservancies are home to more than 1,600 elephants.

Kimana town is a leading tomato producer and a place where researchers at the Route to Food Initiative, a food rights programme, have previously reported the use of a cyanide substance on the crop.

Isaac Lekolool, the head of veterinary and capture services at KWS, told Citizen TV that the stomach contents of one member of a herd that roamed Kimana sanctuary included “lots of tomatoes,” suggesting agrochemical poisoning.

Kanga warned that the effects could reach a wider population, as livestock may also eat from farms in the area.

“We have the goats, we have the cattle that are there. Eventually, if this cyanide is truly the one that is in the system, then we are going to see a bigger impact.”

On Tuesday, KWS announced it was investigating the deaths of the elephants from 24 June and 24 July in Amboseli. It said 10 of the elephants had shown signs of partial paralysis before dying and that preliminary tests had detected a potential toxic substance.

Benson Leyian, the CEO of Big Life Foundation, a conservation organisation that operates in the area surrounding Amboseli national park, said the elephant deaths were a cause for concern.

“Thanks to decades of community-centred conservation, the Amboseli elephant population is one of the best protected in Africa, and elephant poaching has been virtually eliminated here. Aside from losses during periods of severe drought, we haven’t seen a cluster of elephant deaths like this for some time,” he said.

In a statement, the International Fund for Animal Welfare described the deaths as “deeply alarming,” adding the incident “reinforces why we must continue investing in science, monitoring, and collaborative conservation efforts”.

“Every elephant lost is significant – not only for the species, but for the health of the ecosystems they help sustain and the communities that live alongside them,” it said.

Farmers and herders in Kenya have in the past poisoned wildlife in retaliation for eating their crops and livestock.

In Zimbabwe, poachers have killed dozens of elephants by lacing watering holes and salt licks with the chemical compound.

The Amboseli ecosystem is a major source of tourism revenue, but tensions have been building in recent months as local leaders demand the handover of the park’s management and operations to the government of Kajiado county, where it is located. Earlier this month, a court suspended the county government’s takeover.

articles.title: 'Worst aquarium ever' review sends whaling museum's sales soaring 250%
articles.excerpt:
Maurene Calago was posing underwater for photos in the Philippines when a whale shark approached unnoticed and nudged her arm, prompting a quick retreat to the surface to avoid further contact.

A mus...
articles.body_text:
Maurene Calago was posing underwater for photos in the Philippines when a whale shark approached unnoticed and nudged her arm, prompting a quick retreat to the surface to avoid further contact.

A museum is cashing in after a one-star Google review calling it the "worst aquarium ever" became an unexpected viral hit.

The New Bedford Whaling Museum in Massachusetts, which highlights the history, science and art of whaling rather than marine animals, embraced the one-star review by boldly printing the phrase on T-shirts, sweatshirts and tote bags.

The merchandise has since gone viral on social media — sending sales soaring by 250% in just one week, The Associated Press (AP) reported.

MYSTERY OF GOLD COIN SHIPWRECK FINALLY UNMASKED AFTER 30 YEARS: 'FANTASTIC CONCLUSION'

The now-famous review was posted on Google in 2020 after a visitor mistakenly referred to the museum as an aquarium, writing that it was "the worst aquarium ever."

Rather than ignore the criticism, staff turned it into a merchandise design last fall, featuring the review on the back and a whale skeleton on the front.

The shirt pictured above is part of the New Bedford Whaling Museum's merchandise inspired by the one-star Google review. (Anna Albrecht/The New Bedford Light via AP)

The shirts have recently gained national attention after they were featured in multiple news outlets, helping to introduce the museum to an even wider audience.

"They took a chance on something, and it obviously hit," Amanda McMullen, president and CEO of the museum, told the AP.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Adding to the irony, the museum opened a 250-gallon saltwater tank earlier this year featuring local marine life, including blue crabs, sea stars and northern puffer fish, as part of a partnership with the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth's School for Marine Science and Technology.

The unexpected success reflects the institution's personality, said Annelise Conway, chief engagement officer at the Whaling Museum.

The New Bedford Whaling Museum in Massachusetts, pictured above, showcases the history, science, art and culture of whaling through exhibits that include whale skeletons. (David L. Ryan/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

"There isn't a strategy to be authentic," Conway told the AP. "It just sort of happens."

"The person who sold you your ticket is the person who is modeling the merchandise," Conway added.

The museum's decision to embrace the joke has also won over social media users, who praised it for turning the review into a marketing success.

"I love it. Kudos to the museum for leaning into the joke and embracing it," one Reddit user wrote.

The museum's decision to embrace the joke also earned praise on social media, where users applauded its clever marketing. (Tim Graham/Getty Images; Anna Albrecht/The New Bedford Light via AP)

Another commenter joked, "I think it takes courage to walk into a museum with the word 'Whaling' in the name and think, 'I bet there's a dolphin show.'"

Others said the museum deserves the newfound attention.

"It's honestly a great museum," a user commented. "I love that it's gone viral because it's just a wonderful place to support."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Whaling Museum for comment.

The Associated Press contributed reporting.

Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Only the Middle East crisis is preventing a drop in UK interest rates
articles.excerpt:
Bank’s wariness about inflationary pressures from the conflict lie behind decision to hold steady at 3.75%

There is a threat of high inflation coming to the UK but only from the conflict in the Middl...
articles.body_text:
Bank’s wariness about inflationary pressures from the conflict lie behind decision to hold steady at 3.75%

There is a threat of high inflation coming to the UK but only from the conflict in the Middle East, which could keep oil prices high for much longer than was expected when Donald Trump first began attacking Iran.

It is the war that makes the difference between a benign outlook for inflation and one that puts it back on a rising trajectory, senior UK central bankers believe.

The Bank of England’s monetary policy committee was clear in its decision on Thursday to hold interest rates at 3.75% that underlying pressures on inflation are almost entirely absent in the domestic economy. Prices are stable and, without the war, would be rising steadily at the central bank’s 2% target.

Threadneedle Street officials are worried that retail prices will ratchet up if companies spot a way to increase them, taking advantage of a general expectation among consumers that the war has raised the costs of production. They also fear that workers will see another rise in inflation coming and pitch for a major increase in wages.

They haven’t seen any of these trends yet. If anything, the opposite is true and the spillover, or second-round effects from rising energy and transport costs, remain muted.

Supermarkets have proved resilient and kept food inflation low. Services companies – for so long after the pandemic a source of rising prices – have managed to restrict increases this year.

As the Bank’s quarterly review says: “So far, there are few signs of second-round effects. But there is not enough evidence yet to rule out this risk, and the MPC will continue to monitor evidence closely.”

Annual wage increases are low across the private sector, at 2.8% in the second quarter of this year. They are expected to rise to 3% in the third quarter, but that increase keeps wage increases at a level Bank officials are comfortable with.

As for companies capitalising on a period of rising prices whether or not it actually affects them, the official data does not show that happening across the manufacturing, construction or services industries.

The three MPC members who voted to increase the cost of borrowing this month acknowledge that neither workers nor firms have reacted to inflation. They argue that the figures we have seen – the latest being the drop in the consumer prices index (CPI) to 2.6% in June – are a reflection of cost pressures, or more precisely the lack of them, going into the conflict. Once prices begin to rise again, workers and companies are bound to react, they argue, embedding inflationary pressures into the UK economy even if the Middle East war is settled.

The majority on the MPC focused more on the labour market and a rise in unemployment and sharp fall in vacancies over the last three years. They also see that financial markets have reacted by raising mortgage and commercial lending rates, tightening the screw on homebuyers and firms without the Bank making a move itself.

If anything, businesses that want to invest and with that employ more people could do with a boost from lower interest rates.

It is only Donald Trump’s failure to confect an exit from the Middle East crisis that stands in the way of that.

The Bank’s forecasters expect inflation to peak at 3.2% next spring, but say it could be much higher, at 4.1%, if the war persists and Brent crude prices go back above $100 a barrel and stay there.

The National Institute of Economic and Social Research said this week that the UK had already lost the equivalent of £28bn in growth this year as a result of the Middle East conflict.

The Bank’s warning that it might need to raise rates if the war continues means the impact on businesses, consumers and mortgage borrowers could, unless Trump pulls back, be much more severe.

articles.title: Detained Ugandan opposition leader Besigye in intensive care, wife says
articles.excerpt:
Detained Ugandan opposition leader Kizza Besigye has been hospitalised in an unresponsive state after he collapsed during a court hearing on Wednesday, according to his wife.

Besigye, who has been in...
articles.body_text:
Detained Ugandan opposition leader Kizza Besigye has been hospitalised in an unresponsive state after he collapsed during a court hearing on Wednesday, according to his wife.

Besigye, who has been in prison since late 2024 on treason charges, is now “unconscious, unable to speak, and unresponsive”, his wife, Winnie Byanyima, said in a post on X on Thursday.

He has been admitted to the intensive care unit at Mulago National Referral Hospital in the capital, Kampala, added Winnie Byanyima, who also ‌heads the United Nations AIDS programme UNAIDS.

Byanyima has called for her husband to be transferred out of Mulago hospital, a public facility, and into a private facility where he can be treated by his personal physician.

“[Besigye’s] family is saying he needs special treatment and they do not trust the government hospital,” reported Al Jazeera’s Catherine Soi from Nairobi in neighbouring Kenya.

“There’s a lot of frustration. The court has not granted that permission for him to be transferred.”

Besigye, 70, was seen falling into the dock during his Wednesday courtroom session while protesting against his trial without lawyers of his own choosing, after authorities also detained and charged his main lawyer, Erias Lukwago.

“Before he collapsed, he cried out that he was being injured,” said Byanyima.

Ingrid Turinawe, a close confidant of Besigye, told The Associated Press that she and others were not allowed to see Besigye at Mulago hospital.

“He is in the ICU, and he is not responding to anything,” she said, adding that Besigye’s personal physician was able to see him several hours after he collapsed.

Besigye, a former ally-turned-critic of longtime President Yoweri ‌Museveni, has been in custody since November 2024. He was jailed together with his aide Obeid Lutale in Kenya and ⁠both were repatriated to Uganda where they were subsequently charged with treason.

Besigye’s lawyers, ⁠supporters and rights activists say ⁠that the charges are politically motivated and that his prolonged detention is part of an ongoing crackdown on opponents by ‌Museveni.

Both Museveni and his son, military chief Muhoozi Kainerugaba, have already weighed in against Besigye.

Kainerugaba, alleging that Besigye plotted to kill his father, has previously described the opposition figure as “a dead man walking”. And Museveni himself has said Besigye must answer for “the very serious offences he is alleged to have been planning”.

In recent days, prosecutors have moved to present evidence they say will prove Besigye and others plotted to overthrow the government

Museveni, 81, was declared winner of the last election in January although the results were rejected by ‌runner-up ‌Bobi Wine, who has since gone into exile in the United States.

articles.title: HMRC fines Airbus £6.4m for breaching rules on export of sensitive technology
articles.excerpt:
Company self-reported offences that led to tax authority’s largest out-of-court settlement for such breaches

Airbus has been fined £6.4m in the UK after the European aerospace company admitted to mul...
articles.body_text:
Company self-reported offences that led to tax authority’s largest out-of-court settlement for such breaches

Airbus has been fined £6.4m in the UK after the European aerospace company admitted to multiple breaches of rules designed to stop sensitive goods such as military hardware falling into the wrong hands.

The company, which sits at the heart of the European defence industry, said it had paid the settlement to the UK’s tax authority, HM Revenue and Customs, after self-reporting breaches that occurred before November 2022.

HMRC said the offences related to a failure by Airbus to keep records of the export or transfer of controlled technology over a sustained period.

The UK’s export control licensing regime is designed to prevent strategic goods such as military items and goods that can be used in weapons of mass destruction programmes being sold overseas or to sanctioned individuals and countries.

The £6.4m payment is the highest out-of-court settlement ever reached by HMRC for strategic export offences and more that 10 times higher than the more than £569,100 that an Aberdeen-based division of energy company Petrofac paid to HMRC last month for breaching Russia sanctions regulations.

While Airbus cooperated with HMRC’s investigation, its failure to follow the rules is particularly notable, given the pivotal role it plays in Europe’s defence sector, working on projects including the Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet and the A400M heavy cargo aircraft.

“The UK operates a strict licensing regime […] to ensure military equipment does not fall into the wrong hands,” said Edwige Hill, deputy director of HMRC’s fraud investigation service.

“We use a range of powers to ensure effective controls and enforcement on military goods, which contributes to the UK’s national security. This settlement shows we will not hesitate to take action.”

Failing to keep accurate records of transfers of controlled technology as per the conditions of three of their Open General Export Licences (Ogels).

Multiple occasions failures to keep registers in relation to Ogels.

Failing to keep accurate records contrary to the conditions of one of their Ogels.

A failure of licence conditions on a standard individual export licence (SIEL).

An Ogel is a reusable, pre-approvied licence for multiple shipments of items generally considered low-risk. An SIEL is a more detailed permission, requiring government approval for a specific quantity of items going to a single, named end-user.

The fine was issued to Airbus Operations Limited (AOL), a UK division of Airbus, whose manufacturing headquarters are in Toulouse, France.

In its statement to investors, the company said: “AOL fully cooperated with the investigation and implemented appropriate remediation measures. This settlement closes and fully resolves the matter.”

Sanctions lawyer Nigel Kushner, chief executive of law firm W Legal, said the fine would shake up compliance. “This is a wake up call for UK exporters. It is not enough to obtain licences or rest on your laurels utilising pre-approved licences available to all.

“It is critical to comply with the licence terms, in particular record keeping and updating registers. The failure to do so is an offence in itself as Airbus have been reminded to its cost.”

In 2020, Airbus agreed to pay a record £3bn in penalties after admitting it had paid huge bribes on an “endemic” basis to land contracts in 20 countries.

articles.title: Families to no longer be housed in billionaire-owned tower after suffering without air con
articles.excerpt:
Some residents in glass-fronted block say they are still ‘fighting to stay cool’ in Britannia Point in south-west London

As the fourth heatwave of the year hit the UK on Wednesday, Benice Bodah and h...
articles.body_text:
Some residents in glass-fronted block say they are still ‘fighting to stay cool’ in Britannia Point in south-west London

As the fourth heatwave of the year hit the UK on Wednesday, Benice Bodah and her three teenage sons braced for more scorching temperatures inside their south-west London home. The two-bedroom flat has a built-in air-conditioning unit, but it has worked only intermittently in the almost three years since the family were placed in temporary accommodation at Britannia Point in Colliers Wood. “It has not been easy, but what can we do?” said Bodah, 48.

Several councils have now agreed to stop housing families in emergency accommodation in the glass-fronted block after the Guardian revealed they were told they couldn’t use the built-in air-conditioning during heatwaves as it had “not been offered as an amenity” for them. The 19-storey building is owned by Criterion Capital, set up by the billionaire property magnate Asif Aziz. The temporary tenancies can last from weeks to years and are managed separately by letting agencies, including London-based Aura Assets Management.

Wandsworth council, which has placed residents in the block, is now making “immediate” plans to remove their tenants from the tower. A Wandsworth council spokesperson said: “As ever, the welfare of residents is our priority and we are working at pace to ensure suitable alternative accommodation is available.”

Sutton council said it had already stopped placing people there, and was “working closely with all remaining Sutton residents in the building to ensure they are able to move to other accommodation”. Croydon council said it faced very high demand for temporary accommodation, and was not removing people, but had raised concerns with Criterion and that council staff had been carrying out “welfare checks” with those in the block.

Stuart Neaverson, a Labour councillor in Merton who has been assisting residents, has called on other councils which have placed residents in the building to follow suit. “Criterion Capital, who own the building and the air conditioning units, need to explain how this could ever happen and why some residents are still going without while temperatures hit 35C,” he said.

A spokesperson for Criterion Capital said: “As the freeholder, we engage with our leaseholders and encourage them to work with local authorities to support tenants in these unprecedented circumstances.” Aura Assets Management has been approached for comment.

Since the Guardian reported that temporary accommodation households were prohibited from using in-built air conditioning, some have been receiving letters saying they could “feel free to use” it if it was working, at a cost of between £35 and £50 each month. However, some tenants are still without working units and others have said the additional charge is unaffordable.

By Wednesday evening, the unit in Bodah’s flat was working, but she said she has no choice but to keep it switched off because she cannot afford the extra cost.

Several temporary residents with tenancies managed by Aura told the Guardian on Wednesday that repeated complaints over inoperative air conditioning units have been left unresolved, in some cases, for more than a year.

One tenant, Mahad Maalin, who is living with his 81-year-old mother, had given up on the air conditioning unit after the issue was not resolved last summer. Like Bodah, he said he would not pay the cost of running it for the remaining month of summer, and instead has two fans and keeps the blinds drawn.

Another tenant, Sabrina Walters, raised concerns over her children’s health as her one-year-old daughter was overheating and her 12-year-old suffered cluster nose bleeds, which can be caused by overheating.

“I’m not fussed about myself, but when it comes to my child’s health, especially at that age: she’s one year old, she didn’t ask to be over-dehydrated,” said Walters. “She’s clammy, so you can tell it’s her body fighting to keep cool. That really pissed me off.”

The family escaped the heat of their flat by going outside, which they said was cooler, or would spend time in one room with multiple fans. The windows in their third-floor flat don’t extend fully.

It was only after Walters raised the matter with her local MP that her air-conditioning unit was turned back on, after a two-week outage. She said other residents, including a mother of two, have told her that their air conditioning units remain broken. “I felt bad even saying mine is on to be honest,” said the 31-year- old.

Before councils announced they had removed their tenants from the tower, Walters was relieved to soon be moving elsewhere. “I don’t like having to feel like I have to argue to live somewhere,” she said.

Earlier this year Criterion Capital was accused of trying to mass evict tenants in the weeks leading up to the banning of no-fault evictions, which it has denied.

Aura previously told the Guardian the air conditioning was now “fully operational” and when asked about the email sent to a resident saying tenants in temporary accommodation were not given access to air conditioning, said it was “issued by the building management” based on “information and operational arrangements in place at the time”.

articles.title: Record absence of world’s oldest head of state reignites health speculation
articles.excerpt:
Cameroon’s president has not made statement or been seen since leaving for ‘brief private stay’ at Swiss hotel on 7 June

A record 53-day absence of the world’s oldest head of state has renewed specul...
articles.body_text:
Cameroon’s president has not made statement or been seen since leaving for ‘brief private stay’ at Swiss hotel on 7 June

A record 53-day absence of the world’s oldest head of state has renewed speculation in his native Cameroon about whether he is dead or alive, even though discussing his health is illegal in the country.

On 7 June, 93-year-old Paul Biya departed for Switzerland for what officials described as a “brief private stay” alongside his wife, Chantal. Almost two months later, neither the president nor the first lady have addressed the country or been seen publicly.

Biya, who took office in 1982 after a seven-year stint as prime minister, has taken increasingly long absences from Cameroon in recent years, spending much of his time at the five-star InterContinental hotel in Geneva.

No official timetable has been announced for the president’s return from his latest trip abroad, leaving Cameroonians to rely on a succession of conflicting statements from government officials.

The minister of communication, René Emmanuel Sadi, said Biya was in good health and “working from Geneva, where he currently resides”.

“Reports claiming otherwise are pure fantasy and malicious manipulation aimed at destabilising opinion,” he added. Jacques Fame Ndongo, a senior official from the ruling party and the higher education minister, said Biya had been “meticulously following the files submitted to him by his aides … wherever he is”.

The labour minister, Grégoire Owona, gave a different explanation, saying the president was on annual leave and comparing him to regular Cameroonian citizens. “Paul Biya, elected by the Cameroonian people and paid by them, is a worker who has the right to annual leave,” he said. “His employer is obliged to grant it. He informed his employer before leaving and will do the same upon his return.”

Cameroonian authorities banned discussion of Biya’s health in October 2024, during another absence. Nevertheless, local media have published claims in recent weeks that he is critically ill, and jokes about Biya being a work-from-abroad president or a remote-work president, have resurfaced on social media.

Mamadou Mota, the vice-president of the opposition Cameroon Renaissance Movement party, said Biya’s latest absence had created a “glaring institutional vacuum”. “A country cannot be governed by remote control while critical socioeconomic challenges go unaddressed,” he said.

Last November, Biya was sworn in for his eighth consecutive seven-year term, a month after a presidential election marred by widespread allegations of irregularities and voter suppression. Although the Constitutional Council dismissed post-electoral complaints by opposition parties, many of them refused to recognise the outcome, arguing that the election had further eroded public confidence in Cameroon’s democratic institutions.

Biya has yet to name a government since being sworn in for his latest term. With parliamentary and municipal elections expected in early 2027, many are worried that the ripple effect of that and his prolonged absence could disrupt the electoral cycle.

Cameroon has the largest economy in central Africa, but unemployment rates, high inflation and poor public infrastructure are stymieing the prospects of its young people, who make up about two-thirds of its estimated population of 30.6 million.

“Politics should be about serving the people, but the [ruling] CPDM [party] appears more interested in holding on to power than addressing the concerns of Cameroonians,” said Kohtem Sambit, the secretary general of the opposition Movement for Patriotism and People’s Prosperity.

“The minister of the economy borrowed more than 21bn [Central African francs] in the name of the Cameroonian people, saying it was approved by Mr Biya,” Sambit told the Guardian. “How do we justify this? You do not see the person who signed, nor do you know his whereabouts. That debt will be paid by the public.”

Referring to Owona’s remarks, Sambit said: “If the president is on annual leave, he is still accountable to the Cameroonian people because he is paid with taxpayers’ money. His whereabouts should therefore be disclosed.”

Another opposition party, the Social Democratic Front, has argued that the issue is not whether the president has a constitutional right to travel, but rather the government’s failure to explain the extension of what had initially been described as a brief private visit. Another opposition leader, Patricia Tomaïno Ndam Njoya, of the Cameroon Democratic Union, has called for an impartial procedure to determine any “temporary or permanent incapacity of the head of state”.

In April, parliament reintroduced the office of vice-president as part of a constitutional overhaul, but the position has yet to be filled, leaving Cameroon without a designated deputy should the president become incapacitated. As Biya’s son and stepson reportedly jockey for position, public disagreements between cabinet ministers have become commonplace.

Last week, the party’s secretary general, Jean Nkuete, convened a rare meeting of senior party officials. The CPDM described the gathering only as an “important working session” and released neither an agenda nor further details. Attempts to obtain comment from senior party figures were unsuccessful. Several party officials have declined interview requests, citing personal reasons.

For the businessman Nji Lucas, the president’s prolonged absence has also become an economic concern. “I do not have confidence because it is almost as if the country is on autopilot,” he said. “No serious investor wants to commit resources in a country where there is uncertainty over political leadership. There is no trust, and investors require certainty before making long-term decisions.”

articles.title: Florida Gators coach reveals damning clip of ESPN host sniffing a high-heel as foot feud escalates
articles.excerpt: OutKick host Dan Dakich shares insights on the congressional hearing concerning college sports and player transfers, with Nick Saban expected to testify. Dakich also criticizes Steph Curry's 10-year s...
articles.body_text:
OutKick host Dan Dakich shares insights on the congressional hearing concerning college sports and player transfers, with Nick Saban expected to testify. Dakich also criticizes Steph Curry's 10-year sportswear deal with Chinese brand Li-Ning, questioning the NBA's relationship with China and civil rights.

We're two days away from August, and the college football season is already starting to heat up.

New Florida Gators head coach Jon Sumrall and ESPN football analyst Dan Orlovsky have been going back and forth this week over the most offseason topic of all time: pedicures.

ESPN'S DAN ORLOVSKY WEIGHS IN ON FLORIDA COACH JON SUMRALL'S PEDICURE PREFERENCES, IMMEDIATELY GETS ROASTED

That's right. You read that right. Pedicures.

Sumrall's wife let the cat out of the bag last week that the new UF coach has a secret passion for pedicures, saying that it's his "favorite extra thing to do," and that he gets one "every two weeks during football season."

Relatively harmless interview, and one that, frankly, I didn't think would get much play given the news cycle.

Orlovsky hopped on ESPN's 'Get Up' this week, and angered America when he declared that he was "completely against pedicures for dudes."

Florida head coach Jon Sumrall watches drills during spring practice at Sanders Practice Fields in Gainesville, Fla., on Thursday, March 12, 2026. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

"You're a dude. You're not supposed to get pedicures. I am so against this. You should not be getting pedicures... I'd rather have awful feet than get pedicures," he continued.

Everyone is entitled to their opinion, and Orlovsky made his stance clear. In turn, Sumrall took to X and stuffed the ESPN analyst in a locker with a photo so damning, I'm not even sure Orlovsky can come back from it:

Hand up, I forgot that picture/video of Dan Orlovsky existed. For those who don't follow ESPN religiously (all of you, I hope), that's a clip from a few years back on 'First Take' when Orlovsky, for some reason, decided to smell host Molly Qerim's shoe live on air.

My God. What a scene. What a moment for ESPN.

How does Dan Orlovsky, in good faith, make the pedicure comments when he KNOWS that clip is lingering in the ether? If I knew that footage existed, I would never, ever, ever, hop on ESPN and say a single word about feet.

I'd keep my mouth shut, my head down, and my eyes forward, and just pray nobody ever brings it back up.

Head coach Jon Sumrall of the Florida Gators waits to take the field before the Orange and Blue Game at Ben Hill Griffin Stadium on April 11, 2026, in Gainesville, Fla. (Getty Images for ONIT)

PS: I don't agree with Orlovsky because I know plenty of dudes who get pedicures (well, just two, but still), but I also don't think it was the dumbest thing I've ever heard someone say. It's locker room talk. Guy speak. Clubhouse banter.

If you're in a locker room and say you get pedicures, you're gonna catch flack, even if the other dudes in there get them, too. That's how we operate.

ESPN Broadcaster Dan Orlovsky speaks before the game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Detroit Lions at M&T Bank Stadium on Sept. 22, 2025 in Baltimore, Maryland. (G Fiume/Getty Images)

I have no idea how the Gators are going to be this season. I assume pretty mediocre given the past decade, but maybe I'm wrong.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

I do know that Jon Sumrall is off to a blazing start with this takedown of Dan Orlovsky. We need more of this at UF. Things have gotten so bland around here.

articles.title: California lifeguard speaks out on heartstopping ocean rescue: 'I love what I do'
articles.excerpt: Founder of Drown Zero Wyatt Werneth joins 'Fox & Friends' to discuss the dramatic video showing a 16-year-old lifeguard battling powerful 8-10 foot surf waves and rip currents to rescue a 10-year-old ...
articles.body_text:
Founder of Drown Zero Wyatt Werneth joins 'Fox & Friends' to discuss the dramatic video showing a 16-year-old lifeguard battling powerful 8-10 foot surf waves and rip currents to rescue a 10-year-old boy in Santa Cruz, Calif.

A 16-year-old lifeguard whose daring rescue of a 10-year-old on Saturday went viral finally spoke out about the harrowing save in a Wednesday statement.

Ryder Williams, the teen hero whose daring rescue of a young boy at Santa Cruz Beach on Saturday captivated the nation, described the episode in a statement released by his employer, California State Parks.

"I was at the waterline 15 yards downcoast of Tower 2 making a safety contact when I looked up and saw a child about 20 (yards) up from the tower lose his footing in ankle deep water," the statement opened.

OFF-DUTY ICE OFFICER RELIES ON 'SIXTH SENSE' TO SAVE DROWNING CHILD BEFORE DELIVERING MESSAGE TO CRITICS

Sixteen-year-old lifeguard Ryder Williams repeatedly disappeared beneath towering waves while refusing to let go of a child swept into dangerous California surf in Santa Cruz, California on July 25, 2026. (Scott Vander Dussen/Instagram @Santacruznow)

"I radioed it in, threw my radio and sunglasses at the base of my tower as I ran toward the kid. I put my fins on my wrist, popped my buoy and entered the water to get ahold of the child. Due to the volatility of the water, I was unable to tube up the victim. After the first wave I was unable to pull him out because he was limp and the waves were pushing so hard. There were two to three more waves before lifeguard Aaron Bohnen entered the water to help me. There were bystanders who jumped in to try to help, and I yelled at them all to get back to shore," Williams' statement continued.

"Once Bohnen and I got the kid to shore I was instructed to get the med bag from Bohnen’s unit and we assessed the child. Shortly after, I got back into my tower where I returned to provide lifeguard services for the rest of my shift," he continued.

‘HERO' MOM DIES AFTER USING LAST STRENGTH TO SAVE 4-YEAR-OLD SON FROM FLORIDA RIVER

"I’m grateful to have had the opportunity to return the child to his family safely. This is my job and I love what I do. I’m thankful to my fellow lifeguards who perform rescues just like this every day," Williams' statement concluded.

Witnesses say the dramatic rescue lasted far longer than the viral video shows, with the teen lifeguard refusing to release the child despite punishing surf. (Scott Vander Dussen/Instagram @Santacruznow)

Williams' heroics earned him national attention, praise and even an invitation to the White House.

MISSING GRAND CANYON HIKER, 83, RESCUED AFTER GETTING SEPARATED FROM COMPANION

"We’re going to bring this heroic young man, and his family, into the White House with, perhaps, the boy he saved, to give him a High Civilian Honor. Very brave, he deserves it!" the White House wrote in an X post attributed to President Donald Trump.

Williams' rescue was one of 34 rescues in the Santa Cruz district over the weekend, California State Parks said in a statement obtained by FOX 2 KTVU.

"All California State Park lifeguard towers were staffed, there were 6 units on, a two-person rescue water craft team, three permanent lifeguard units, and a lifeguard supervisor working in Pajaro Coast," California State Parks also said of the weekend.

Witnesses say the dramatic rescue lasted far longer than the viral video shows, with Ryder Williams refusing to release the child despite punishing surf. (Scott Vander Dussen/Instagram @Santacruznow)

The 10-year-old boy Williams rescued was identified by KTVU as being named Nathaniel. His father, Sumit Rai, praised Williams' efforts in an interview with KTVU.

"It was a remarkable effort to bring him back to shore. I mean Ryder fought the sea," he told the outlet.

"It's really hard to fight that, and my son was unconscious. He weighs about 100 pounds, and he was limp, so that's basically dead weight that he had to carry and hold onto to pull back to shore," he continued.

"It's so easy to let go, and he knew that if he lets go then he's gonna basically just float away, and he's gone. That's the end of it, and he would have died," Rai concluded.

Fox News Digital contacted California State Parks for comment and additional information.

articles.title: NFL employees’ troubling driving incidents mount, costing jobs and putting others at risk
articles.excerpt:
Bodycam footage shows Tony Romo using a cop car to stretch before taking his sobriety test. (Credit: Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office)

Many years ago, before drunk-driving charges were euphemized as...
articles.body_text:
Bodycam footage shows Tony Romo using a cop car to stretch before taking his sobriety test. (Credit: Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office)

Many years ago, before drunk-driving charges were euphemized as driving while intoxicated, Dan Marino liked to imbibe a little. But he also enjoyed getting around South Florida because he was the quarterback of the Miami Dolphins, not a hermit.

Marino understood his stature in the community and what an unacceptable pratfall a drinking and driving charge would be on charges of his reputation. So he bought a limousine. And he hired a driver.

That driver, who happened to be the father of future NFL great and current Carolina Panthers general manager Dan Morgan, would drive Marino everywhere, making sure the star quarterback, who liked a few drinks now and then, never had any issues on the road.

Miami Dolphins quarterback Dan Marino broke Fran Tarkenton's NFL career completion record with his 3,687th career completion on his fourth completion of the game. Marino finished the day with 3,702 career completions during a game against the Indianapolis Colts at Joe Robbie Stadium in Miami, Florida, on Oct. 8, 1995. (CHRIS BERNACCHI/AFP via Getty Images)

TONY ROMO ARRESTED IN MILWAUKEE FOR ALLEGED OWI OFFENSE: REPORT

The NFL, its players and coaches could definitely use more of Dan Marino's thinking now because events in the past couple of years suggest the league has something of a driving problem.

Consider what has happened this month so far:

Rueben Bain Jr of the Miami (FL) Hurricanes speaks to the media during the 2026 NFL Scouting Combine at Lucas Oil Stadium on Feb. 25, 2026, in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Justin Casterline/Getty Images)

VIKINGS SUSPEND ASSISTANT GERALD ALEXANDER AFTER GUILTY DUI PLEA

The Washington Commanders fired tight end coach Ben Steele on the eve of training camp following a DWI arrest in June.

"Certainly really wish the best for Ben and his family," Commanders general manager Adam Peters said this week. "A lot of thought was put into that decision and, you know, it was unfortunate but hoping for the best for him and his family."

Before the draft, OutKick reported that University of Miami defensive lineman Rueben Bain Jr. got into an accident in October 2025 and was cited for reckless driving. That followed a March 2024 fatal accident in which Bain hit another car on I-95 in South Florida, setting off a chain reaction accident that eventually left one of his passengers non-responsive.

Bain was drafted in the first round by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, but the Top 10 prospect dropped to the No. 15 overall slot.

In this screen grab taken from dash camera video provided by Bill Nabors, two speeding sports cars, left and second from left, cause a chain-reaction crash on the North Central Expressway, in Dallas, Saturday, March 30, 2024. Dallas police said Wednesday, April 10, 2024, that Kansas City Chiefs' wide receiver Rashee Rice faces charges including aggravated assault after he and another speeding driver of a sports car caused a chain-reaction crash on a Dallas highway. (Bill Nabors via AP)

Kansas City Chiefs receiver Rashee Rice served 30 days in jail from May to June because he tested positive for THC (marijuana) and the reason we know this is because those tests are part of a probation agreement stemming from his well-chronicled driving conviction.

Rice in July 2025 pleaded guilty to third-degree felony charges (collision involving serious bodily injury, and racing on a highway causing bodily injury) following a high-speed March 2024 crash in Dallas.

Fox News Digital compiled records of 21 driving incidents involving NFL people dating back to 2024 that speak to drinking and driving, reckless driving or simply bad decision-making behind the wheel when viewed individually.

But when one understands NFL-connected people – not including their families – are involved in more than one traffic-related mishap per month on average, it could signal a problem.

An NFL spokesman could not be reached for comment on this matter, but a league source told Fox News Digital this is an individual and club matter.

Clubs instruct their employees not to drink and drive, something they probably should already know. Some clubs connect players and others with rideshare programs or tell players to call club security if they feel unsure of their ability to drive.

But a large percentage of these incidents, like Shanahan's head-on collision, do not involve alcohol.

More NFL drivers apparently could learn something from the Dan Marino example.

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

articles.title: Zac Brown Band's John Driskell Hopkins says he's 'chasing the clock' after ALS diagnosis
articles.excerpt:
John Driskell Hopkins told Fox News Digital that he's been trying to fit in as much as possible since his diagnosis in 2021.

Zac Brown Band's John Driskell Hopkins is opting to look at his ALS (amyot...
articles.body_text:
John Driskell Hopkins told Fox News Digital that he's been trying to fit in as much as possible since his diagnosis in 2021.

Zac Brown Band's John Driskell Hopkins is opting to look at his ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) diagnosis in a different light and is trying to make everyday count.

Over a decade after the Ice Bucket Challenge surfaced on social media, it is making a comeback. During an interview with Fox News Digital about the challenge, Hopkins explained that after his diagnosis in 2021, he's been "chasing the clock" ever since.

"I'm almost busier now than I was before because I'm trying to get so much done. I'm tryin' to fit it all in. I'm taking more family vacations. I'm in the studio more than I should be. I'm still on tour with Zac Brown Band right now. You know, my fingers work. My voice works, it's been compromised, but most of the set, no one would notice," Hopkins, a founding member of Zac Brown Band, said.

John Driskell Hopkins of Zac Brown Band was diagnosed with ALS in 2021. (Derek White/Getty Images for The Recording Academy)

He continued, "And I'm playing different things on stage, but they still don't make sense. You know, I'm chasing the clock more than I ever have been. And what I worry about is that that is causing me stress, which might be exacerbating my condition. So it's a bit of a catch-22, you know, I've created."

ZAC BROWN BAND'S JOHN DRISKELL HOPKINS FIGHTS ALS DIAGNOSIS: ‘CRYING SUCKS’

Acknowledging the reality of his diagnosis, Hopkins said that he's looking toward the future where he might not be able to sing.

"I hope that my progression continues to be slow and that I can sing for a long time, but who knows?" he said.

In 2014, Hopkins and the Zac Brown Band participated in the ALS Ice Bucket Challenge on social media – years before his diagnosis. At the time, Hopkins had no idea what the disease was, let alone that he would be diagnosed one day.

"I'm chasing the clock more than I ever have been."

WATCH: Zac Brown Band's John Driskell Hopkins is 'chasing the clock' after ALS diagnosis

"I didn't even know what it was. I mean, I think a lot of people in the band that did the challenge with me understood that it was neurological and fatal, but we didn't have any clue as to how it affected the body more," he began.

"Certainly not how cases were increasing. I mean, we have seen an explosion of neurodegenerative diseases and I can only, generally point to maybe its toxicity. You know, maybe in the world where we're just consuming a lot more things that are doing us harm. That's all I can guess. But I would have never thought… I was indestructible in 2014, you know?"

With several notable public figures recently diagnosed with ALS, the Ice Bucket Challenge has begun resurfacing across social media. Hop and his team at Hop On A Cure have now joined in, sharing their own Ice Bucket Challenge video and passing the challenge on to fellow ALS organizations, as well as the Zac Brown Band.

MICHAEL J. FOX SAYS GOING PUBLIC WITH PARKINSON'S WAS 'HELL' ON WIFE TRACY POLLAN

Hopkins told Fox News Digital he's glad the trend has come back around this summer. Hopkin's nonprofit organization and the Zac Brown Band posted videos on Instagram in July participating in the challenge.

"It's very popular, and it's fun in the summer. It's been a really hot summer this year, all over the world. And we were in London with 95 degree days, and they never see that," Hopkins said.

John Driskell Hopkins and wife Jennifer started the nonprofit, Hop On a Cure, in 2022. (Emilee Chinn/Cincinnati Reds)

When asked how he's been able to stay strong during his diagnosis, Hopkins told Fox News Digital that he doesn't feel strong at all.

LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I don't feel strong, people often ask me where my strength comes from, but I feel incredibly weak, not just physically. You know, I'm an actor, I have a theater degree, so I'm acting strong," he said.

WATCH: John Driskell Hopkins talks about the viral ALS Ice Bucket Challenge

Hopkins was diagnosed with ALS just before Christmas in 2021 and announced his diagnosis in May 2022. After his diagnosis, Hopkins and his wife, Jennifer, founded the nonprofit organization, Hop On A Cure, to help accelerate research to prevent, reverse and ultimately cure ALS while also raising awareness and supporting families affected by the disease.

At the time of his diagnosis, Hopkins emphasized that his disease had been slowly progressing, allowing him to continue touring and performing with the band.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

During his interview with Fox News Digital, Hopkins said he's in a different position than 99% of ALS patients because he is still able to plan for the next calendar year.

John Driskell Hopkins feels fortunate to still be planning for 2027 amid his ALS diagnosis. (ANGELA WEISS/AFP via Getty Images)

"The fact that I still see next year in my future puts me in a different position than 99.9% of ALS patients. The fact that I'm looking to my calendar for '27. I'm gonna be at the 30a Songwriters Festival '27, and maybe I won't be able to sing what I can now, but maybe I will, you know, we just don't know, and I appreciate you recognizing that reaction as strength, but to me, it's getting up every day that I can and doing what I do," Hopkins concluded.

Janelle Ash is an entertainment writer for Fox News Digital covering Hollywood, celebrity culture and breaking entertainment news through exclusive reporting, interviews and in-depth storytelling.

articles.title: Fetterman unloads on reporter from 'trash' anti-Israel outlet, asks why it loves 'Hamas and Iran'
articles.excerpt:
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., expresses deep concern over the Democratic Party's changing stance on Israel and the recent U.S.-Iran strikes on ‘Sunday Morning Futures.’

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., had ...
articles.body_text:
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., expresses deep concern over the Democratic Party's changing stance on Israel and the recent U.S.-Iran strikes on ‘Sunday Morning Futures.’

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., had a fiery exchange Wednesday with a reporter from the anti-Israel outlet Drop Site News, accusing the outlet of loving Iran and terrorist groups like Hamas and Hezbollah.

In a video shared by Drop Site's Capitol Hill reporter Julian Andreone, Fetterman appeared amused when the reporter told him which outlet he represented.

"Oh, you're Drop Site," Fetterman reacted as he kept walking.

"It's like a race between who's the more pro-Hamas — Drop Site or Zeteo," he quipped, referring to the far-left outlet founded by former MSNBC host Mehdi Hasan.

FETTERMAN TROLLS THE DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA AS ISRAEL KILLS HAMAS TERRORISTS: 'CRY HARDER'

Sen. John Fetterman had a combative exchange with a reporter from the anti-Israel outlet Drop Site News. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Fetterman, the most outspoken supporter of Israel among Senate Democrats, had a message for Drop Site viewers.

"I want your viewers to see how much I love to watch Israel eliminating the Hamas leadership," he told Andreone. "I know that upsets a lot of your viewers and a lot of your founders. But I think it's a great thing."

"So there's no news coming out of me. I'm going to always back Israel," Fetterman continued. "The question is, where does your trash outlet come from and who's funding it?"

Andreone pushed back, saying the site's readers fund the outlet, citing "46,000 individual donors."

SEN JOHN FETTERMAN PLEDGES TO BE 'LAST MAN STANDING' IN THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IN SUPPORT OF ISRAEL

Sen. John Fetterman has become one of the most vocal supporters of Israel among Democratic lawmakers. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Fetterman took aim at Drop Site News co-founder Jeremy Scahill, who went viral earlier this month for lambasting Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., over whether the Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7 was justified.

"Your founders think it's appropriate to attack and kill Israeli civilians. That's really — that should be the news overall," Fetterman said. "Now you're sticking a microphone in my face… I think the question is why does Drop Site love Hamas and Iran and Hezbollah so much? I think that's the news."

"I mean, are you OK with taking your paycheck from these kind of people?" he then asked the reporter.

CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS

Drop Site News co-founder Jeremy Scahill. (Jim Spellman/WireImage)

As Andreone attempted to ask Fetterman whether he was "OK" with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu being in the United States, Fetterman replied, "I'm OK," and added, "I love killing Hamas leadership" before the elevator doors closed.

Drop Site News did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Fetterman had a separate exchange Wednesday with a Zeteo reporter, where he labeled the outlet "pro-Hamas" while speaking with one of its reporters.

Hasan referred to Fetterman, who is reviled by anti-Israel figures for his staunch support of the Jewish state, as a "broken-brained, racist Democrat" in an X post about him meeting with Netanyahu.

Joseph A. Wulfsohn is a media reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to joseph.wulfsohn@fox.com and on Twitter: @JosephWulfsohn.

articles.excerpt:
Lawmakers scrap planned committee vote and seek further assurances that president’s ‘anti-weaponization fund’ is dead

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Todd Blanche’s nomination to bec...
articles.body_text:
Lawmakers scrap planned committee vote and seek further assurances that president’s ‘anti-weaponization fund’ is dead

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Todd Blanche’s nomination to become attorney-general stalled last night as lawmakers scrapped a planned committee vote.

Key Republicans, senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis, had demanded further assurances about the settlement of president Donald Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service (IRS).

Cornyn and Tillis have demanded additional assurances in writing that the ‘Anti-Weaponization Fund’ is dead and have pressed for clarification on the scope of the tax immunity deal.
