articles.title: Bank of England holds interest rates at 3.75% as inflation fears mount
articles.excerpt:
Split vote comes as Iran war is rekindled and oil price climbs back above $90 a barrel

The Bank of England has kept UK interest rates on hold as it warned that a further escalation in the Iran war co...
articles.body_text:
Split vote comes as Iran war is rekindled and oil price climbs back above $90 a barrel

The Bank of England has kept UK interest rates on hold as it warned that a further escalation in the Iran war could drive inflation above 4% next year, adding to cost-of-living pressures on households.

Against a volatile backdrop in the Middle East conflict, the Bank’s monetary policy committee voted by six to three to keep its key base rate at the current level of 3.75%.

As Donald Trump’s renewed attacks on Iran drive up global energy prices, the Bank warned that an “adverse scenario” involving a drawn-out war and oil prices remaining above $100 a barrel could drive UK inflation to a peak of 4.5% by the middle of 2027.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, briefly rose above that level last week before falling back, amid fears that the violence across the region could shatter the world economy’s earlier resilience to the war. The oil price was trading above $90 a barrel on Thursday.

In a decision taken after UK inflation dropped by more than expected in June, Threadneedle Street said there were signs the impact from the war could still be contained because Britain faced a sluggish growth outlook and rising levels of unemployment.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said: “Inflation has fallen faster than we’d expected, but the conflict in the Middle East continues to mean high and volatile energy prices. That will cause inflation to rise again later this year. However the conflict unfolds, our job is to make sure any increase in inflation is temporary and that it comes back to our 2% target.”

Publishing its central forecast, involving the oil price falling back to about $71 a barrel, Threadneedle Street said it still expected inflation in the UK to a peak at about 3.2% later this year as households come under pressure from higher fuel and energy prices.

The interest rate decision comes as Andy Burnham pushes to lower the cost of living after announcing a sweeping package of support for households and businesses in his first week as prime minister.

Under his plans, electricity bills in Great Britain will be cut by an average of £45 a year from October, after he said the government would remove VAT from them. The Bank expects the policy, alongside a £2 cap on bus fares, to reduce the headline inflation rate by 0.1 percentage point.

Official figures show inflation in the UK fell by more than expected in June to 2.6%, from a peak of 3.8% last year. It had been on track to fall close to 2% before the outbreak of the Iran war.

The Bank said a loose labour market and higher borrowing costs for households and businesses compared with before the Iran war would reduce inflation over time, with conditions before the conflict more “benign” than they were before previous global shocks, including the Covid pandemic and Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

However, the MPC warned that it “stands ready to act as necessary” to prevent inflationary pressures from becoming entrenched.

Highlighting the risk of stubbornly high inflation, Catherine Mann, an external economist on the MPC, joined her fellow committee members Megan Greene and Huw Pill in dissenting against the majority of the panel with a vote to raise rates immediately to 4%.

Greene, another external member, and Pill, the Bank’s chief economist, had previously been outvoted in pushing for a quarter-point rise at the last MPC meeting amid concern about inflation.

Financial markets had priced in a more-than-90% probability of Threadneedle Street keeping borrowing costs on hold, with the outside chance of a rise. Investors expect a rise in borrowing costs to 4% before the end of the year.

The news comes after the US Federal Reserve held borrowing costs unchanged on Wednesday and its new chair, Kevin Warsh, unnerved some investors worried over its readiness to tackle high inflation.

After a press conference that analysts said was light on detail, US borrowing costs rose to the highest level since 2007 amid concern the Fed would not be able to contain the energy price shock from the Iran war.

articles.title: 'Woke' Smithsonian exhibit lionizes embattled Fauci amid conservative scrutiny of museum's messaging
articles.excerpt: Dr. Anthony Fauci faces intense scrutiny from the Senate Homeland Security Committee, repeatedly invoking the Fifth Amendment. Senators questioned Fauci regarding NIH funding directed to the Wuhan lab...
articles.body_text:
Dr. Anthony Fauci faces intense scrutiny from the Senate Homeland Security Committee, repeatedly invoking the Fifth Amendment. Senators questioned Fauci regarding NIH funding directed to the Wuhan lab via EcoHealth Alliance, the use of aborted fetal tissue in coronavirus research, and his shifting advice on mask mandates and lockdowns. Lawmakers challenged the scientific basis for many pandemic-era policies and Fauci's documented private remarks.

The embattled former face of the United States' COVID-19 response is prominently displayed and heroically framed at the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History — as the network of Smithsonian institutions face scrutiny over woke messaging from government officials.

Dr. Anthony Fauci, formerly the head of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), has a prominent place at the museum's "Entertainment Nation" exhibit.

"As a deadly pandemic ravaged the nation, major sports leagues found themselves at the center of a debate over 'reopening' the country," a placard dedicated to Fauci says.

A placard in the "Entertainment Nation" exhibit at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. honors Dr. Anthony Fauci. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

"Amidst a cacophony of misinformation and denial, advice from Dr. Anthony Fauci, the nation’s leading epidemiologist, urged leagues to make decisions about resuming play 'based on scientific evidence and public health judgment,'" it continues. "When baseball became the first league to retake the field, Fauci threw the ceremonial opening pitch—wearing a facemask in a stadium empty of fans."

A diary kept by Fauci while the pandemic raged, recently exposed by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., shows a man fixated on his own fame, who acknowledged answers to controversial questions in private, but said the opposite in public.

Dr. Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, throws out the ceremonial first pitch before the game between the New York Yankees and Washington Nationals at Nationals Park on July 23, 2020, in Washington, D.C. (Getty Images)

One of those controversial questions dealt with the origin of the virus. COVID-19 may have originated in an National Institute of Health (NIH) funded facility in China. While Fauci recognized privately that the virus may have accidentally escaped a lab, he stalwartly maintained the opposite in public. Fauci critics who suggested otherwise, including other doctors, were castigated. Fauci also insisted that the government was not conducting controversial gain-of-function research. That later proved false.

FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

Alongside the Smithsonian's heroic characterization of Fauci as a man of science, the museum prominently features that Washington Nationals baseball cap, signed by the doctor, that he wore while throwing out the first pitch when MLB resumed play after lockdowns.

A Washington Nationals cap worn by Dr. Anthony Fauci, complete with his signature, in the "Entertainment Nation" exhibit at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

Fauci also repeatedly denied that he was behind the damaging pandemic-era lockdowns, but acknowledged in his diary that mayors and health officials in the country's largest metropolitan areas, including New York City and Los Angeles, were taking his advice to shut their municipalities down.

Diary posts also show that the doctor, often framed as a humble lifelong public servant, was obsessed with the attention he received during the pandemic. He extensively documented flattering news stories about himself, bragging in May of 2020 that his "national and international fame is explosive and really unimaginable" and that it was "not hyperbole" to say he was "the most famous and talked about person in the country."

TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

The pandemic claimed 1.2 million American lives.

Fauci was grilled on Capitol Hill Wednesday before the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, chaired by Paul. He invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination 111 times, failing to answer a single question.

The "Entertainment Nation" exhibit at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

The Smithsonian is dealing with government scrutiny of its own, both from congress and the White House.

The American History museum's director, Anthea Hartig, was grilled before congress last week over sexually explicit imagery, Mickey Mouse being linked to racism and a museum toolkit discussing "objectivity" as a feature of White supremacy.

The museum's MASS Action Toolkit, a mid-2010s anthology for museums that references the 2014 Ferguson, Missouri, police shooting of Mike Brown and subsequent Black Lives Matter protests. It links politeness and being on time to white supremacy.

The White House chastised the taxpayer-funded museum for pushing "one-sided, divisive political narratives."

The "Entertainment Nation" exhibit at the Smithsonian National Museum of American History in Washington, D.C. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

"American taxpayers should not be funding institutions that undermine our country or promote one-sided, divisive political narratives," White House official Lindsey Halligan told Fox News Digital. "The Smithsonian Institution should present history in a way that is accurate, balanced, and consistent with the values that make the United States of America exceptional."

The White House report also released a report on July 4 that criticized the Smithsonian's portrayal of American history, and more recently, President Donald Trump ordered the National Park Service to place signs outside the museum directing visitors and passersby to an online resource that he says portrays an "accurate" version of American history.

He also blasted the museum as "woke" and "OUT OF CONTROL" on TRUTH Social.

Fox News' Charles Creitz and Jasmine Baehr contributed to this report.

Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: New audio released following Nolan Wells disappearance doesn't show 'anything nefarious': retired FBI agent
articles.excerpt:
A caller aboard the boat that brought Nolan Wells to Horn Island tells a Sea Tow dispatcher the vessel is sinking with seven people onboard on July 4. (Credit: MDMR)

A retired FBI agent says that new...
articles.body_text:
A caller aboard the boat that brought Nolan Wells to Horn Island tells a Sea Tow dispatcher the vessel is sinking with seven people onboard on July 4. (Credit: MDMR)

A retired FBI agent says that new audio released following Nolan Wells' disappearance and death doesn't show "anything nefarious."

Wells, 18, went missing July 4 after a boat trip with friends to Horn Island, a barrier island off Mississippi's Gulf Coast. Crews searched the area for two days before a National Parks Service ranger found his remains on the island's northwestern tip on July 6.

Wells' friends returned to the mainland that afternoon without him. Jackson County Sheriff John Ledbetter has said investigators believe Wells chose to remain on the island, and it wasn't until later that night that his mother learned from one of his friends he was missing, prompting her to report it to authorities.

Fox News Digital obtained a recording of a call made to Sea Tow on the evening of July 4 by someone aboard the boat, who said the vessel was taking on water as it prepared to return to the mainland. The individual said there were seven people onboard.

SEARCH CALLED OFF AFTER BODY MATCHING MISSING TEEN NOLAN WELLS FOUND OFF MISSISSIPPI COAST

Nolan Xavier Wells disappeared on the Fourth of July while boating with friends, according to authorities. (Jackson County Sheriff's Department via Facebook)

"Hey, we’re at the west tip of Horn, and our bilge pump stopped working. We’re sinking. Can y’all please come?" an individual can be heard saying to the Sea Tow dispatcher.

When the dispatcher asked how far the water is coming inside the boat, the individual replied, "It’s coming up... we’re just sinking. I don’t know. We’re going down though."

"And is everyone on board and in good health otherwise?" the dispatcher asked.

"Yeah, everyone is on board," the individual on the boat responded.

The man heard talking to the Sea Tow dispatcher requested someone to come help un-sink the boat and get it towed back to the Fort Bayou launch in Ocean Springs, Mississippi.

NOLAN WELLS INDEPENDENT AUTOPSY DOESN'T POINT TO FOUL PLAY, FORMER MEDICAL EXAMINER SAYS

Nolan Wells smiles on the field while playing wide receiver for Southwest Mississippi Community College. (Christine Wonsley/Facebook)

The Sea Tow dispatcher spoke with a separate boat captain, who said he was on the phone with the boat's owner.

"It sounds like a bunch of kids on board on Horn Island," the dispatcher said. "He’s saying the boat is sinking and he’s on Horn Island... It’s just unfortunate, he’s just a kid... there’s a lot going on... I’m guessing they’re all under 18... He wants you guys to go out there and un-pump the boat and then tow it in?"

The dispatcher then spoke with a captain, who said he was already on the phone with a man who owned the boat, a relative of the teen who called, and said those on the boat were in a "panic" because the boat wouldn't crank.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"It sounds like a bunch of kids on board on Horn Island," the dispatcher told the captain. "He’s saying the boat is sinking and he’s on Horn Island. It’s just unfortunate, he’s just a kid. It’s a lot going on.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

"He wants you guys to go out there and un-pump the boat and then tow it in," the dispatcher said.

The captain said the boat's owner told him the teens didn't "need any help right now, but if something changes, he'll call me back."

Former FBI agent Jonathan Gilliam told Fox News Digital he doesn't believe the Sea Tow audio points to any signs of foul play, as some people on social media have claimed.

WATCH: Retired FBI agent says nothing 'nefarious' in newly released Nolan Wells boat audio

"I don't hear anything nefarious... it just sounded like there was a lot of stuff going on, that they were taking on water — not panic as much as this young person was trying to resolve a situation in a party atmosphere."

Gilliam also pointed out that the call itself undercuts the idea of a cover-up.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"By the way, they're taking on water. They're going to be calling for assistance, which could lead to authorities. If they had done something, that'd be a very bad time for a person who'd done something nefarious to call out people and for them to get away with something. So I don't think it added anything to the conspiracies of something having occurred knowingly in a nefarious manner."

Several of Wells' friends told authorities he "chose to remain at the island" with an unidentified female rather than return to the mainland with the group he arrived with, according to a Mississippi Department of Marine Resources police report obtained by Fox News Digital.

According to the police report, authorities "did not have reason to believe there were any water related exigencies or emergencies and he believed the most likely scenario was Nolan rode in on another vessel but did not have his phone in his possession to make contact with family."

During a July 22 news conference, attorney Ben Crump revealed that an area of "red discoloration" was found on Wells' head, but said Dr. Roger Mitchell, who performed an independent autopsy, couldn't come to a conclusion on a cause or manner of death "pending further investigation." An official autopsy into Wells' death hasn't been completed.

Wells was a wide receiver at Southwest Mississippi Community College and had hopes to play at the Division 1 level, according to Crump, an attorney for his family.

Adam Sabes is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Adam.Sabes@fox.com and on Twitter @asabes10.

articles.title: Trump accused China of an 'election security nightmare' but then undercut his own warning
articles.excerpt:
President Donald Trump claims Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea have the capability to compromise U.S. election infrastructure.

Less than two weeks after accusing China of carrying out an "unprece...
articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump claims Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea have the capability to compromise U.S. election infrastructure.

Less than two weeks after accusing China of carrying out an "unprecedented election security nightmare," President Donald Trump has not changed his posture toward Beijing and is moving ahead with plans to host Chinese President Xi Jinping in September.

"This data loss presents an unprecedented election security nightmare," Trump said in a July 16 address. "The intelligence even shows that China assigned a data exploitation unit specifically to this new project."

Intelligence officials, he said, "worked to actively suppress and downplay information about the extent of China’s sinister election meddling."

TRUMP’S UPBEAT CHINA MESSAGE COLLIDES WITH DEEPENING BEIJING RIVALRY

Trump did not claim China changed votes or altered election results. Instead, he argued Beijing engaged in an influence campaign aimed at shaping U.S. public perceptions.

But within days of the address, Trump undercut the urgency of his own warning. Asked whether China would face consequences, he said the alleged activity "took place a long time ago" and suggested it reflected the broader intelligence rivalry between the two countries.

"They do things and we do things to them," Trump said July 21 in remarks to reporters. "I’ll be honest, we do things to them, too. It’s not a one-way street."

President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping prepare for a key summit in May. (Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/Getty Images)

So far, the fallout has been directed almost entirely inward. Trump ordered investigations into U.S. officials who handled the intelligence, while his trade and diplomatic engagement with Beijing has continued largely unchanged.

Trump’s posture toward TikTok has undergone a similar shift. He sought to ban the platform during his first term over national-security concerns tied to its Chinese ownership but joined it during the 2024 campaign. Five days after Trump’s address, most Cabinet members launched official accounts after the Justice Department cleared federal employees to use TikTok under its new U.S.-controlled ownership.

It also remains unclear when Trump first learned of the intelligence or whether he knew about it before traveling to Beijing in May. A White House official confirmed Xi's Sept. 24 visit will proceed but did not answer questions about when Trump was briefed or whether anyone accused of withholding the intelligence remains in government.

The Chinese embassy could not immediately be reached for comment on the planned visit.

Newly declassified records released by the administration provide fresh details about China’s alleged collection and analysis of American voter information and reveal an internal intelligence debate over whether Beijing’s broader activities amounted to election interference. But the documents also establish less than some of Trump’s rhetoric appeared to suggest.

CHINA DISMISSES TRUMP ELECTION INTERFERENCE ACCUSATIONS AS 'ENTIRELY FABRICATED,' THREATENS COUNTERMEASURES

During the July 16 address, Trump said China had acquired 220 million U.S. voter files containing names, addresses, phone numbers and political affiliations. He said Beijing assigned a unit to exploit the information and which had the potential to use it to register voters or engage in other "nefarious activities."

Trump called the findings "stunning" and the broader vulnerabilities "a cyber threat aimed at the very heart of our democracy."

The president accused intelligence officials of working to "actively suppress and downplay" China’s "sinister election meddling." He cited an internal message saying officials had "deliberately massaged" a pending President’s Daily Brief and another in which an FBI official described "running a shadow government."

'SHADOW GOVERNMENT': TRUMP CLAIMS INTEL COMMUNITY BRAGGED ABOUT HIDING CHINESE MEDDLING

Trump directed the Justice Department, FBI, CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence to investigate. He said those responsible should be fired and potentially prosecuted.

The roughly 270 pages of released records show that Chinese entities amassed and analyzed large quantities of American voter information.

The seal of the Central Intelligence Agency is displayed in the foyer of the original headquarters building in Langley, Virginia, Sept. 18, 2009. (Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The figure at the center of Trump’s announcement appears to come from a record showing that a Chinese entity possessed an unspecified dataset containing approximately 204.8 million American voter records. The document does not identify its source or explain how it was obtained.

Other records describe China analyzing registration information from 18 states and a Chinese actor downloading publicly available historical voter information from six states. The documents do not show that China altered voter rolls, changed ballots or penetrated vote-counting systems.

The documents also include a raw FBI report alleging that China planned to manufacture fraudulent U.S. driver’s licenses that could be used to cast mail ballots for Joe Biden. The allegation came from a single uncorroborated source, and the report was recalled the day it was distributed and never reissued.

There was no evidence that any fraudulent votes were actually cast.

Emily Harding, director of the Intelligence, National Security, and Technology Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote that China "likely gained little advantage" from voter records that were largely publicly available or available for purchase.

Harding wrote that the internal exchanges showed "an honest, and valuable, analytical debate" rather than a cover-up. She noted that the recalled FBI report relied on unreliable third-hand information and said references to the election were removed from one briefing so a specialized election-security team could address the issue.

Trump did not explain which American activities he considered comparable to China’s collection and analysis of voter information.

There is some public record behind Trump’s suggestion that the intelligence competition runs both ways — but China does not hold free national elections.

Trump authorized the CIA in 2019 to conduct a covert influence campaign against China, Reuters reported in 2024. According to three former U.S. officials, operatives used false online identities to circulate damaging but fact-based information about Xi’s government and attempt to shape public opinion inside China.

The CIA declined to confirm the program. Documents leaked by former National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden also showed the National Security Agency penetrating Chinese networks, including the systems of telecommunications giant Huawei.

Trump expressed a similar view during his May visit to Beijing, although he was speaking then about Chinese espionage more broadly.

President Donald Trump trailed by Chinese President Xi Jinping greets other officials at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing.  (Kenny Holston-Pool/Getty Images)

"They spy on us," Trump told Fox News host Sean Hannity during the trip. "We spy on them too, I guess."

Trump otherwise used the visit to promote closer economic ties. He traveled with leading American executives, called Xi a "great leader" and said it was an "honor" to be his friend.

The White House later announced that the two countries had agreed to establish boards of trade and investment. China also committed to purchase 200 Boeing aircraft and at least $17 billion in American agricultural products annually through 2028, according to the administration.

Preparations for Xi’s visit continued after Trump’s address.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi July 22 to lay the groundwork for what he called a "very positive" visit but said Trump’s election allegations were not discussed. Rubio added that it would be "reckless and irresponsible" for the two powers not to maintain a relationship.

China has denied interfering in the 2020 election. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian called the allegations "entirely fabricated" and urged the United States to stop using China as an election issue.

articles.body_text:
Americans are facing a deepening affordability crisis but at least Trump and co have ... 250 new Cadillac Escalades

This was originally published in This Week in Trumpland. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday

Gas prices are up almost a dollar a gallon since the day Donald Trump took office; mortgage rates just hit their highest level in nearly a year, and over the weekend a prominent economist said the Iran war is costing the average US household more than $1,200.

Americans are struggling through a deepening affordability crisis caused largely by Trump’s ill-fated war against Iran. They are in need of a boost, something to lift the spirits. Perhaps the president could give a speech, letting the people know that we are all in this together.

Or, he could give a speech announcing that the White House has just ordered 250 brand new Cadillac Escalades, giant SUVs which have a suggested retail price of more than $90,000 each and cost significantly more to customize for secure uses.

“We ordered 250 Escalades. That’s how we look sharp in those cavalcades, you know,” Trump said during a rambling, hour-long address at a General Motors facility in Michigan.

“We look sharp in those Escalades. Our guys are very spoiled. They’re very spoiled. They like the Escalade. So do I.”

I’d like to think I would look sharp in an Escalade. But, like most people in the US, I cannot afford one: especially if, as seems likely, the White House orders the armored version of the SUV, which can cost more than $300,000. And then, of course, I’d have to fill the 24-gallon gas tank.

The symbolism of Trump’s gesture, his fiddling with car specifications while Rome burns, is consistent with his Lucille Bluth-like behavior in recent weeks. He’s dismissed “affordability” as a term concocted by Democratic political consultants to criticize his presidency, introduced a new round of tariffs likely to push up prices, and refused to sign a rare bipartisan housing bill. It’s still shocking. Even Scrooge didn’t order a new horse and cart as Tiny Tim’s health declined.

Yet here we are, in 2026, with a billionaire president crowing about spending at least $22m of Americans’ money on a fleet of luxury SUVs, an act which seems extremely unlikely to boost morale.

“Hey I know inflation is out of control and a lot of folks can’t afford basic necessities, but at least we’re tackling waste fra ud and abuse by buying… *checks notes* 250 Escalades for the government,” the Angry Staffer account wrote on X, capturing much of the mood.

The announcement of the car purchase was a baffling move in what was a confusing speech. Trump’s address in Michigan was supposed to be about US auto manufacturing, but instead his remarks took on transgender rights, “Marxist protesters” and how, should Democrats win control of the government: “In one year, the country will be absolutely bankrupt. You’ll live in squalor. You’ll live in fear. You won’t have police. You won’t have firemen. You won’t have anybody.”

Trump also disclosed to the crowd that he was “sort of a clean freak, I like clean”, before claiming he had been awarded “man of the year” in Michigan 25 years ago. The latter was an interesting claim, because Trump has been claiming to have been awarded this Michigan man of the year title for a decade, and it never happened.

“Approaching 10 full years after Trump debuted the ‘Man of the Year’ lie, nobody has ever been able to find any evidence for it,” CNN’s Daniel Dale wrote.

“The state of Michigan does not give out a ‘Man of the Year’ award, Trump has never lived in the state, and he and his team have never specified who or what entity supposedly gave him this award and when.”

It’s all very well for the president: swanning about the midwest bulk-buying massive SUVs, “liking clean”, living in a fantasy world where he is handed awards left right and center.

It’s hard to see, however, how this display of opulence and this dabbling in make-believe helps everyday Americans. We’ll have to see what Trump has planned next to lift the mood. Perhaps he could announce a new caviar supplier, or a wholesale purchase of top hats. Or maybe he could settle for just slathering gold all over his office. Time will tell.

articles.title: Trump tells foreign students: overstay your visa, face the consequences
articles.excerpt:
Federal Trade Commission chairman Andrew Ferguson highlights efforts to ensure the H-1B program serves its intended purpose of bringing in specialized labor on ‘America’s Newsroom.’

Amid all the nois...
articles.body_text:
Federal Trade Commission chairman Andrew Ferguson highlights efforts to ensure the H-1B program serves its intended purpose of bringing in specialized labor on ‘America’s Newsroom.’

Amid all the noise in Washington and simultaneous lack of legislation coming out of Congress, there have been some quiet wins for accountability in our visa system.

One recent win is an administrative final rule that requires foreign students to comply with their visas. Administrative rules govern how the government implements the law in practice.

Most foreign students who qualify get an F-1 visa, which allows them to study at the undergraduate or graduate level. Some get a J-1, which is for international exchange visitors.

RUBIO PUSHES BACK ON INDIA'S CONCERNS OVER US VISA CURBS, SAYS POLICY MUST BE 'AMERICA FIRST' UNDER TRUMP

When student visa holders arrive here, they are given permission to enter under what’s called "duration of status." That means that as long as they are full-time students, they can stay.

President Donald Trump is reining in student visas that have been abused by foreign students. (Photo: iStock/Getty Images Plus)

An earlier rule allows students, while still on their student visas, to work in "Optional Practical Training" for a year, with another two years if they have STEM degrees. The definition of STEM is 16 pages long and generous. Because foreigners on OPT are working using their student visa (remember – "duration of status") their employers are not required to pay into Social Security and Medicare. That’s a discount of up to 15% for hiring foreign workers instead of Americans.

"Duration of status" combined with OPT incentivizes marginal students not to complete their degrees in due course and, as they originally claimed they would, go home.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ORDERS GREEN CARD APPLICANTS TO LEAVE THE US, APPLY FROM THEIR HOME COUNTRIES

The education-migration complex is desperate to keep the foreign student gravy train on the rails. They make the new rule seem as if it is cutting off opportunity. Quite the opposite: it’s about asking for responsibility.

It’s not hard to complete a bachelor’s degree in four years, especially for foreign students. Americans can apply to college knowing they’ll need to work or apply for aid and grants. Foreigners, meanwhile, are required to show consular officers in their visa interview that they can afford the entire course of study, including tuition, lodging and incidental costs. They are not, in theory, supposed to work.

If they decide to earn a master’s after their BA, or even a PhD, the new rule just means they have to go home, apply for a new visa, and show the consular officer they are credible students, can afford the entire course of study and intend to return home when done.

TRUMP PUTS ASYLUM LAWYERS ‘ON NOTICE’ WITH NEW FRONT IN WAR ON FRAUD

That’s what is really freaking out the edu-crats. Many foreign students intend to stay in the U.S. Some never go to school at all; these get dropped from the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) maintained by DHS. They should then be deported, but many make frivolous asylum claims to remain.

Others do go to school, but drag it out over many years, taking minimal classes to maintain status while working, often illegally. Schools don’t mind, as long as the fees keep coming.

But we should mind. America doesn’t need to import this type of low-motivation student.

The education-migration complex is desperate to keep the foreign student gravy train on the rails. They make the new rule seem as if it is cutting off opportunity. Quite the opposite: it’s about asking for responsibility.

What America needs even less are students who come here pre-programmed with hostility to the United States, Western civilization and capitalism, who spend their time protesting on campus.

Some foreign students on campuses across the United States have been here for years, spending far too much time and energy protesting Israel, capitalism, ICE and Western civilization instead of hitting the books and getting a degree. These permanent students aren’t adding to our national prosperity, security, or unity.

America wants students who come, study and finish their degrees. The left will tell you that foreign students are all the best of the best. Not so. As a consular officer, I did thousands of student visa applications in Africa, Asia and Europe. I’ve seen everything from applicants with full scholarships at MIT and Harvard to those wanting to study English at a community college near their uncle, who just happens to own a motel or gas station.

America welcomes legitimate students. We will always have room for the most talented and entrepreneurial to stay. But our universities are not there to facilitate mass economic migration.

The unemployment rate for recent American college graduates is 5.7%, higher than the national average. They need our support, not millions of foreign graduates to compete with.

The new rule on student visas is timely and welcome. Future presidents would be wise to keep it instead of caving to the education and migration lobby.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM SIMON HANKINSON

Simon Hankinson is a senior research fellow in The Heritage Foundation’s Border Security and Immigration Center and author of "The Ten Woke Commandments (You Must Not Obey)" from Academica Books.

articles.title: Daily eating habit linked to better brain health in older adults, new research suggests
articles.excerpt: Dr. Mary Claire Haver breaks down how the menopause shift rewires metabolism, raising abdominal fat and inflammation, and reveals why tracking strength and fat distribution beats relying on the number...
articles.body_text:
Dr. Mary Claire Haver breaks down how the menopause shift rewires metabolism, raising abdominal fat and inflammation, and reveals why tracking strength and fat distribution beats relying on the number on the scale.

Eating within a shorter daily window could help support brain health as people age, according to new research.

Preliminary findings presented at NUTRITION 2026 — the American Society for Nutrition’s annual meeting in Maryland — suggests that older women who ate within eight to nine hours per day saw slight cognitive improvement compared to those who spread their meals over about 12 hours each day.

The small six-month trial included 47 postmenopausal obese or overweight women aged 50 to 79. They were each advised to reduce their daily food intake by about 500 calories.

INTERMITTENT FASTING'S REAL BENEFIT MAY COME AFTER YOU START EATING AGAIN

The participants were divided into two groups. One ate in a time-restricted window within an average of 8.2 hours, usually from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. The other group ate across a 12.3-hour window, according to a news release.

Both groups saw weight-loss results, but the shorter-window group scored higher on cognitive tests. (iStock)

Both groups lost about 15 pounds over six months, but those in the shorter eating-window group performed better on cognitive tests measuring spatial planning and problem-solving.

The shorter-window group also showed fewer errors on memory and learning tests, but no meaningful differences in reaction time or multi-tasking ability.

PEOPLE LOST WEIGHT WHILE EATING SIGNIFICANTLY MORE FOOD — HERE'S THE SECRET

"These outcomes suggest a better ability to remember information during everyday tasks and reduce mistakes related to memory, attention and problem-solving," lead researcher Sue Shapses, PhD, a professor at Rutgers University and Rutgers-RWJ Medical Center, said in a press release. "Reductions in the eating window predicted greater improvements."

Although the pilot study included only a small number of participants, the researchers believe that time-restricted eating may support brain health by regulating circadian rhythm, reducing inflammation and improving metabolic health.

"Think of meal timing as one potential piece of the puzzle rather than a magic bullet."

Losing weight alone can help "ward off some of the aging-related cognitive decline," according to Shapses.

"And these data suggest there may be additional benefits if you stop eating four hours prior to going to sleep and reduce food intake to eight to nine hours per day, compared to the usual eating window of 12 hours per day."

People who are overweight or obese tend to face a higher likelihood of developing dementia as they age, the researchers said. (iStock)

Women, as well as adults who are overweight or obese, tend to face a higher likelihood of developing Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia as they age, according to the researchers.

Lauri Wright, PhD, director of nutrition programs and associate professor at the USF College of Public Health, who was not involved in this research, reflected on these findings in an interview with Fox News Digital.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"This is an interesting study because it suggests that when we eat may matter in addition to what and how much we eat," she said. "That suggests meal timing itself may have played a role, not just weight loss."

"The results are promising, but we need larger, longer studies before recommending time-restricted eating specifically to improve brain health."

Brain imaging should be performed within the first several hours after seeking medical attention for a stroke, a doctor advised. (iStock)

Experts are still learning about how intermittent fasting affects the brain, although "several biological mechanisms are being considered," Wright noted.

"Giving the body a longer overnight break from eating may improve insulin sensitivity, reduce chronic inflammation, support healthy circadian rhythms and allow cells more time for repair and maintenance," she said. "Those processes are all linked to healthy brain aging."

From a practical standpoint, eating within a shorter daily window often leads people to consume fewer calories, which can promote weight loss, according to New York-based certified holistic nutritionist Robin DeCicco.

"We know that maintaining a healthy weight helps with virtually everything," she told Fox News Digital. "Eating within a restricted window helps people cut calories."

"When you fast or ... have periods of time where you're not just eating throughout the whole day, it does help to lower markers of inflammation and certain sources of oxidative stress."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Many people have reported "feeling better" when fasting, DeCicco noted — especially those who have inflammatory conditions, which can include neurological disorders like Alzheimer’s and dementia.

"When you're fasting, you're giving your organs a chance to rest, you're giving the digestive system a chance to ‘rest and digest,’" she added.

Fasting gives the organs a chance to "rest and digest," an expert said. (iStock)

Intermittent fasting isn’t the only way to support cognitive health, Wright countered.

"Regular physical activity, adequate sleep, controlling blood pressure and blood sugar, avoiding smoking, maintaining social connections and following an overall healthy dietary pattern, such as the Mediterranean diet, have much stronger evidence for protecting cognitive function over time," she said. "Think of meal timing as one potential piece of the puzzle rather than a magic bullet."

Intermittent fasting "isn’t appropriate for everyone," Wright warned, adding that she would advise against it for children and teens, pregnant or breastfeeding women, anyone with a history of an eating disorder, and people with diabetes who are taking insulin.

DeCicco agreed that fasting should be recommended and monitored by a medical professional, especially for those who take certain medications or have certain conditions.

Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Huckabee warns of 'biblical ignorance' as he defends conservative support for Israel
articles.excerpt:
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee argues that being America First means standing with Israel and U.S. allies.

As some on the right become more skeptical of the U.S.-Israel relationship, U.S. Am...
articles.body_text:
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee argues that being America First means standing with Israel and U.S. allies.

As some on the right become more skeptical of the U.S.-Israel relationship, U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee warns that the trepidation is fueled by what he calls "biblical ignorance" and a misunderstanding of what it means to be "America First."

Speaking to Fox News Digital ahead of the 15th anniversary of the U.S. Israel Education Association's founding, Huckabee rejected the idea that putting America first means pushing away allies. Rather, he argued that support for Israel is aligned with U.S. interests and the religious convictions held by many Christians.

"When I look at the things on the right what I see is that there's biblical ignorance," Huckabee said. "People who say, 'you know, God has no longer got a promise that he's keeping to the Jewish people,' and I'm thinking 'well, that's news to God because he doesn't break a promise."

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee says resentment towards the Jewish state on the right is fueled by "ignorance" of the Bible and a misunderstanding of what it means to be "America First." (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)

CHRISTIAN LEADERS HOLD EMERGENCY SUMMIT IN JERUSALEM TO CONFRONT GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM

"If God broke his promise to the Jews, then what makes me, as a Christian, think that he won't break his promise to me?" he added.

In addition to being the former governor of Arkansas, Huckabee was also ordained as a Baptist minister and served as President of the Arkansas Baptist State Convention, giving him a perspective shaped by both politics and faith.

The ambassador also dismissed notions that Christians are not welcomed or allowed to worship freely in Israel. He told Fox News Digital that he plays bass guitar in his church praise band every Sunday and that "nobody throws a chair at me."

Skepticism and outright hostility toward Israel has become more prevalent in recent years in some corners of right-wing media and among more heterodox podcast stars, such as Joe Rogan, who said Wednesday that there was no doubt Israel was guilty of "genocide" in Gaza.

TRUMP THREATENS 'MAJOR MILITARY PUNISHMENT' FOR IRAN OVER FUTURE HOUTHI ATTACKS

However, the ambassador's concerns go beyond theological debates. Huckabee argued that some conservatives have misinterpreted the "America First" movement as one of pure isolationism.

"There's another thing on the right that I'm concerned about. People who say, 'Look, I'm an America First person,' I say 'I am too.' I was MAGA before anybody knew what MAGA was," Huckabee told Fox News Digital. "America First has never meant America only."

Ambassador Mike Huckabee argues that some on the right who are turning against Israel are doing so because of a misunderstanding of what it means to be "America First." (Maâayan Toaf (GPO)/Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

The ambassador explained that America's interests do not stop at its borders, particularly when it comes to combatting enemy threats.

He pointed to Iran, saying that the regime has spent decades calling for "death to America." Huckabee also cited Iranian proxies across the globe and the threats they pose as key reasons why the U.S. cannot afford to ignore what happens overseas. For Huckabee, the threats emanating from Iran and its proxies reinforce his belief that putting America first does not mean turning inward.

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee speaks to Fox News Digital during an interview at the American embassy in Jerusalem, Israel. (Yoav Dudkevitch/ TPS-IL)

"They've never changed their message that they want to murder us. So, when people tell you for 47 years their goal is to kill you, you're pretty stupid if you don't pay attention to that, and even more stupid if you do nothing about it," he said.

Rachel Wolf is a media and culture reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Book returned to Australian library – 150 years overdue
articles.excerpt:
The book, Antiquities of Athens, was handed back to Kiama library by a man who found it bricked into a wall

An Australian public library has had a book returned an estimated 150 years late after bein...
articles.body_text:
The book, Antiquities of Athens, was handed back to Kiama library by a man who found it bricked into a wall

An Australian public library has had a book returned an estimated 150 years late after being found behind a wall during a home renovation.

The book, Antiquities of Athens, published in 1858, was returned to the library in the seaside town of Kiama, south of Sydney, by a man who had found it inside a tea crate bricked into a sealed fireplace

“We’ve never had anything that old come back to us,” library manager Michelle Hudson said.

“I follow lots of libraries on social media and often you’ll get things that are maybe 30 or 40 years old when they’re cleaning out estates and stuff like that.”

The book’s finder did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The late return fine would be around A$28,000 (US$19,500), allowing for inflation, Hudson said. That was calculated on the British three pence a week overdue fee that was printed on the inside cover of the book, along with a list of rules that applied when the library opened in 1872.

But Hudson said there was no way of tracing the final borrower who had accrued the debt. The library journal from the 1870s that recorded who borrowed a book and when had been lost.

“Unfortunately, we have a missing link. There’s nothing in the book that tells us who the last borrower was,” Hudson said.

Library rules in the 1870s stated that a book had to be returned and an overdue debt paid before another book could be borrowed.

“Maybe that’s why they never returned it to us,” Hudson said.

Under the antiquated rules of the day, up to three books could be borrowed by households in which at least six members were “known to be able to read”.

The book, which has some water damage from its years under a chimney, was marked as No 506 in the library’s original collection of around 1,000 books, Hudson said.

She expects the book was lost within a few years of the library opening.

The returned book will be displayed in the library’s local history collection.

“We’re not going to allow it to go back out again. We don’t want to wait another 150 years for this book to be returned,” Hudson said.

articles.title: Three people found dead on small boat in Channel crossing attempt
articles.excerpt:
Group of migrants found unresponsive off coast of Dunkirk after attempting to reach UK

Three people have died while trying to reach the UK on a small boat after one of the busiest days for Channel cr...
articles.body_text:
Group of migrants found unresponsive off coast of Dunkirk after attempting to reach UK

Three people have died while trying to reach the UK on a small boat after one of the busiest days for Channel crossings this year.

The group of migrants were found dead on a boat off the coast of Dunkirk on Thursday morning, the French coastguard said.

Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that the government’s plan to curb Channel crossings was “working” but there was “more to do”.

The boat was spotted at around 6am and the three people on board were found to be unresponsive. They were taken to shore by rescue crews before paramedics confirmed they had died, according to a translation of a statement from maritime authorities in Cherbourg-en-Cotentin.

Wednesday was one of the busiest days for small boat crossings so far this year, with a steady stream of attempts throughout the day amid hot, sunny weather and calm sea conditions.

articles.title: AFC president doubles down on FIFA, calling World Cup plan ‘unacceptable’
articles.excerpt: Asian Football Confederation ‌(AFC) president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa has branded FIFA’s lack of consultation over its plan ⁠to sell stakes in ⁠the World Cup to private investors “totally...
articles.body_text:
Asian Football Confederation ‌(AFC) president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa has branded FIFA’s lack of consultation over its plan ⁠to sell stakes in ⁠the World Cup to private investors “totally unacceptable”, saying the move undermined the sport’s existing continental structure.

The Bahraini’s unusually forthright comments were made in a letter sent on Thursday to ⁠the regional body’s 47 member associations, which was seen by the Reuters news agency.

FIFA on Tuesday said it planned to create a $20bn commercial subsidiary to run the World Cup and its other events, drawing ⁠criticism from regional confederations, including the AFC, which said they were blindsided by the announcement.

“The AFC notes with great concern and disappointment that it was not consulted by FIFA at any level prior to the public announcement of this proposal,” Sheikh Salman wrote.

“And nor has it received any detailed governance, financial or legal ‌analysis of the proposal and its potential repercussions, which is totally unacceptable.

“Furthermore, the AFC is deeply concerned that FIFA’s unilateral actions appear to undermine the very foundations of continental football, which are based on solidarity, cooperation and transparency.”

The Kuala Lumpur-based AFC is one of FIFA’s six confederations and is responsible for running regional club and national team competitions across a vast expanse that encompasses continental Asia, the Middle East and Australia.

The Bahraini said the proposal would not succeed without the support of ⁠all of the confederations.

Sheikh Salman called for FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s proposal ⁠to be “thoroughly examined and discussed through the appropriate legal and governance channels” and questioned the tight timeline given to member associations to approve the plan.

Infantino said in a letter to all 211 football associations this week that they would receive $40m each ⁠if they agreed to FIFA’s proposal by September 19.

“The AFC is also surprised that the current timeline allows an extremely limited period for consideration of ⁠a proposal of such significance, when such decisions should never be ⁠rushed,” wrote Sheikh Salman.

He asked the confederation’s members to avoid making a decision on the proposal until the AFC had engaged in further discussions with FIFA.

“The AFC kindly requests all [member associations] to await the outcome of these consultations and the completion of the ‌necessary review processes before reaching any position regarding the proposal,” he wrote.

“I assure you that the AFC remains fully committed to working constructively with all [member associations], FIFA and stakeholders to advance the interests of ‌football ‌and ensure that the continued growth of the game is built on a foundation of trust, transparency and unity.”

Al Jazeera has asked FIFA for a response to the letter from the AFC.

articles.title: Missile that left crater deep inside Poland was probably Russian - Polish PM
articles.excerpt:
The missile landed close to the village of Tarnawa Kolonia deep inside Polish territory

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said an object that crashed into a field in eastern Poland in the early h...
articles.body_text:
The missile landed close to the village of Tarnawa Kolonia deep inside Polish territory

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said an object that crashed into a field in eastern Poland in the early hours of Thursday was probably a Russian missile.

The unidentified object caused a 10m-wide (33ft) crater a short distance from the village of Tarnawa Kolonia, about 100km (62 miles) from the border with Ukraine during a Russian attack on the city of Lviv.

"All the indications are that it was a Russian Kh-101 ballistic missile, but we want to be 100% certain about the type of missile and who launched it," Tusk said during a specially convened meeting in Lublin.

Ukraine's acting Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said earlier on Thursday that a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile had "crossed into Poland as part of Russia's massive strike against Ukraine, violating Nato airspace".

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said about 20 objects were seen close to Polish airspace overnight and pyrotechnical analysis was being carried out to determine the identity of the object that fell near Tarnawa Kolonia.

Poland's military had detected the object at about 03:40 on Thursday (01:40 GMT) and had sent an F-16 fighter jet to intercept it before it disappeared minutes later from radar systems.

Tusk said there were no reports of casualties but the incident was being treated as serious.

The Polish leader had met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Lublin the previous evening as Zelensky was returning from talks with US President Donald Trump.

articles.title: Socialism's war on success has a new champion — and he’s running for Senate in Michigan
articles.excerpt: Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers discusses the growing influence of Democratic socialists across the country. He also discusses his potential opponent Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and his u...
articles.body_text:
Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers discusses the growing influence of Democratic socialists across the country. He also discusses his potential opponent Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and his unclear stance on the DSA.

The summer’s collective uplift from our nation’s 250th birthday and the United States’ role in co-hosting the World Cup has collided with the ominous spread of socialism among the American left. The dangerous philosophy is no longer confined to Ivy League faculty lounges or deep-blue enclaves of New York City, either. In next month’s primary in my home state of Michigan — a critical national battleground — Democrats could nominate Abdul El-Sayed for the U.S. Senate.

El-Sayed may try to distance himself from the "socialist" label and his long-standing ties to the Democratic Socialists of America, or DSA, but his platform speaks for itself. For starters, he not only boasts the support of prominent socialists Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., but has also recently campaigned with them in Michigan. Furthermore, he has gone out of his way to link himself to self-described democratic socialist and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Last summer, his campaign even ran ads declaring, "Zohran won. Abdul is next."

Like the private jet-flying, multiple-home-owning Sanders, El-Sayed is a hypocrite. He has demonized high earners while earning an income in 2025 that puts him squarely in the top 1%. He has also advocated for "Medicare for All" and railed against employer health plans while his wife allegedly operates a medical practice that appears not to accept Medicare or any insurance at all.

SOCIALIST-BACKED DEM WHO RIPPED THE WEALTHY CRACKS STATE’S TOP 1%, TAX RETURNS SHOW

But perhaps most troubling is the radical economic agenda El-Sayed seeks to bring to Washington. One staple of his stump speech is his criticism of "corporate oligopoly" and his demand for a "muscular" Federal Trade Commission, or FTC. On that front, El-Sayed’s campaign draws directly from the anti-business orthodoxy pushed by Lina Khan, former chair of the FTC under President Joe Biden and current chair of the board of the New York City Economic Development Corporation.

Under Khan’s watch, sweeping federal investigations and punitive lawsuits became standard operating procedure, sending a chill through innovators and entrepreneurs nationwide. Her time leading the once-bipartisan agency was mired in hostility toward enterprise, job losses and internal agency mismanagement. By echoing Khan’s rhetoric, El-Sayed is not just pandering to the far left but also preparing to execute her ideas in the Senate. Their shared worldview appears to treat success as suspect and the federal government as a weapon to punish companies for innovating, competing and winning in the marketplace.

Unfortunately, key pillars of this agenda are already surfacing. Take the recently revived American Innovation and Choice Online Act, or AICOA. Having failed to advance in previous Congresses, it’s back this summer as living proof of an anti-business and anti-growth philosophy.

RAHM EMANUEL WARNS DSA AGENDA DOESN'T PLAY WELL OUTSIDE 'UPPER WEST SIDE OF MANHATTAN'

Among other harmful provisions, the bill establishes a financial threshold above which tech companies would be subject to punitive, European-style regulations. Should the legislation become law, federal regulators will have sweeping authority to single out and penalize American companies for being successful innovators.

If elected, it’s a good bet El-Sayed won’t just support this regulatory overreach; he will champion its expansion, putting Michigan’s job creators and critical industries in the crosshairs.

For my friends on the right who are watching the rise of socialism with glee and viewing it as a glide path to victory in the general election, think again. In a challenging midterm political environment, anything can happen. To win public support, we need to do more than just paint our opponents as extremists.

We must, as Ronald Reagan said, put forward our own bold colors and not pale pastels. We must be clear about how and why free markets provide opportunities, especially for younger audiences who are already nervous about their future amid the rise of artificial intelligence. History shows us that innovation leads to more jobs and opportunities. But that can’t happen if we cede leadership to China out of fear of the unknown or surrender the economic argument to the likes of Mamdani, Khan and El-Sayed, who will replace optimism with fear tactics.

That means articulating a clear, affirmative vision for economic growth: cutting burdensome regulations that stifle investment and hurt startups, defending free-market competition, and ensuring that American enterprise remains the envy of the world.

A former four-term chairman of the Republican National Committee, Ronna McDaniel is the chair of the Competitiveness Coalition and CEO of the Michigan Forward Network.
