The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, says the cut to the fuel excise was always meant to be temporary and the government had spent the last few months ensuring fuel supply amid ongoing tension in the Middle East.

Albanese said he would consider revisiting the cuts in the future if the war in the region drags on, but said the decision to step down the cuts had been telegraphed with a “lot of notice”.

double quotation markWhat we’ve moved to is permanent cost-of-living support. The tax cuts that came in on July 1, the increase in the minimum wage, the move of paid parental leave to six months – all of these measures are making a difference on cost of living.

eSafety commissioner says Telegram case comes amid ‘heightened security environment’ in Australia

Julie Inman Grant said the case comes at a time when Australia is “facing a heightened security environment against the fresh backdrop of the Bondi tragedy, the royal commission into antisemitism, and Asio’s assessment that Australia’s terrorism threat level remains ‘Probable’”.

double quotation markIt is more important than ever that digital platforms meet their obligations to protect the Australian community. Australians have the right to expect that services operating and generating revenue in this country are responsible for preventing platforms from being used to spread material that can radicalise, incite violence, and cause real world harm.

Inman Grant added that some of the alleged offending content remained on Telegram. She said court action was ongoing, but when asked if the app could be banned from Australia she had this to say:

double quotation markWe could apply to the federal court and ask that the service be ceased. We’ve never used those powers. We’ll see how this all plays out and whether that kind of action is warranted.

eSafety takes Telegram to court over terror content

The eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, has taken messaging service Telegram to court over its alleged failure to detect and remove pro-terror material from its platform, including videos of terrorist executions and mass shootings.

The eSafety commissioner conducted a year-long investigation into the platform and alleges Telegram has failed to comply with Australian codes and standards regarding pro-terror material.

The content allegedly identified includes the livestreamed Christchurch mosque shooting from 2019, and the Buffalo mass shooting in New York from May 2022.

eSafety alleges the material was uploaded to Telegram nearly three months prior to its removal.

The company could face fines of up to A$54.6m.

Albanese says government providing support to Australian in Syria facing death penalty

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, says the federal government is providing assistance to an Australian man facing the death penalty in Syria over the alleged murder of a fellow national.

AAP reports Gold Coast man Patrick Stevenson, 20, has been detained for seven months in Syria over the alleged shooting death of another Australian man, Abdullah Glen Charles Burgess, in December.

The penalty for premeditated murder in Syria is punishable by death.

However, Stevenson could be spared execution under Syria’s legal system if Burgess’s widow grants forgiveness in the form of a blood-money payment.

double quotation markLegal processes will take their course overseas, of course, and that is appropriate. I feel for the families of the person who’s lost their life, and we’ve connected with them and providing support for them.

We’re also providing support for the family of the person who’s been charged.

Australia does not have a diplomatic presence in Syria, which has limited the ability for consular support.

Bird flu is spreading locally. How bad could it get?

Australia has entered a new phase in dealing with the incursion of deadly H5N1 bird flu, with authorities confirming on Wednesday that local transmission of the highly virulent strain had taken place.

“We have had what is suggestive of local transmission for the first time,” Julie Collins, the federal minister for agriculture, fisheries and forestry, said on Wednesday afternoon, after 11 new suspected detections were reported in South Australian birds.

Now that authorities believe transmission of H5 strain is occurring locally, what does this mean for Australia’s wildlife, and how bad could things get?

Police and government have been under pressure after multiple deaths

The announcement said NSW police will still respond in situations “where the police are the most appropriate agency to attend”.

The ministers said its approach was shaped by the UK’s “right person, right care” model, which sees health workers rather than police attend mental health callouts if there is no crime being committed and no risk to life.

Police and the government had been under pressure to enact reforms after the deaths of Clare Nowland, Steve Pampalian, Jesse Deacon and Krista Kach in 2023 while under mental health distress. The pressure grew again after public housing resident Collin Burling died last year after he begged for help while restrained by police.

Last week, the coronial inquest into Deacon’s death, who was fatally shot by police after he was reported to be self-harming, began before the NSW coroner’s court. His mother, 82-year-old Judy Deacon has since become one of the state’s loudest voices for change in how police respond to mental health incidents. One of the changes he has called for is a change to how Triple 0 calls are triaged.

NSW government to roll out health-led response to mental health crises

The Minns government is rolling out a health-led response to mental health emergencies following long-fought for reform in the wake of multiple deaths at the hands of police.

The police minister, Yasmin Catley, and mental health minister, Rose Jackson, announced on Thursday people experiencing a mental health crises who call triple zero will, under the change, be connected with a new team of mental health experts who would assess their needs, provide support and connect them with the care they need.

The change, funded by $270m over 10 years, will also establish a hub in NSW ambulance that will provide real-time clinical advice to first responders.

Eight new mental health acute assessment teams, which will include a paramedic and specialist mental health nurse, will also be set up and based in areas of high need, operating 12 hours a day, seven days a week.

Albanese says Victorians will have a choice between Ben Carroll ‘and chaos’

Albanese said he welcomed Ben Carroll’s election in Victoria as the next premier and looks forward to working with him.

The prime minister was also asked about One Nation’s surging support in the state before its November election and had this to say:

double quotation markVictorians will have a choice between Ben Carroll and a Labor government, and chaos. … That’s the choice that they will have. And a chaotic Victorian government with people involved in One Nation. …

I want to see a Victorian government that looks after the interests of Victorians, that continues to invest in health and education …

I look forward to working with Ben Carroll, and I will continue to advocate for him to remain premier of Victoria beyond November. Because I think that is very much in the interests of Victorians.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, says the cut to the fuel excise was always meant to be temporary and the government had spent the last few months ensuring fuel supply amid ongoing tension in the Middle East.

Albanese said he would consider revisiting the cuts in the future if the war in the region drags on, but said the decision to step down the cuts had been telegraphed with a “lot of notice”.

double quotation markWhat we’ve moved to is permanent cost-of-living support. The tax cuts that came in on July 1, the increase in the minimum wage, the move of paid parental leave to six months – all of these measures are making a difference on cost of living.

‘The likelihood of the RBA raising interest rates has fallen. Have we finally come to our senses?’

Greg Jericho has a piece this morning on the latest inflation figures. He writes:

double quotation markThe June inflation rate of 3.8% ended any real prospect of a rate rise next month, despite investors assuming the Reserve Bank would rather raise rates than not.

There is a certain ghoulishness when it comes to economics and especially inflation. A “good” number will inevitably be dull news, whereas a bad number – one that is higher than expected or just higher – can lead to all manner of gnashing of teeth and wailing as the topic quickly shifts to interest rates.

Atlassian tightens tracking of staff AI use

Software firm Atlassian has sought to tighten tracking of its staff’s AI spending by introducing “wallets” with monthly caps of up $2,000 for each employee, amid an explosion in costs at other tech companies.

The move by Atlassian, which recently cited AI as part of the reason behind cutting 1,600 staff, bucks the trend of others in the tech sector who encouraged employees to use as much of the technology as possible, dubbed “tokenmaxxing”. Some companies have reportedly introduced leaderboards for employees who used the most AI in their work.

Tokens refer to the measurement of a response AI gives to a prompt. OpenAI has said one token is about four characters, and something like the US Declaration of Independence amounts to 1,695 tokens. OpenAI’s flagship model, GPT-5.6 Sol, has a charge of US$5 for every 1m tokens, while Anthropic’s Claude Fable and Mythos models are US$10 for every 1m tokens.

Under tokenmaxxing, the costs quickly add up.

articles.title: Frozen pizza brand celebrates 50 years by throwing every topping you can think of on a pie
articles.excerpt: WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert continues to face intense scrutiny for her leadership missteps, especially surrounding Indiana Fever superstar Caitlin Clark. But despite mounting criticism, some in ...
articles.body_text:
WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert continues to face intense scrutiny for her leadership missteps, especially surrounding Indiana Fever superstar Caitlin Clark. But despite mounting criticism, some in the media are rushing to shield her.

Frozen pizzas have been a staple of freezers for decades, a useful option for a late-night snack or a contingency plan when you mess up the better dinner you were trying to cook.

And, for 50 years, one of the biggest players in the game has been Red Baron.

Now, the pizza brand is celebrating its 50th anniversary by dumping just about anything you can think of on top of a pie.

REDS FANS GO BERSERK AFTER CATCHER TYLER STEPHENSON'S ABS CHALLENGE WINS THEM FREE PIZZA

If your ideal pie just has a few pepperonis tossed on it, maybe Red Baron's 50th anniversary pizza isn't for you. (iStock)

That's right, they're giving lucky winners the chance to go to town on a pizza with 50 toppings.

Baron von Richthofen himself could never have imagined when he was shot down during the Fourth Battle of Ypres that this would be his legacy...

You can enter to win one on the company's website, but I don't even think I could name fifty pizza toppings. If someone locked me in a room and said I couldn't come out until I did, I'd probably get about 25 before I started panicking.

KFC PLANS TO TEST A NEW PROTOTYPE CALLED OPEN HOUSE

Red Baron is celebrating fifty years with a fifty-topping pizza. (iStock)

I'd get to arugula, and then I'd be like, "Sh--; someone has to have put rhubarb on pizza, right? RIGHT?!"

A lot is happening on that pie, maybe too much.

I don't usually go too far beyond sausage, pepper, and onion on my bespoke pies, and I'm not averse to keeping it au naturel and going plain.

But I'm open to experimentation on the pizza front and would be open to popping this into the ol' General Electric oven and seeing what it's all about.

Hell, I went on a cruise earlier this year, and they had grape and gorgonzola pizza. I thought that broke some laws (good thing we were in international waters at the time), and it turned out to be one of the best pizzas I've ever had.

Certainly not a daily driver like a nice Hot-N-Ready or a pie from the mom & pop joint down the street. But if you want to put the top down and let your hair blow in the wind, that's when you bust out a flashy pizza like a grape and gorgonzola or, in this case, everything they had on hand at the Red Baron plant.

articles.title: El-Sayed in the hot seat for another foreign rental property, nearly $300K in additional income
articles.excerpt: Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., accused Democratic Senate rival Abdul El-Sayed of withholding his full tax returns while earning $300,000 in outside income and promoting what she called "junk health care...
articles.body_text:
Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., accused Democratic Senate rival Abdul El-Sayed of withholding his full tax returns while earning $300,000 in outside income and promoting what she called "junk health care cures" through his podcast. (Credit: WJBK)

Moments ahead of a primary debate on Monday night, Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed released a new financial disclosure, revealing new details about he and his wife’s assets worth up to $2.1 million.

The disclosures, which come a week ahead of a heated primary election between El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., shed new light on El-Sayed’s financials but questions still remain about the specifics of his wealth. While, broadly, much of their information was already known through reporting he did last year, the 2026 filing adds three key additions.

El Sayed and his wife listed a rental property in Dubai worth up to $250,000, a liability to a company in Dubai worth up to $100,000 and a tweak to El-Sayed’s employment status in Michigan.

SOCIALIST-BACKED DEM WHO RIPPED THE WEALTHY CRACKS STATE’S TOP 1%, TAX RETURNS SHOW

Abdul El-Sayed, candidate for US Senate in Michigan, speaks before U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) takes the stage at Mumford High School on May 3, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)

Past reporting had already show that El-Sayed’s wife owned a rental property in Ann Harbor, Michigan and another one in Bangalore, India.

The Dubai property makes a third real estate holding. The debt, worth between $50,000 and $100,000, is a liability owed to Majid Al Futtaim Tilal, a real estate development company that specializes in luxury residential projects. And finally, the filing adds that El-Sayed worked as a consultant for Wayne County, Michigan, with an income of $72,000. At the same time, the filing lists a salary of $82,750 — also for Wayne County. The consulting is a change from a salaried position listed at $278,900 the year before.

"Know many people who own rental properties in three countries?" Prominent gun-control activist Shannon Watts posted on X.

"Why are all the socialists rich????" Democratic analyst Rachel Bitecofer posted on X.

In total, both the 2025 and 2026 filings put El-Sayed’s net worth between $870,000 and $2.1 million.

The Michigan race has drawn national attention as Stevens, a more establishment candidate with the backing of Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., squares off against El-Sayed’s progressive promises to challenge the U.S.-Israel relationship, abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and provide universal healthcare. His platform has drawn support from fellow progressives such as Sens. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Bernie Sanders, I-Vt.

WATCH: SURFACED VIDEOS OF DEM SENATE CANDIDATE BACKING 'DEFUND THE POLICE' CONTRADICT RECENT DENIALS

Michigan U.S. Sen. candidate, Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., speaks with media after a debate at WoodTV studios on Tuesday, July 7, 2026, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Kristen Norman)

With a groundswell of support among progressives, Stevens has sought to paint El-Sayed as a far cry from the middle-class working-family base he claims to champion, needling El-Sayed over his net worth in a debate last month.

"Look, I am the only one running for United States Senate in Michigan who is not a millionaire," Stevens had said at the time.

At the debate on Monday, Stevens resurfaced the filings and what she characterized as a lack of transparency.

"You have not released your tax returns," Stevens reminded him. "You talk about getting money out of politics and putting money in people’s pockets, but still no one knows who’s putting the money in your pocket," Stevens said.

El-Sayed, who filed the Senate report right before the debate, said he had made the necessary disclosures, sidestepping the comment about his tax returns.

DEM PRIMARY ERUPTS AS ESTABLISHMENT FAVORITE DISMISSES RIVAL AS ‘CELEBRITY CANDIDATE’

Abdul El-Sayed, candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, speaks before U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., takes the stage at Mumford High School on May 3, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)

"This is a distraction from the issues in your life," he said at Monday’s debate.

El-Sayed’s most recent disclosures follow an application for an extension which allowed him an extra 90 days to finalize his 2026 paperwork. That extension would have allowed him to submit his disclosures on Aug. 13 — a week after the primary. When confronted about the timeline, El-Sayed pledged on a podcast earlier this month to submit his disclosures before the election.

El-Sayed’s campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment about the disclosures or the timing of its submission.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia seeks international coalition against Houthis in Red Sea
articles.excerpt: Saudi Arabia is seeking to build an international coalition to protect shipping in the Red Sea from attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, people familiar with the deliberations have told the Reuters news agency...
articles.body_text:
Saudi Arabia is seeking to build an international coalition to protect shipping in the Red Sea from attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, people familiar with the deliberations have told the Reuters news agency.

The composition of the coalition has not yet been finalised and is being discussed with dozens of countries, the sources said.

Tensions in the Red Sea are rising, denting the global economic outlook already under stress due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

On July 20, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, accusing its leaders of imposing “an unjust and oppressive siege” on Yemen for nearly 12 years, “plundering our resources and imposing a comprehensive blockade”.

Since then, the Houthis said they have launched attacks on Saudi vessels in the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia responded with air strikes on what it said were Houthi military facilities at Yemen’s Hodeidah port used to threaten commercial shipping.

The Saudi Center for International Communication did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

The blockade has opened a new front against the United States and its allies in the wider US-Israel war on Iran, expanding attacks on tankers carrying energy and other supplies to waters beyond the Gulf and pushing oil prices higher.

“Gulf states have been trying to avoid this [expansion] throughout the US-Iran conflict. They do not believe this is their war to fight, and they have said repeatedly they don’t want to get dragged into it,” said Al Jazeera’s Victoria Gatenby.

Saudi Minister of Foreign Affairs Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud received phone calls from his counterparts in Qatar, Kuwait and Bahrain, during which the diplomats “stressed the importance of continuing efforts to de-escalate tensions”, according to his office.

They also condemned attacks by Iran and “its affiliated militias in Iraq and Yemen”, and emphasised continued coordination and stronger joint action through the Gulf Cooperation Council.

In Yemen, a minister of the internationally recognised government accused Houthi rebels of working under Iranian guidance to establish a system to impose fees for ships transiting the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait.

Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani described “the move as a dangerous escalation aimed at transforming one of the world’s most strategic maritime corridors into a permanent source of funding for the militia’s military and terrorist activities”.

articles.title: Nicaragua’s Daniel Ortega aims to bar ‘traitors’ from future elections
articles.excerpt: Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega aims to exclude “traitors” and “coup-plotting” opposition members from elections, while also seeking to extend the presidential term from six to seven “renewable” ye...
articles.body_text:
Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega aims to exclude “traitors” and “coup-plotting” opposition members from elections, while also seeking to extend the presidential term from six to seven “renewable” years, according to a draft constitutional reform sent to Congress.

Congress President Gustavo Porras previewed the content of the reform on Tuesday, according to several media outlets, though he did not provide many details.

The proposal is expected to be approved in September. It follows recent statements by the president that there would be no elections in the Central American nation, as a means of preventing the opposition from “seizing the government”.

“Our system of government, under the presidency of the people, proposes to be organised with an effective term of seven renewable years,” Porras said as he read the proposal.

A previous constitutional amendment was passed in 2024 that extended the presidential term from five to six years and elevated Rosario Murillo, Ortega’s wife and then-vice president, to the position of co-president.

It also postponed planned elections until late 2027.

Opponents criticised those moves as an effort to keep the presidential family in power indefinitely.

Ortega, a former Marxist rebel, began his fourth consecutive term in January 2022 after winning an election the previous November, amid growing criticism and sanctions from much of the international community, led by the United States and the European Union.

He helped overthrow the right-wing dictatorship of the Somoza family in the late 1970s and has been the longest-serving leader in the Americas since returning to power in 2007.

Nicaragua has been in the midst of a political crisis since April 2018, when Ortega responded to antigovernment protests with a crackdown that killed more than 300 people, according to human rights organisations.

articles.title: Israel slams Canada for statement opposing West Bank settlement expansion
articles.excerpt: The Canadian government has issued a statement reaffirming its opposition to Israeli expansion in the occupied West Bank, where settlers have carried out widespread and violent attacks on Palestinian ...
articles.body_text:
The Canadian government has issued a statement reaffirming its opposition to Israeli expansion in the occupied West Bank, where settlers have carried out widespread and violent attacks on Palestinian communities.

Wednesday’s statement prompted a tit-for-tat on social media with the Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which sought to dismiss Canada’s concerns as misguided.

In a post, Global Affairs Canada, the country’s foreign ministry, underscored that Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory are illegal under international law.

The expansion of such settlements has coincided with an uptick in violence in the West Bank. The United Nations reports that 76 Palestinians have died this year in settler attacks.

“Canada condemns the ongoing violence in the West Bank. The expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank must stop. These settlements are illegal under international law and undermine prospects for peace, security and stability,” Canada’s statement reads.

“We call for the de-escalation and protection of civilians. International humanitarian law must be respected, and all civilians must be able to live in safety and security.”

Hours earlier, the Office for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) likewise highlighted the increasing violence and condemned plans for expanding Israeli settlements.

“We are alarmed by the Israeli Government’s announcement to further increase the number of settlements and outposts and open calls by Israeli leaders for revenge and collective punishment against Palestinian communities,” an OHCHR spokesperson said in a statement.

The UN said it had recorded roughly 190 settler attacks in each of the first four months of 2026. At that rate, it estimated that the number of settler attacks could reach about 2,000 by the year’s end, overtaking last year’s total of 1,835.

The remarks from Global Affairs Canada on social media prompted a rebuttal from the Israeli Foreign Ministry, which accused Canada of moving to “embolden terror”.

“A wave of Palestinian terrorism is sweeping Judea and Samaria. Israelis are being murdered and wounded by Palestinian terrorists,” the Foreign Ministry said, using the biblical term for the occupied West Bank favoured by Israeli settlers.

“Yet Canada’s response is not to focus on the terrorists or those who glorify and encourage them, but to condemn Israel.”

Attacks on Palestinian communities have further surged after a deadly incident last week, when a Palestinian man in the village of Tal grabbed a settler’s gun and shot him dead during an incursion into their village.

Heavily armed Israeli settlers often roam into Palestinian areas hoping to spark tensions.

Israeli authorities and settlers alike have framed the incident as an act of terrorism and used it as a pretext to issue a sweeping crackdown on Palestinian communities.

Israel and Canada have previously feuded over Israel’s control of the occupied West Bank, although critics have pointed out that Ottawa has rarely followed up with concrete policy changes to step up pressure on Israel.

In December, Israel denied six Canadian MPs entry into the occupied West Bank, where they had planned to speak with Palestinian officials and human rights advocates.

The National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM) said at the time that the lawmakers had been turned away after being told that Israeli authorities had deemed them a “public safety threat”.

articles.title: Trump appeals $83.3m E Jean Carroll civil verdict to US Supreme Court
articles.excerpt:
Personal lawyers for United States President Donald Trump are appealing to the Supreme Court to reject an $83.3m defamation penalty a jury awarded to writer E Jean Carroll.

Separately, representative...
articles.body_text:
Personal lawyers for United States President Donald Trump are appealing to the Supreme Court to reject an $83.3m defamation penalty a jury awarded to writer E Jean Carroll.

Separately, representatives for the Department of Justice have filed a similar petition this week, seeking the same end goal.

Both have argued that Trump’s statements against Carroll — who claims the Republican leader sexually assaulted her in the Bergdorf Goodman department store — fall within the bounds of his office’s immunity.

“Absent this Court’s intervention, the sitting President is facing nearly a hundred million dollars of personal liability for conduct that was well within the scope of his federal office,” federal lawyers wrote in their filings.

They pointed to the Westfall Act, which shields federal employees from certain civil lawsuits when an alleged harm is “committed within the scope of their employment”.

Trump’s personal lawyers, meanwhile, suggested that the president’s remarks about Carroll could fall under the precedent set in the 2024 Supreme Court case Trump v United States.

That ruling expanded the concept of presidential immunity.

Previously, presidents enjoyed immunity from prosecution for any actions that fell within their constitutional authority. But after the 2024 case, “presumptive immunity” was extended to anything that could be considered an “official act” of the presidency — a term that was left largely undefined.

The precedent, however, only applies to criminal prosecution. It does not include civil cases, like Carroll’s.

Still, Trump’s personal lawyers have sought to widen the 2024 ruling to include civil proceedings. The 2nd Circuit Court of Appeals in Manhattan, however, rejected that approach on September 8 of last year.

In appealing to the Supreme Court, Trump’s legal team argued that his statements about Carroll were voiced as part of his presidential interactions with the public and news reporters. They therefore constitute an “official act”, according to Trump’s court filings.

His lawyers also accused lower courts of sidestepping the question of presidential immunity, which was not raised at the early stages of the litigation.

“This is the first case in our nation’s history in which a court has imposed damages liability on a president for his conduct in office,” the Trump team said in its filings.

“Yet, in upholding the exorbitant $83.3 million defamation judgment here, the 2nd Circuit never even decided whether presidential immunity applies to President Trump’s allegedly defamatory statements.”

For years, Trump has fought a pair of defamation lawsuits filed by Carroll. The first was filed in 2019, after Carroll said he damaged her reputation by claiming she lied about the alleged assault for personal gain.

The second came in 2022, after Trump renewed his accusation that Carroll had lied.

In a social media post that year, Trump called her case “phony”, a “complete con job” and a “complete scam”. He added that he had to defend his reputation from “liars, cheaters, and hacks”.

Trump was no longer president at that time, having lost his first re-election bid to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. He has since mounted a successful re-election campaign in the 2024 presidential race.

The second defamation case was resolved first. In 2023, a jury awarded Carroll $5m, finding Trump liable for both sexual abuse and defamation, though not rape, as Carroll alleged.

The 2019 civil trial, meanwhile, reached a verdict in January 2024. In that case, a jury awarded $83.3m, much of which came in the form of punitive damages, finding Trump liable for sexual abuse and harming Carroll’s reputation.

Carroll, a former columnist for Elle magazine, first made her accusations about Trump’s behaviour public in a 2019 book called What Do We Need Men For? A Modest Proposal.

She gave an account of the Republican leader of cornering her in a department store dressing room in 1996, pulling down her tights and raping her. Trump has denied her accusations, saying, “This woman is not my type.”

In the years since the two jury decisions, Carroll’s lawyers have accused the Trump side of attempting to avoid paying the verdicts.

In June, the Supreme Court declined to hear Trump’s appeal against the initial $5m jury award — which had grown due to accrued interest to nearly $5.8m. A federal judge subsequently ordered the payment to be disbursed this month.

It is unclear whether the Supreme Court will take up Trump’s appeal of the $83.3m defamation verdict.

articles.title: Gina Rinehart lobbied for controversial plan to move 2032 Olympic rowing to crocodile-inhabited river
articles.excerpt:
Decision to host event on Fitzroy River at Rockhampton, 600km north of host city Brisbane, prompted significant backlash

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news ...
articles.body_text:
Decision to host event on Fitzroy River at Rockhampton, 600km north of host city Brisbane, prompted significant backlash

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s richest person, Gina Rinehart, lobbied for controversial plans to host 2032 Olympic rowing events on the Fitzroy River at Rockhampton, documents released by the Queensland government show.

The plans to send rowers 600km north of host city Brisbane – to a river that is natural habitat for saltwater crocodiles, and which prompted significant backlash among the rowing and broader Olympic communities – were announced by the Queensland government in March last year.

The newly elected Queensland government conducted a venues review that was finalised in early 2025.

It used the review process to justify breaking election promises not to build a new stadium. But the decision to send rowing events to Rockhampton went against the review’s recommendations, which suggested rowing be relocated to Sydney and held at the existing facility near Penrith.

Concerns about the Fitzroy River’s suitability go well beyond the most glaring reason – the saltwater crocodiles, which are occasionally found in the water at Rockhampton, which sits just above the Tropic of Capricorn.

International and Australian rowing officials and competitors have raised various concerns, including that a rowing facility built in Rockhampton would become a “white elephant”. There are also concerns any potential course would not it meet the strict technical requirements for international racing regarding weeds, water quality and currents.

The situation has led to brinkmanship: the Queensland deputy premier, Jarrod Bleijie, has said publicly that rowing would be held in Rockhampton or cancelled altogether.

An undated letter from Rinehart to Bleijie obtained by Brisbane Times, but understood to have been sent prior to the government’s decision to move rowing to Rockhampton, lobbies for the relocation of rowing to central Queensland.

Rinehart, a key financial backer of the rightwing One Nation party, and who has extensive mining and pastoral interests, says in the letter that hosting an Olympic event in the “beef capital” would “enable Queensland to tell the iconic Australian story of our pastoralists and farmers”.

“As a supporter of Australian rowing for more than a decade, I am aware that the Australian team often trains on the Fitzroy River and that Rockhampton annually hosts the Queensland state school championships,” Rinehart said.
 “This rowing facility is world class and is already close to major infrastructure, so it offers the potential to save taxpayer money.

“As you would know too, Rockhampton has also always been a major mining town, the nearby Mt Morgan mine was once the biggest gold mine in the world.

“I am told that metals from this mine will produce the gold, silver, and bronze medals for the Olympics! To marry showing where the Olympic medals come from and having Olympic events nearby, sounds to me like a beautiful extra!”

articles.title: Wisconsin Dem socialist gubernatorial hopeful dodges whether she still wants to ‘abolish police’
articles.excerpt:
Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong was asked about appearing on far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker's livestream on MS NOW Wednesday.

Wisconsin democratic socialist state Re...
articles.body_text:
Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong was asked about appearing on far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker's livestream on MS NOW Wednesday.

Wisconsin democratic socialist state Rep. Francesca Hong, the Democratic primary frontrunner in the race for governor, sidestepped repeated questions from Politico reporter Jonathan Martin Tuesday at Marquette University in Milwaukee about whether she still wants to abolish police after a televised debate in which she pledged to preserve law enforcement funding amid scrutiny of her previous position.

"So, this system is not working," Hong said. "If we want to be serious, we better be putting these billions into things we know prevent crime."

Martin asked whether Hong still wanted to abolish police in the long term. Hong did not answer yes or no, instead calling for "systems of care" and redirecting criminal justice spending before a campaign aide ushered her away.

"I believe that we have to be serious about public safety, and I’m going to be a governor that is more serious than anyone else in making sure that we are building systems of care," Hong said.

DEM SOCIALIST RUNNING FOR WISCONSIN GOVERNOR PUSHED 'ABOLISHING THE POLICE'

Gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong speaks on stage during the Wisconsin Democrats 2026 Convention June 14, 2026, in Madison, Wis. (Getty Images for WisDems)

Hong campaign communications director Allison Geyer told Fox News Digital Wednesday the candidate had not changed her underlying values on police and prison abolition, although she now discusses the issue differently.

"Rep. Hong has spoken in the past about police and prison abolition as an aspirational goal, akin to eradicating disease or eliminating poverty," Geyer said. "Her values haven’t changed, but the way she talks about this issue has."

Hours earlier, moderators asked Hong and her four Democratic opponents whether they would sign a state budget cutting police funding. All five said they would not.

"The governor cannot defund police, and I am not here to govern by slogan," Hong said. "I am here to make sure I am the governor that’s most serious about public safety."

SCOTT WALKER: DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS ARE COMING FOR MY STATE. THIS IS HOW WE BEAT THEM

Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong (Matthew Ludak for The Washington Post via Getty Images)

The exchange revived scrutiny of Hong's comments following the 2020 police shooting of Jacob Blake in Kenosha. Hong called for abolishing police in a 2021 social media post after federal prosecutors declined to charge the officer who shot Blake.

"How is 7 bullets in the back not excessive force," Hong said. "Police exist to uphold White supremacy. Defund then abolish. Reform can't be an option. My heart breaks for the trauma the Blake family and their community continues to endure."

She addressed the controversy in a May statement to Fox News Digital but did not say then whether she continued to support abolishing the police.

"There is no way I want to cut resources for public safety," Hong said. "I don’t like crime. I don’t like unsafe streets. I also don’t like when a member of law enforcement abuses their power."

On Tuesday, Hong's campaign told Fox News Digital the candidate did not recall a social media post she made in 2021 calling to "Abolish the Senate" after the body failed to convict President Donald Trump during impeachment proceedings.

DSA CO-CHAIR PUSHES BACK ON SOVIET UNION COMPARISONS, WANTS PRISONS TO BE 'LESS NECESSARY'

Francesca Hong, a Democratic state lawmaker and socialist candidate for Wisconsin governor, speaks to voters at a retirement home July 7, 2026, in Madison, Wis. (Scott Bauer/AP Photo)

Hong's campaign platform calls for state support for noncarceral crime-prevention programs, reentry services, red flag laws, universal background checks and safe-storage requirements. Its public safety section does not call for eliminating police departments or cutting their funding.

A Marquette Law School poll released Wednesday showed Hong at 38% among Democratic primary voters, up from 26% one week earlier. Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes followed at 16%, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley had 7%, and 34% remained undecided. The survey of 407 primary voters had a 6.6-percentage-point margin of error.

Hong’s rise has unsettled Democrats concerned about the November contest against expected Republican nominee Rep. Tom Tiffany.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Joe Zepecki, a Democratic strategist who is not supporting a primary candidate, said Republicans were "trying to pick an opponent they think they can beat."

"Every Democratic campaign should call this out for what it is: a sneaky, underhanded, blatant attempt to meddle in the democratic process," Zepecki said in comments published by Wisconsin Public Radio.

Joel Brennan, a former Wisconsin Department of Administration secretary under Democratic Gov. Tony Evers, is running against Hong for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination.

In a memo published by WisPolitics, Brennan said the ads were intended to elevate Hong, "a candidate they are confident they can beat in November because of her extreme positions on defunding police, abolishing prisons and other views out of step with mainstream Wisconsin values."

Citing a filing with the Wisconsin Ethics Commission, WisPolitics reported that the Republican Governors Association has spent nearly $3.6 million on ads labeling Hong dangerously liberal while emphasizing positions likely to appeal to progressive primary voters.

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

You can send news tips to cj.womack@fox.com and follow CJ on Twitter.

articles.title: Iraq calls Saudi-US attacks a ‘flagrant violation of sovereignty’
articles.excerpt: Iraq’s National Security Council has condemned Wednesday’s Saudi-US strikes against the Iran-backed Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), which killed at least 20 members of the Iraqi paramilitary group....
articles.body_text:
Iraq’s National Security Council has condemned Wednesday’s Saudi-US strikes against the Iran-backed Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), which killed at least 20 members of the Iraqi paramilitary group.

The council meeting, chaired by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, called the attacks on PMF bases in seven Iraqi provinces “a flagrant violation of Iraq’s sovereignty and the sanctity of its lands”.

“An aggression”, according to a statement shared on X, “in contravention of the principles of international law and the United Nations Charter”.

“Any transgression or compromise of Iraq’s security and sovereignty will not be tolerated under any circumstances”, it said.

Saudi Arabia and US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the joint air strikes targeted Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq responsible for attacks on American troops and Saudi energy infrastructure.

The Saudi Ministry of Defence said in a statement that the strikes were “in response ⁠to recent drone attacks” and that Saudi air defences had “intercepted and destroyed several drones that attempted to target petroleum facilities in the Eastern Province and Riyadh regions… launched from Iraqi territory and carried out by Iran-aligned terrorist militias”.

The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella coalition of self-proclaimed resistance groups backed by Iran, had denied any role in the attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying the Saudi claims were “fabrications” and that “any foolish Saudi action will be met with a harsh response”.

The joint Saudi-US attacks, from the Iraqi cities of Kirkuk in the north to Basra in the south, killed at least 20 PMF members and at least four advisers from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), according to Iranian and Iraqi media reports.

Iraqi Prime Minister al-Zaidi was due in the Saudi capital on Thursday, his first visit since taking office, but the visit has been cancelled following the attacks.

Baghdad has complained that US-Saudi “aggression has hindered investigation efforts regarding the alleged targeting of Saudi Arabia”.

“We demand evidence and proof regarding the launch of attacks from Iraq, and no party has provided any evidence,” the spokesperson for the commander-in-chief for Iraq’s armed forces told the Iraqi News Agency.

Funerals were held in Mosul for some of the PMF fighters killed, with mourners calling for revenge. There is also anger on the streets of the capital, Baghdad, where PMF supporters rallied, demanding the expulsion of the Saudi ambassador.

In a statement, the Iran-aligned Iraqi paramilitary group Kataib Hezbollah said it would give the Iraqi government until August 6 to demonstrate it can defend Iraq’s sovereignty.

The group said an immediate response to the US-Saudi attack is “inevitable”.

articles.title: Trump taps veterans to fix illegal alien trucking problem plaguing US roadways
articles.excerpt: Fox News' Kevin Corke reports on a joint investigation by the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Transportation targeting truck driver schools. The probe addresses improper certificatio...
articles.body_text:
Fox News' Kevin Corke reports on a joint investigation by the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Transportation targeting truck driver schools. The probe addresses improper certifications and falsified records, especially concerning the issuance of commercial driver's licenses to non-citizens/

FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump will launch the White House's new Freedom Haulers initiative Thursday, Fox News Digital has exclusively learned, opening new pathways for military veterans to become commercial truck drivers while intensifying the administration's crackdown on illegal immigrant and non-English-speaking truckers.

"President Trump’s administration has made our roads safer by taking illegal alien, non-English-speaking truck drivers off America’s highways. Now, through the Freedom Haulers initiative, the president is expanding opportunities for our veterans by making it easier to obtain commercial driver’s licenses once they conclude their service," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Fox News Digital.

The Trump administration is pairing its crackdown on illegal immigrants and non-English-speaking commercial drivers with a new effort to recruit military veterans into the trucking industry.

Trump, along with Department of Transportation (DOT) Secretary Sean Duffy, Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins and acting Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling, will welcome a truck on West Executive Avenue to announce the initiative.

JOE BIDEN MANDATED ALL NEW VEHICLES COME INSTALLED WITH A 'KILL SWITCH.' THIS REPUBLICAN WANTS TO REPEAL IT

Former President Donald Trump, the Republican presidential nominee, holds a news conference from inside trash hauler at Green Bay Austin Straubel International Airport Oct. 30, 2024. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"By leading a multi-agency process spanning the departments of Transportation, Labor, Veterans Affairs and War, President Trump is bolstering America’s trucking industry, which is crucial to strong supply chains, while helping our nation’s heroes transition to civilian life with quality, good-paying jobs," Kelly added.

The Department of Transportation will expand eligibility for veterans to receive expedited commercial driver's licenses (CDLs), extending the waiver period from 12 months to 24 months after active-duty service.

For veterans who have never driven a heavy commercial vehicle during their military service, CDL training will be offered.

ILLEGAL TRUCKER CASES FUEL GOP PUSH TO CRACK DOWN ON CDL MILLS AS DEMS LARGELY SILENT

Former President Donald Trump, the Republican presidential nominee, holds a news conference from inside a trash hauler at Green Bay Austin Straubel International Airport Oct. 30, 2024. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Indiana and Wyoming will also join the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration's Even Exchange program, allowing military truck drivers to more easily transition into civilian CDLs.

Werner Enterprises, an Omaha, Nebraska-based trucking company attending Thursday's event, will announce plans to hire 1,400 new veteran drivers.

The administration is also highlighting its ongoing crackdown on commercial drivers who fail to meet English-language proficiency requirements or are improperly licensed.

VIRGINIA BUS CRASH THAT KILLED FIVE INVOLVED DRIVER WHO DOESN'T SPEAK ENGLISH, SEAN DUFFY SAYS

Trucks travel on Interstate 80 Nov. 14, 2025, in Albany, Calif. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

The Department of Transportation says it has removed more than 24,000 commercial driver's licenses from the nation's highways under stricter English-language proficiency enforcement.

More than 28,000 CDLs were also canceled after officials determined they had been improperly issued to noncitizen truck drivers.

The White House says the initiative is aimed at improving highway safety while strengthening the nation's trucking workforce.

The announcement comes after a series of fatal crashes involving illegal immigrant truck drivers in states including Florida, California, Indiana and Pennsylvania.

Earlier this month, a Pennsylvania State Police trooper was killed during a roadside inspection when a semitruck driven by a Haitian national struck him. Authorities say the driver had obtained a non-domiciled CDL before the administration's rule changes.

Truck drivers have seen a 7.42% increase in real wages during the Trump administration, compared to a 3% decline in real wages under President Biden, according to DOT.

DOT also says veteran truck drivers experience 42% fewer accidents and cover 98% more miles than non-veteran drivers, arguing the initiative will both improve highway safety and help strengthen America's supply chains.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Megan Moroney cancels show mid-performance, leaves stage in tears
articles.excerpt:
Country music star Megan Moroney told Fox News Digital she is not ‘emotionally available’ for a romantic relationship, putting all her energy into her music career.

Country star Megan Moroney cut her...
articles.body_text:
Country music star Megan Moroney told Fox News Digital she is not ‘emotionally available’ for a romantic relationship, putting all her energy into her music career.

Country star Megan Moroney cut her Denver concert short Tuesday night after becoming too sick to continue performing, later telling fans it was "the hardest decision" she has ever had to make.

The singer took the stage at Ball Arena but struggled through just three songs before stopping the show. Moroney returned to address the audience herself, apologizing as she fought back tears.

"I am obviously extremely sick, and I thought I did everything to make myself better, and obviously, two songs in, I just can't play this show tonight," she told the crowd in a fan-recorded video.

JON BON JOVI ABRUPTLY ENDS MADISON SQUARE GARDEN SHOW AFTER HEALTH SETBACK

Fan-recorded video captures Megan Moroney fighting back tears as she stops her Denver Ball Arena show after just three songs due to illness. (Photo by Rick Kern/Getty Images for CMT)

MEGAN MORONEY STUNS IN ORANGE BIKINI DURING FRIEND'S BAHAMAS BACHELORETTE

Despite ending the performance early, Moroney assured concertgoers she planned to make up for the disappointing night.

"I want to give you guys the show you deserve. ... I'm sorry," she said.

Fans inside the arena responded with encouragement, with one audience member shouting, "That's OK Meg, I love you," as the visibly emotional singer exited the stage.

Ball Arena later confirmed the concert had been canceled because Moroney was feeling under the weather.

The "Am I Okay?" singer shared an emotional Instagram message after ending her concert early, promising Denver fans a rescheduled date. (NDZ/Star Max/GC Images)

"Megan is unable to continue her performance this evening due to illness, and we must end the show at this time," the venue said in a statement.

"Please allow event staff to direct you to the nearest exit, and we will follow up with more information as soon as we're able."

COUNTRY SINGER MEGAN MORONEY SWEARS OFF DATING AFTER MEN 'RUINED' HER BIGGEST MOMENTS

Moroney apologized to fans for canceling her Denver show, saying she was unable to perform at 100% and announcing the concert has been rescheduled. (Megan Moroney/Instagram)

The venue added that updates would be posted on its website and apologized "for the inconvenience" while thanking fans for their understanding and cooperation.

Shortly after, Moroney shared an emotional message with fans on Instagram, explaining that continuing the concert would have meant delivering a performance below her own standards.

"That was the hardest decision I've ever had to make & I'm so sorry to cancel the show tonight," she wrote.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I never ever will give you guys a show that is not 100% and by song 3 I knew that I was not capable of giving that to you tonight."

The "Am I Okay?" singer said she was devastated by the decision, adding, "I'm typing this as I'm quite literally bawling my eyes out in my dressing room & it hurts me so much to disappoint you all."

Moroney also announced that the Denver concert has been rescheduled for Aug. 27. Tickets purchased for Tuesday night's performance will be honored for the new date, and fans unable to attend can request refunds through their original point of purchase.

"I've never had to do this & I'm truly so sorry," she wrote before closing her message with, "i love u guys."

Fox News Digital reached out to Moroney for comment.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

After leaving college, she moved to Nashville. Moroney's "Tennessee Orange" breakthrough helped transform her into an award-winning country sensation. (John Shearer/Getty Images for CMT)

The abrupt cancellation comes as Moroney continues touring following the success of her third album and a string of sold-out performances across the country.

Her emotional apology and promise to return were met with widespread support from fans online, many of whom encouraged the singer to focus on recovering before getting back on stage.

Despite the canceled show, Moroney's music career continues to soar.

After attending the University of Georgia, she moved to Nashville to pursue music full time.

Her 2022 breakout hit, "Tennessee Orange," launched her into the country music spotlight, and she has released three albums since: "Lucky" (2023), "Am I Okay?" (2024) and "Cloud 9" (2026).

Moroney also earned ACM and CMA honors as the country's top new female artist before releasing her latest project, "Cloud 9," in February and launching her current tour in May.

Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: WATCH: Fetterman reveals his ‘one regret’ from COVID era after Fauci testimony
articles.excerpt: Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., spoke with Fox News Digital after attending the Senate hearing with Dr. Anthony Fauci, sharing he wishes he'd been more willing to consider the COVID lab leak theory. (Cred...
articles.body_text:
Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., spoke with Fox News Digital after attending the Senate hearing with Dr. Anthony Fauci, sharing he wishes he'd been more willing to consider the COVID lab leak theory. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., says one of his regrets from the COVID-19 pandemic was not speaking up more forcefully about the possibility that the virus originated in a lab following a heated exchange with Anthony Fauci at a Senate hearing Wednesday.

"Did I have regrets?" Fetterman said. "Well, I did."

Speaking to Fox News Digital after questioning Fauci at the Senate hearing, Fetterman said he regretted not speaking up when the lab-leak theory was dismissed as a "fringe" idea.

CBP INTERCEPTED BIOLOGICAL MATERIALS TIED TO US–CHINA VIRUS NETWORK BEFORE COVID, NEW DOCUMENTS SHOW

U.S. Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., speaks to reporters outside the Senate Chamber during votes on Nov. 10, 2025 on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

"One [regret] for sure was, you know, this idea that it could have come from the lab," Fetterman said. "That was like, you know, crazy, right fringe kind of thing. And I was like, ‘It seemed to make sense to me.’"

During his remarks at the hearing, Fetterman told Fauci that he was not there to attack him, but rather to call out his own questioning and hesitancy throughout the pandemic. He revealed that he was reluctant to publicly support the possibility of a lab origin after it became viewed as what he called a "right-wing kind of theory," even though he thought it deserved consideration.

"I hope the next time this happens, we can follow where the truth is, depending on if there's an R or D after the name or whatever the side is," Fetterman told Fox News Digital.

RAND PAUL BRINGS CIA WHISTLEBLOWER TO SENATE HEARING ALLEGING 'DEEP STATE' COVID-19 CONSPIRACY

"It's a virus, the only side is, really, Americans versus the virus in the future," he told Fox News Digital.

Fetterman shared the same sentiment during the hearing, explaining that he doesn’t want to be "blindsided" by a partisan idea moving forward, arguing that everyone should be "willing to pursue the truth" despite what political party is spearheading it.

He also told Fox News Digital that he knew Fauci was going to plead the Fifth, which Fauci invoked 111 times after claiming Committee Chairman Rand Paul had an "obsession" with putting him behind bars. Fetterman shared that, regardless, he wanted to hold himself accountable for his own approach during the pandemic.

RAND PAUL SEEKS CONTEMPT CHARGES AFTER FAUCI INVOKES FIFTH AMENDMENT MORE THAN 100 TIMES

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., shares his regret about staying quiet on the lab leak theory during the COVID-19 pandemic after delivering remarks at the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing with Anthony Fauci. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"I know Dr. Fauci was gonna take the Fifth," Fetterman said. "So just like I said, I expressed my one regret, [not] being more willing to push that idea," Fetterman said, referring to the possibility of a lab leak.

Fetterman also spoke about his acknowledgement that while many lost their lives to the pandemic, countless businesses were also devastated by the pandemic — calling it a "different kind of death."

"I've had loved ones die from COVID, but I also met and I've heard from countless people that lost their businesses," Fetterman said. "That's devastating."

Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Senator’s F-bomb bashing of Fauci rocks Internet: ‘High-heat fastball!’
articles.excerpt:
Sen. Bernie Moreno teared into Anthony Fauci for his COVID-19 policies, accusing Fauci of being interested in meeting with celebrities than administering to the American people.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R...
articles.body_text:
Sen. Bernie Moreno teared into Anthony Fauci for his COVID-19 policies, accusing Fauci of being interested in meeting with celebrities than administering to the American people.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, tore into Dr. Anthony Fauci, who served as President Joe Biden's chief medical advisor and was a key government spokesman during the COVID-19 pandemic, dropping an F-bomb during Wednesday's congressional hearing.

Fauci was issued a subpoena by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., as part of a congressional investigation into the origins of COVID-19 and the federal government's response to the pandemic. Paul, who chairs the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, and his Republican colleagues have long accused Fauci of misleading Congress and the American people about the origins of the virus, federal funding for research at the Wuhan Institute of Virology in the Chinese city where the virus first emerged and the nature of so-called gain-of-function research, which alters pathogens to study how they may become more transmissible or dangerous.

"Here I am sitting in front of you six years later saying, who the f--k do you think you were for doing that?" Moreno said. "It is a total disgrace what you did to this country."

FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

A split image shows Bernie Moreno and Anthony Fauci. (Allison Robbert / AP)

Moreno's remarks came after he argued the government's COVID-19 guidance, including mask mandates, social distancing recommendations and school closures, harmed Americans. He said "moronic" politicians' implementation of Fauci's guidance led to arrests, recounting the story of an Ohio mother who was arrested for not wearing a mask during an outdoor high school football game.

"When that story broke, I said to myself, I cannot stand idly on the side and watch this happen," Moreno said. "It was about six years ago today that I decided I'm going to give up my businesses, sell them all, run for office, run for the United States Senate."

Moreno then asked Fauci whether he would apologize to the American people, prompting Fauci to invoke the Fifth Amendment. Throughout the hearing, Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment more than 100 times rather than answer lawmakers' questions.

RAND PAUL SEEKS CONTEMPT CHARGES AFTER FAUCI INVOKES FIFTH AMENDMENT MORE THAN 100 TIMES

Fauci served as chief medical adviser to President Donald Trump during the COVID-19 pandemic before later continuing in the role under President Joe Biden. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

At the beginning of his allotted time, Moreno called on audience members to stand if they had questioned the government's COVID-19 guidelines and were made to feel "like less than a human being" or suffered consequences for failing to comply, such as being fired from their jobs or refusing the vaccine. Moreno's request prompted audience members sitting behind Fauci to stand. Moreno asked Fauci to turn around and face them, but he refused.

Moreno accused Fauci of being more interested in rubbing elbows with celebrities such as Kim Kardashian, referring to a Zoom call Fauci participated in with her and more than a dozen other celebrities, than serving as a public health official.

Moreno's fiery exchange with Fauci quickly drew praise from conservative commentators and Trump administration officials on social media.

"Fauci should go to jail. Full stop," Fox News contributor Joe Concha wrote on X.

White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung praised Moreno's line of questioning.

"Senator @BernieMoreno throwing a high-heat fastball!"

Former NIH Director Anthony Fauci testifies before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in Washington, D.C., on July 29, 2026. Fauci was expected to be questioned about his diary entries during his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. (Getty Images)

Jace Yarbrough, a Republican congressional candidate in Texas' 32nd District and an Air Force veteran, thanked Moreno for confronting Fauci and described what he said was pressure placed on service members who declined the COVID-19 vaccine.

"I am one of the service members who refused the COVID shot," Yarbrough wrote on X. "Many were removed from service, lost their livelihoods, or received career-ending reprimands simply for declining the shot."

"Thank you @berniemoreno for taking this man to task and standing up for those who were targeted by his regime."

Philip Letsou, Moreno's chief of staff, also reacted to the exchange, writing on X, "Never seen a moment quite like this in Congress."

"We have no comment on anything Senator Moreno had to say other than he is completely wrong," David Schertler, Fauci's attorney, said in an email to Fox News Digital.

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

articles.title: Paul Finebaum eviscerates Illinois' Bret Bielema after his claim that the SEC is stuck living in the past
articles.excerpt:
Dan Dakich reacts to Greg Sankey saying the SEC is exploring options outside of the NCAA.

ESPN's Paul Finebaum has offered a rebuttal to Bret Bielema and the Illinois head coach's nonchalant yet note...
articles.body_text:
Dan Dakich reacts to Greg Sankey saying the SEC is exploring options outside of the NCAA.

ESPN's Paul Finebaum has offered a rebuttal to Bret Bielema and the Illinois head coach's nonchalant yet noteworthy comments about the SEC wanting to live in the past. Finebaum brought out the receipts, too, which don't exactly put Bielema in the best light.

While speaking at Big Ten media days on Tuesday, Bielema elected to take a not-so-subtle shot at the Southeastern Conference.

"[SEC commissioner] (Greg) Sankey, I know he's gotta protect the SEC, and they kinda wanna live in 2005 forever," Bielema said while at the podium. "But, I think the forward thinking of where we are in college football is an awesome thing."

Head coach Bret Bielema of the Illinois Fighting Illini speaks to the media during the 2026 Big Ten Football Media Days at Hilton Chicago on July 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) (Justin Casterline/Getty Images)

ILLINOIS COACH BRET BIELEMA FIRES BACK AT NOTRE DAME AD OVER RECENT REMARKS: 'JUST JOIN A CONFERENCE'

There is absolutely no valid argument to be had against the fact that the Big Ten sits on the throne of college football at the moment with programs from the conference winning three straight national championships. Sure, the SEC won the four before the Big Ten built its recent run, but in today's reality, the Big Ten reigns supreme.

That, however, isn't what Bielema said, he elected to take a jab at the SEC as a whole, which includes some of the most rabid fan bases in all of sports, for being stuck looking into the rearview mirror.

Head coach Bret Bielema of the Illinois Fighting Illini speaks to the media during the 2026 Big Ten Football Media Days at Hilton Chicago on July 28, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) (Justin Casterline/Getty Images)

The exact comments from Bielema are rather rich given the fact that he has a history of coaching in the SEC, which Finebaum was quick to remind people of in his response to the head coach.

"He never fails to be the village idiot at Big Ten Media Days," Finebaum said during ESPN's 'Get Up' on Wednesday. "I have no earthly idea where that came from, why he said it. First of all, 2005, since that moment in time, the SEC has only won 13 national championships.

"Let’s go back to Bret Bielema in the SEC at Arkansas. He didn’t make it. His last year, he was 1-8 in the SEC. His overall record in the SEC is 11-29. He was a complete and total disaster. But he always shows up there and gives us something to laugh about, but mostly to laugh at him."

ARKANSAS ATHLETIC DIRECTOR HUNTER YURACHEK DEMANDS SEC CHANGE GAME TIMES FOR RAZORBACKS' FOOTBALL TEAM

ESPN/SEC Network Analyst Paul Finebaum is on set prior to the college football Playoff Semifinal game at the Chick-fil-a Peach Bowl between the Georgia Bulldogs and the Ohio State Buckeyes on Dec. 31, 2022 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, Georgia. (Michael Wade/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Finebaum did make an error during his rebuttal.

Bielema wasn't 1-8 in the SEC during his final season with the Razorbacks. He was actually 1-7, for whatever that is worth. His final campaign with the Hogs at 4-8 in 2017 did come on the heels of three straight winning seasons, but Bielema never came close to meeting expectations in Fayetteville during his five-year tenure, winning just 11 conference games.

articles.title: Two people accuse Epstein of sexual conduct at Michigan fine arts school
articles.excerpt:
Report on Interlochen Center for the Arts details sexual allegations against 47 faculty and staff members since 1950s

Two people who attended a prestigious Michigan fine arts school reported conduct ...
articles.body_text:
Report on Interlochen Center for the Arts details sexual allegations against 47 faculty and staff members since 1950s

Two people who attended a prestigious Michigan fine arts school reported conduct of a sexual nature by Jeffrey Epstein, a major donor, according to an investigation that also uncovered dozens of allegations spanning decades against nearly 50 other people.

Interlochen Center for the Arts operates a summer camp and performing arts school that draws students from around the world. It hired a law firm in 2024 to investigate reports of sexual abuse by faculty and staff. Subsequently, it expanded the work to include information about Epstein, the 66-year-old financier who killed himself in jail in 2019.

Interlochen removed Epstein’s name from a lodge after he was convicted of sex offenses in Florida in 2008. The building, renamed the Green Lake Lodge, was recently demolished after the US justice department released millions of pages about him that had been compiled over the years.

Sanghavi law office says it collected 70 accounts from alumni alleging “physical conduct of a sexual nature” by 47 faculty and staff members affiliated with Interlochen from the 1950s through the 2010s, most before 2000.

“The information gathered during this investigation is, simply, devastating,” the 97-page report says, noting that alumni reported grooming, flirting, sexual touching and sex.

Interlochen said it has provided names of people accused of misconduct to Grand Traverse county authorities in northern Michigan to determine what steps, if any, might be taken. None are currently employed there and more than a third are dead.

“We are deeply sorry for the harm experienced by members of our community and extend our apologies to those impacted by abuse at Interlochen,” president Trey Davey and board chair Barrett Rollins said in a letter to the community posted online.

“While the vast majority of the incidents described in the investigation took place many decades ago, and reports of abuse at Interlochen have significantly decreased over the past 25 years, the passage of time does not diminish the experiences of our alumni,” they said. “Sexual abuse committed by an adult in a position of power or trust against a student is wrong, then and now.”

Interlochen today “is fundamentally different from the institution described in this report”, Davey and Rollins wrote, with comprehensive safety policies and a changed culture.

Epstein, who played the bassoon, was an Interlochen camper in 1967. He donated more than $400,000 to the school between 1990 and 2003.

Two women told investigators that Epstein engaged in conduct of a sexual nature with them, one of them at the Interlochen lodge that bore his name.

He brushed against her body “over her clothes, in a manner in which he indicated was accidental”, according to the report.

Epstein also paid for her to visit him in New York while she was a student. She said “every time he was ‘handsy’ with her, she would freeze until he would stop”, the report states.

The other woman said she gave Epstein a massage at his home, according to the report, and he may have asked her to remove her top. She never had any further contact with Epstein or his girlfriend, Ghislaine Maxwell.

Outside of the school investigation, at least two Interlochen alumnae made allegations of grooming and abuse against Epstein and Maxwell, according to federal records and media reports. Their identities were not made public.

One testified against Maxwell in 2021 when she was convicted of sex trafficking. It is unclear whether those women spoke to the law firm hired for the Interlochen investigation.

articles.title: Giants outfielder suffers late-night scooter accident while already dealing with foot injury, team says
articles.excerpt:
San Francisco Giants outfielder Harrison Bader was involved in a bizarre accident while already dealing with plantar fasciitis. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)

Harrison Bader's season has ...
articles.body_text:
San Francisco Giants outfielder Harrison Bader was involved in a bizarre accident while already dealing with plantar fasciitis. (This video contains AI-assisted content.)

Harrison Bader's season has gone from bad to worse.

The San Francisco Giants outfielder has been limited to just 30 games due to injury, and when he's been on the field, it has not been pleasant.

Bader is hitting just .170 with a .198 on-base percentage and .358 slugging percentage, as he's dealt with plantar fasciitis for the second time in his MLB career.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

San Francisco Giants outfielder Harrison Bader heads to the dugout after hitting a grand slam against the Chicago White Sox on May 23, 2026, at Oracle Park in San Francisco. (Larry Placido/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

But this week, the Giants announced that Bader had a "scooter accident" on "Saturday night/early Sunday morning," which further injured his foot.

Bader is now set to get an MRI for the new injury.

Bizarrely enough, this is not the first time Bader has gotten into trouble with a scooter. While playing for the University of Florida in 2014, he was suspended for 19 games for drunkenly crashing a scooter into a parked truck.

Harrison Bader of the San Francisco Giants is on deck during an MLB game at Chase Field in Phoenix, Arizona, on May 19, 2026. The Diamondbacks defeated the Giants 5-3. (Christian Petersen/Getty Images)

MLB PROSPECT PROVIDES POSITIVE UPDATES AFTER FRACTURING VERTABRAE IN SCARY OUTFIELD COLLISION

Bader is in the first year of a two-year pact with the Giants, which is worth north of $20 million. The Giants are his seventh team.

The 2021 Gold Glove Award winner spent nearly six full seasons with the St. Louis Cardinals before being traded to the New York Yankees in 2022. He then had a brief stint with the Cincinnati Reds before spending time with the New York Mets, Minnesota Twins and Philadelphia Phillies.

Harrison Bader #9 of the San Francisco Giants prepares for a game against the Arizona Diamondbacks at Oracle Park in San Francisco on May 25, 2026. (Andy Kuno/San Francisco Giants/Getty Images)

The Giants, meanwhile, are tied for the second-worst record in the National League and figure to trade just about anyone they can ahead of next week's deadline.
